articles.title: Singapore, Indonesia Ready to Address Bilateral Issues Including Haze, Minister Says
articles.full_text:
For several weeks tension between the two neighbors has been growing over a range of issues including transboundary haze and energy supplies.
Singaporean Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan and Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir speak to the press after a meeting in Jakarta, Indonesia, Oct. 27, 2026.
Singapore and Indonesia are prepared to do what is necessary to manage their differences over transboundary haze, energy supplies, and other bilateral issues, Singaporean Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said yesterday.
Speaking with the press in Jakarta after a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto at his home in Bogor, West Java, the Singaporean envoy said that “communication has occurred at the highest level” between Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Prabowo in recent weeks, according to the official transcript of his comments.
“It sets the political commitment on both sides to do what is necessary, and now we’ll have to implement those plans, execute that commitment,” Balakrishnan said. He did not give further details on what he discussed with Prabowo.
The two neighbors have experienced growing friction over the past several weeks over a range of bilateral issues. Among the most pressing are the haze caused by raging forest and peatland fires in Indonesia, which have pushed air pollution levels in Singapore to hazardous levels. Singaporeans have become increasingly frustrated by the apparent inaction of the Indonesian authorities to respond to, and prevent, the fires, which are an annual occurrence.
There have also been tensions related to the recent threat of global index provider MSCI to downgrade Indonesia to “Standalone Market” status due to a lack of transparency in its stock market – in particular, comments by a former minister that Singaporean state investment firms had pressured MSCI to downgrade the country. Finally, earlier this week, Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore in order to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs, to the chagrin of the Singaporean government.
All of these issues have prompted tense words from leaders in both countries. On October 15, as Singapore choked under some of its worst air pollution in more than a decade, Prime Minister Wong said that the government was looking into Indonesian companies that could be responsible for the fires in Indonesia, and potentially take action against them under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on October 19 that Singapore will “sustain pressure” on these companies even after the haze passes.
Similarly, on the question of the gas export cut, Wong said on Sunday that Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honor their commitments.” He added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the steps needed to protect its rights and interests. The Indonesian government claims that the 9 percent reduction was within contractual limits, but Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia did not help matters when he suggested that Jakarta might cut off energy supplies to nations that did not respect Indonesia – a possible reference to Singapore’s statements about the haze issue.
Balakrishnan’s three-day visit, which concludes today, is aimed at preventing these diplomatic spot fires from developing into a more serious bilateral conflagration. On Tuesday, he met with Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir, after which the two sides announced a joint task force to coordinate investigations into companies responsible for setting the fires, which have taken place across Borneo and Sumatra.
After the meeting, Arrmanatha told the press that addressing the haze issue was a “top national priority” for Prabowo, adding that “no border should shield those who profit from burning our forests.”
Speaking yesterday, Balakrishnan said that he was not in a position to provide details about the composition and staffing of the task force, but said that it would “deal with this issue, exchange information, to facilitate each authority’s work in our respective jurisdictions.” He added that “given the commitment at the senior level for both countries, we will get this done quickly, promptly, and effectively.”
Singapore and Indonesia also announced a new hotline to handle bilateral differences.
Arrmanatha told the press that the Indonesia-Singapore relationship is “mature enough” that leaders could speak candidly with one another. “What matters is not what we differ, but how we resolve our differences constructively, respectfully, and openly,” he said. Balakrishnan described the talks with Indonesia’s new foreign minister as “very fruitful and sincere.”

articles.title: Hegseth Seeks to Reassure Southeast Asia of US Security Commitment to the Region
articles.full_text:
Speaking at the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting in Cebu, the U.S. secretary of war pledged to “defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners.”
U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks during the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Informal Meeting in Cebu, Philippines, Oct. 28, 2026.
U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth yesterday sought to reassure Southeast Asian counterparts on Wednesday of Washington’s commitment to the region, pledging that the superpower would “let our actions speak for themselves.”
Hegseth made the comments in an address to the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) in Cebu, Philippines, where he once again outlined President Donald Trump’s vision of a “more stable, secure, and prosperous Pacific.”
“The approach we’re taking we described as strong, quiet, and clear – strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics,” he said, according to the official transcript of his remarks.
In line with this approach, the U.S. would “let our actions speak for themselves, but clear enough that our friends, our partners, and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners.”
To support that, Hegseth said that the U.S. would back that commitment with practical cooperation, such as “strengthening maritime domain awareness, improving interoperability, and advancing cooperation among our navies.”
“These are not symbolic things. They are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do,” he added. “Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together and build confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict.”
Hegseth’s promise of “pragmatism, openness to dialogue, respect for counterparts, and proud nationalism,” a reiteration of the realist theme of his address to the Shangri-La Dialogue in May, in principle aligns well with ASEAN’s own modus operandi. But just how reassuring this would have been to Southeast Asian interlocutors attempting to deal with the volatility and caprice of the second Trump administration remains unclear.
Most Southeast Asian nations, and particularly those with outstanding maritime disputes with China, would likely welcome sustained or enhanced U.S. security cooperation. This is especially important for the Philippines, which has the distinction of being both a U.S. treaty ally and a South China Sea claimant state that disputes China’s maximalist claims to the vital waterway. The past few years have seen growing tensions between Beijing and Manila in contested parts of the South China Sea, where the two sides have engaged in a string of dangerous confrontations.
In his own remarks to the ADMM, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. said that ASEAN values the United States’ “sustained engagement” with the region’s defense establishments, pointing out that “a robust U.S. presence is necessary for peace and stability in Southeast Asia and in the broader Indo-Pacific region.”
Even then, the erratic nature of current U.S. foreign policy would likely be a source of consternation in most, if not all, ASEAN capitals. Southeast Asia has been hit hard by the effects of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran earlier this year, which exposed the heavy dependence of most nations on imported oil and refined fuels from the Gulf. The Trump administration’s erratic tariff policy – Southeast Asian nations were among the heaviest hit by Trump’s initial “liberation day” tariff announcement – has also impacted the region’s economies, and prompted some nations to begin diversifying their trade partnerships. On top of this, the U.S.’ staunch support for Israel, and its role in the Israeli assaults on Gaza, remains a subject of concern in Muslim-majority Southeast Asia.
Even in terms of security cooperation and military deployments, a traditional area of strength, the U.S. walks a fine line between supporting deterrence by bolstering Southeast Asian defense capacity and actions that ratchet up tensions with China. While the Trump administration has dialed down tensions with Beijing, its highly disruptive war on Iran, the accompanying rhetoric of which has hardly eschewed “needless escalation or public theatrics,” naturally raises the question of whether this U.S. administration, or a future Trump-ite administration, could bluster its way into some sort of conflict with China.
Greg Poling, director of the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C., told Reuters that Hegseth would get an opportunity to discuss the above issues with ASEAN counterparts, although he expected that concrete cooperation would be concentrated among “like-minded” countries.

articles.title: The Impact of the Philippine Supreme Court’s Recent Landmark Rulings
articles.full_text:
Two important rulings on political dynasties and the budget system could have significant implications for the Marcos administration.
The Supreme Court building in Manila, Philippines.
The Philippine Supreme Court issued two major decisions over the past two months that could affect not just the work of Congress but also the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and the candidates who may run in the 2028 national and local elections.
In September, the Court ruled that Congress is mandated by the 1987 Constitution to pass a bill prohibiting political dynasties. This month, the Court nullified some aspects of the previous national budget because the item on unprogrammed appropriations increased the president’s spending program.
A few powerful clans have long dominated Philippine politics, which has entrenched inequality and elite rule. After the fall of the Marcos dictatorship in 1986, framers of the new Constitution wanted to democratize political participation by banning political dynasties. But in the end, they left it to Congress to define what a political dynasty is and pass a law prohibiting them. This ultimately doomed the Constitutional intent to ban dynasties because the few families that dominated both houses of Congress would not legislate against their own interests.
Responding to the petition against the failure and refusal of Congress to pass a law banning political dynasties over the past 39 years, the Court unanimously ruled that this was a “grave abuse of discretion. It reminded legislators that the provision against dynasties “is not merely an aspiration but a constitutional command.” The Court acknowledged that it cannot compel a co-equal branch of government “to perform a discretionary act,” but it noted that the case is “highly exceptional” because of the grave abuse of discretion and “manifest injustice.”
There are pending bills on the abolition of dynasties, and even President Marcos has signaled his support for the measure. However, critics pointed out that the House version endorsed by the president’s son would merely regulate dynasties, and if passed into law, families like the Marcoses and the Dutertes can still field multiple candidates in several elective posts at the same time.
The release of the Court ruling was therefore timely since it can be used as a reference for legislators in finalizing the bill to end dynasties once and for all and allow a new breed of leaders a greater chance to serve in government.
Another landmark decision of the Court released this month was about the unprogrammed appropriations in the previous national budget. The Court ruled that these were unconstitutional because of Congress’s increase of the Special Road Fund, which resulted in an increase in the president’s total recommended appropriations. It added that there should be no lump sums in unprogrammed appropriations and that this budgetary item “needs clear limits and safeguards to preserve fiscal discipline, transparency, and accountability.”
Simply put, the Court reiterated its earlier ruling against the pork barrel system. Lump sum funds inserted by Congress or budget items that expanded the discretionary spending of the president are “constitutionally infirm” since they can be turned into a corruption-prone pork barrel distribution program.
Again, the Court ruling was timely, since the Senate will tackle the House-approved 2028 budget bill next month. It could become a point of contention between the two chambers, especially since most House members are reliant on pork barrel funds to boost their electoral chances. Meanwhile, the Marcos government has asked the Court for a partial reconsideration and clarification on some matters of the ruling pertaining to funds that have already been spent.
The budget ruling could revive the clamor for accountability since it validated the assertion of progressive lawmakers and anti-corruption watchdogs that the Marcos government has drafted a budget that institutionalized and expanded suspicious items in the unprogrammed appropriations.
Even Vice President Sara Duterte cited the Court decision to castigate Marcos for his role in enabling the rampant corruption in the bureaucracy. Duterte has no credibility to speak on this issue since she herself is embroiled in a corruption scandal, but her statement highlights how the ruling can spur the demand to hold the Marcos administration accountable for budget-related controversies.
The two Supreme Court rulings pose a challenge to the work of Congress, whose sessions will resume next month. The Senate can initially rework the budget bill before the review of the Bicameral Committee. But in the end, it is not just Congress that will be put in the spotlight but President Marcos, who has to persuade the public that he acted in good faith when he signed and implemented a budget law that contains unconstitutional provisions.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Artificial Intelligence Warfare
articles.full_text:
Faced with multipronged challenges, the country has gradually incorporated AI into its security strategy.
For the first time in its volatile history, Pakistan topped the Global Terrorism Index this year, recording 1,045 terror incidents and 1,139 related deaths in 2025. The fatalities have risen further in 2026, with the third quarter of the ongoing year showing an 83 percent hike in terrorism-linked deaths as compared to the second quarter. 
This surge comes amid external security woes. Last year, Pakistan and India came the closest that they have to a full-fledged war since the turn of the century, and reportedly to the brink of nuclear war. Pakistan is also engaged in persistent cross-border clashes with Afghanistan. Meanwhile, the ongoing Iran-U.S. war is reconfiguring militancy in Balochistan, after Islamabad and Tehran exchanged drone and missile strikes on each other’s territories in 2024. 
Faced with these multipronged challenges, Pakistan has gradually incorporated artificial intelligence (AI) into its security strategy.
Last year, Pakistan unveiled its National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2025 to regulate AI usage. Pakistan’s military forces have already deployed AI to enhance their capabilities through research units, such as the Army Center of Emerging Technologies and the Pakistan Air Force-run Center for Artificial Intelligence and Computing (CENTAIC). 
Pakistan has also unveiled a gamut of AI-enabled military weapons, including equipment manufactured by the state-owned Global Industrial & Defense Solutions (GIDS). These include unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs), such as Shahpar-II, and the Spider Anti-UAV system. Pakistan and India used numerous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in the 2025 clashes, with Islamabad deploying YIHA-III drones manufactured by the Turkish defense contractor Baykar in addition to Shahpar-II. 
Drones are being extensively used along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border according to Pakistan Army sources. “We are facing the double threat – from the Afghan Taliban, and local terrorist groups – and we are countering these by using drones for surveilling and also for striking targets, especially in remote areas,” an official working with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s newly formed Police UAV Division told The Diplomat.
Military sources reveal that Pakistan is also close to deploying robots. “Law enforcement authorities already have robots in bomb disposal units. Robots are also performing reconnaissance tasks, including in border areas. Now we are working on using robots to lead clearance operations, along with transporting ammunition and supplies in military operations in [Khyber] Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan,” said a senior officer.
The security agencies have already run drills with Chinese robotic wolves. There are plans to produce similar machines indigenously, as well as humanoid and bipedal robots.
“To keep pace with India, and to nullify terrorist groups, we are always integrating new technologies in military and law enforcement agencies. However, the biggest challenge is developing our capacity due to the lack of resources and the economic challenges,” Lieutenant General Talat Masood, a former secretary of Pakistan’s Ministry of Defense Production, told The Diplomat. In this regard, Pakistan continues to benefit from Chinese architectural support for CENTAIC. Beijing is also helping Islamabad use facial recognition technology, as Pakistani security agencies gradually expand its deployment to sensitive areas, including border checkpoints and terror hotspots.
Along with fortifying security capacities, however, the Pakistani state is also using these AI-powered technologies to maintain the military establishment’s stranglehold and quell any regional or political dissent. The Diplomat has learned that the military’s media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), is allocating resources for “narrative building.” In addition to producing various forms of media, the ISPR also employs tech professionals to engage in countering what the establishment deems to be “anti-state propaganda,” a misnomer for critiques of the armed forces, the country’s military leadership, and their policies. 
“A good chunk of money is going into algorithmic filtering and monitoring, and tools are being used to erase social media anonymity and target individuals accordingly. Many professionals in the IT sector and the media industry are working on these projects,” revealed a senior digital media professional working at one of Pakistan’s largest media houses. 
The investment to “counter anti-state propaganda” has significantly increased following the ouster of former premier Imran Khan in 2022. The ensuing anti-army sentiment has meant that Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, and its activists, have especially been under the gun. However, the same digital tools are being wielded to suppress dissidents in Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. 
Similarly, Pakistani citizens are vulnerable to Islamist persecution, with digital blasphemy laws still providing allowance for the use of modern technology to fatally impose antediluvian punishments. This is in stark contrast with the image of moderation and reform that the Pakistani governments wants to show in front of the global audiences, especially as part of its recent role as the mediator between the U.S. and Iran.
A lack of transparency allows the state and the military establishment to deploy technology and AI beyond the realms of the already loosely defined “national security.” The National Security Policy 2022-2026 “has no mention of Artificial Intelligence,” said security analyst Abdullah Khan, the managing director of the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. “How can we deliberate over its pros and cons, when there is no official declaration of how these technologies are being used?” 
Lieutenant General Talat Masood, the former Ministry of Defense Production secretary, said that transparency can only be ensured, and any overreach into the domain into fundamental rights can only be nullified, by having credible checks on the abuse of power. “The command needs to be held by a representative civilian government, which would require a revamp of the state’s power structure, so that the military and civilian can keep charge of their respective domains,” he said.
Those who defend the state’s position argue that compromising on certain freedoms is part and parcel of counterterror policymaking, especially when the situation is as grave as the one Pakistan faces today. But critics maintain that any compromises need to be justified with successful outcomes of technology and AI incorporation. So far, that hasn’t happened.
“All terror trends have increased over the past five years. There are hardly any counterterror successes for us to gauge,” said Khan of the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies. “[The state] is currently in the responsive mode, whereas militants are in the offensive mode” when it comes to using technology.
“We need to change that, and enhance our own capacities beyond intelligence gathering and monitoring. When it comes to actual incorporation of technology in counterterror operations, we are still at the infancy stage,” he added.
As technology impacts the state’s role as a guarantor of its citizens’ security and freedom, it is evident that Pakistan is struggling on both fronts. And it is likely to stay that way, as long as the omnipotent military establishment continues to arbitrarily impose its whims.
For the first time in its volatile history, Pakistan topped the Global Terrorism Index this year, recording 1,045 terror incidents and 1,139 related deaths in 2025. The fatalities have risen further in 2026, with the third quarter of the ongoing year showing an 83 percent hike in terrorism-linked deaths as compared to the second quarter. 
This surge comes amid external security woes. Last year, Pakistan and India came the closest that they have to a full-fledged war since the turn of the century, and reportedly to the brink of nuclear war. Pakistan is also engaged in persistent cross-border clashes with Afghanistan. Meanwhile, the ongoing Iran-U.S. war is reconfiguring militancy in Balochistan, after Islamabad and Tehran exchanged drone and missile strikes on each other’s territories in 2024. 
Faced with these multipronged challenges, Pakistan has gradually incorporated artificial intelligence (AI) into its security strategy.
Last year, Pakistan unveiled its National Artificial Intelligence Policy 2025 to regulate AI usage. Pakistan’s military forces have already deployed AI to enhance their capabilities through research units, such as the Army Center of Emerging Technologies and the Pakistan Air Force-run Center for Artificial Intelligence and Computing (CENTAIC). 
Pakistan has also unveiled a gamut of AI-enabled military weapons, including equipment manufactured by the state-owned Global Industrial & Defense Solutions (GIDS). These include unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs), such as Shahpar-II, and the Spider Anti-UAV system. Pakistan and India used numerous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in the 2025 clashes, with Islamabad deploying YIHA-III drones manufactured by the Turkish defense contractor Baykar in addition to Shahpar-II. 
Drones are being extensively used along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border according to Pakistan Army sources. “We are facing the double threat – from the Afghan Taliban, and local terrorist groups – and we are countering these by using drones for surveilling and also for striking targets, especially in remote areas,” an official working with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s newly formed Police UAV Division told The Diplomat.
Military sources reveal that Pakistan is also close to deploying robots. “Law enforcement authorities already have robots in bomb disposal units. Robots are also performing reconnaissance tasks, including in border areas. Now we are working on using robots to lead clearance operations, along with transporting ammunition and supplies in military operations in [Khyber] Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan,” said a senior officer.
The security agencies have already run drills with Chinese robotic wolves. There are plans to produce similar machines indigenously, as well as humanoid and bipedal robots.
“To keep pace with India, and to nullify terrorist groups, we are always integrating new technologies in military and law enforcement agencies. However, the biggest challenge is developing our capacity due to the lack of resources and the economic challenges,” Lieutenant General Talat Masood, a former secretary of Pakistan’s Ministry of Defense Production, told The Diplomat. In this regard, Pakistan continues to benefit from Chinese architectural support for CENTAIC. Beijing is also helping Islamabad use facial recognition technology, as Pakistani security agencies gradually expand its deployment to sensitive areas, including border checkpoints and terror hotspots.
Along with fortifying security capacities, however, the Pakistani state is also using these AI-powered technologies to maintain the military establishment’s stranglehold and quell any regional or political dissent. The Diplomat has learned that the military’s media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), is allocating resources for “narrative building.” In addition to producing various forms of media, the ISPR also employs tech professionals to engage in countering what the establishment deems to be “anti-state propaganda,” a misnomer for critiques of the armed forces, the country’s military leadership, and their policies.
articles.summary: Faced with multipronged challenges, the country has gradually incorporated AI into its security strategy.

articles.title: Lula’s Election Win in Brazil Is a Relief for China
articles.full_text:
Lula’s victory secures the most important destination for Chinese foreign direct investment in the Western Hemisphere and ends a winning streak for Trump-supported candidates.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a signing ceremony at the Great Hall of the People, Beijing, May 13, 2025.
On October 4, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva finished the first round of Brazil’s presidential election behind his main rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro and an open ally of U.S. President Donald Trump. Flavio Bolsonaro had taken 47 percent of valid votes against Lula’s 45 percent. Because no one topped 50 percent of votes, however, the race went to a second-round runoff.
The first post-election poll gave Bolsonaro a six-point lead in the head-to-head contest. Three weeks later, Lula won with 51.76 percent, a margin of roughly 4.3 million ballots, securing an unprecedented fourth term. His victory came after intense popular demonstrations in leading cities such as Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Belo Horizonte, as well as a new social media strategy boosted by political allies.  
Lula’s comeback matters well beyond Brasília. Since late 2025, Latin America has seen a regional shift toward right-wing regimes. Bolivia, Chile, Honduras, Costa Rica, Colombia, and Peru all elected conservative governments, most of them endorsed by Washington. 
Brazil was meant to be the crowning piece of Trump’s foreign policy, seeing as it is the largest market in the region and one of the only ones who did not agree on Trump’s Shield for the Americas initiative. Instead, Brazil has opted for a pragmatic foreign economic policy, trying to negotiate with both China and the United States.   
Washington’s strategy has been referred to as the “Donroe Doctrine,” claiming the United States’ right to assert its interests in the region in security terms. In practice that has meant rewarding ideological allies and treating Chinese influence as a central opposing force. 
A series of electoral victories seemed to confirm the effectiveness of Trump’s approach to the region. Rodrigo Paz ended two decades of Movimiento al Socialismo (MAS) rule in Bolivia in October 2025. José Antonio Kast won Chile in December. Nasry Asfura took office in Honduras after Trump threatened to cut aid if he lost. In June 2026, Colombia elected the Trump-endorsed outsider Abelardo de la Espriella, and Keiko Fujimori finally won Peru on her fourth attempt. Moreover, Argentina’s right-wing President Javier Milei continues to be an ally. 
Tensions between Brazil and the United States have been accumulating in Trump’s second term. In July 2025, the U.S. president imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on Brazilian goods over the prosecution and later incarceration of Jair Bolsonaro and sanctioned the Supreme Court judge overseeing the case. 
On May 26, 2026, Trump received Flavio in the Oval Office, and on June 2, a day after his administration proposed a fresh 25 percent tariff on Brazilian goods, Trump praised him publicly. Flavio asked Washington to postpone the tariffs until after the voting period, but it was too late: a Datafolha poll found that 52 percent of Brazilians saw the tariffs as an effort to help his campaign, but ultimately hurting the Brazilian economy. 
Until 2030, Brazil and Mexico, the two largest economies in Latin America, will be governed by center-left leaders, both of whom refuse to pick a clear side between Washington and Beijing. For a doctrine premised on sorting the hemisphere into aligned and unaligned camps, this is a strategic setback for Trump, precisely at a moment where the leader faces low approval rates at home. 
Beijing’s Geoeconomic Influence in the Region Is Growing
For China, Brazil is now a strategic partner. In 2025 it was the single largest destination for Chinese outbound investment worldwide, absorbing 10.9 percent of the total, according to the China-Brazil Business Council (CEBC). Chinese investment in China reached $6.1 billion, up 45 percent, far outpacing both Brazil’s overall foreign direct investment (FDI) growth of 4.8 percent and China’s global outbound growth of 1.3 percent. 
Overall Brazil accounts for almost two thirds of China’s FDI in South America, with a total stock of $85.5 billion, distributed across 355 projects, between 2007-2025.
China continues to invest heavily in Brazil’s electricity sector, spanning renewable generation and transmission. Automotive investment rose 66 percent to $965 million as BYD began production at the former Ford complex in Camaçari, Bahia (Northeastern Brazil), and Great Wall Motors at the former Mercedes-Benz plant in Iracemápolis, São Paulo. Geely has sealed an alliance with Renault do Brasil and plans local production in Paraná (Southern Brazil) this year. 
Beyond investment, bilateral trade hit a record $171 billion in 2025. China bought nearly 80 percent of Brazil’s soybean exports. These ties survived even Jair Bolsonaro’s hostile rhetoric. But a Flavio government that owed its political capital to Washington would have faced intense pressure to slow Chinese investment, and it would have inherited brand-new legal tools to do so (more on this below). 
After his loss, Flavio Bolsonaro immediately fled Brazil, heading secretly to the United States via Argentina, amid fears of being convicted of ties to money laundering schemes.  
Brazil and the Race for Technology and Critical Minerals
Lula signed Law 15.506/2026 on September 16, creating Brazil’s first National Policy on Critical and Strategic Minerals (PNMCE) and a council, the CIMCE, attached to the presidency. The stakes for investors are considerable: Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves and leads global niobium production, with newly found lithium and nickel reserves. 
China still controls roughly 90 percent of rare earth processing and magnet manufacturing and the United States was seeking to secure privileged access to exploration of this sector in the Brazilian market. 
The new law has two main aspects: promotion and regulation. The first key is promotion in an industrial policy style. Brazil’s government will provide up to 7 billion Brazilian real in support for firms aiming to raise production and processing of critical minerals, as well as tax credits of up to 1 billion real a year between 2030 and 2034, tied to value-adding and processing on Brazilian soil. 
The second aspect is regulation. The newly formed council, led by the president, must approve direct or indirect changes of control in companies holding rights to critical minerals, as well as international supply agreements that could affect Brazil’s economic or geopolitical security.
On paper, this created a screening mechanism that can be used as a hurdle for Chinese state capital, depending on the elected administration. A senior official at the Ministry of Mines and Energy said in October that scrutiny would concentrate on business groups or financing backed by foreign governments, while purely domestic deals may be exempt. 
Today, the most visible foreign investors in Brazilian rare earths are American. In April 2026, USA Rare Earth acquired the Serra Verde Mining Complex, Brazil’s only commercial producer of rare earths, for $2.8 billion, in a deal backed by the U.S. government, including $565 million in direct funding from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation. 
Meanwhile, between 2024-2025 three Chinese state-owned enterprises invested more than $1.2 billion in acquisitions of copper, nickel, niobium and lithium mines in Brazil. BYD has held lithium rights in Minas Gerais region since 2023.
Under Lula, the CIMCE is likely to wield screening as an industrial policy filter, asking how much value stays in Brazil. The new law rewards precisely what Chinese firms can offer and Washington struggles to: refining know-how, battery materials capacity, and captive demand from EV plants already operating in Brazil. Under a Flavio government, however, the same powers could easily have been aligned with Washington’s geoeconomic de-risking agenda. 
Beijing’s position in Latin America rests less on ideological affinity than on economic gravity. Even the leaders that are sympathetic to U.S. regional influence, from Kast in Chile to Fujimori in Peru, still count China as their largest trading partner, and the Chinese-built port of Chancay now anchors Peru’s Pacific trade, for example. Brazil, on the other hand, remains a non-aligned political actor and a market where Chinese firms already have an established presence in EVs and energy. 
The new critical minerals law suggests that there will be ample competition in the future, as long as investors can also earn their place by processing locally, even as the dispute for geoeconomic influence in the region continues to grow in different sectors and areas.

His victory came after intense popular demonstrations in leading cities such as Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Belo Horizonte, as well as a new social media strategy boosted by political allies.

articles.title: Tokayev Proposes Dipping Into National Fund to Turn Kazakhstan into a ‘Big Construction Site’
articles.full_text:
In his annual state of the nation address, Tokayev laid out an ambitious spending spree focused on infrastructure and investment.
“Kazakhstan must turn into one big construction site,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proclaimed in his October 28 national address, proposing that the government dip into the National Fund, to the tune of 6.5 trillion tenge (approximately $14.4 billion at the current exchange rate) to fund projects through 2029. 
That represents more than 21 percent of the National Fund, a sovereign wealth fund created in 2000 and supplied by tax revenues from oil and gas companies. RFE/RL reported that the fund currently holds around $66.7 billion. Tokayev’s new ambition scraps a previous goal, stated in 2022 in the wake of the Qandy Qantar events as part of his “Fair Kazakhstan” pitch, to increase the National Fund’s assets to $100 billion by 2030.
From 2026 through the first two months of 2027, Tokayev said in his recent speech, 1.5 trillion tenge ($3.3 billion) would be allocated for social projects.
“I am confident that no one will object if we call this initiative a ‘People’s Construction Project,’” Tokayev said. In his subsequent remarks, he wandered through a smorgasbord of initiatives, mentioning a handful of specific efforts already underway, and spoke more generally about a huge range of ambitions. 
“Particular focus should be placed on developing logistics infrastructure,” he said. Here Tokayev spoke at length about the importance of logistics – from roads to rail to air transport – in furthering Kazakhstan’s development. 
Tokayev mentioned the Bakhty-Ayagoz rail line, which runs from Ayagoz in eastern Kazakhstan to the Chinese border and is expected to be completed by the end of 2027. He noted the start of construction in August of the the Aral-Caspian Highway, which “will shorten the route along the Trans-Caspian Corridor by approximately 1,000 kilometers, reducing cargo delivery time to three days.”
Tokayev took time to put special emphasis on the quality of roads – a perennial complaint in Kazakhstan – and criticize “executive bodies at the center and locally” who have treated the issue like a football.
“They kicked the issue around and did everything possible to drown the problem in an impassable swamp,” Tokayev, who has been president of Kazakhstan since 2019, said.
After discussing the importance of developing air corridors – “huge profits are literally flying past our country” – Tokayev shifted to energy. He stated the ambition for Kazakhstan to achieve a “sustainable energy surplus” by 2029, on the back of a full range of energy sources, from “clean coal” to renewables like solar. Nuclear power, he said, is of “fundamental importance,” praising as the “correct decision” the approval of a referendum on the topic in 2024. That referendum took place under heavy government pressure on critics of nuclear power. 
Closely related is the hot topic of critical minerals. On that, Tokayev cautioned that “new businesses should not create obstacles for existing businesses in the local area.” He specifically referenced Qarmet, which until 2023 was known as ArcelorMittal Temirtau. That year it was acquired by the the Qazaqstan Investment Corporation. Tokayev obliqued referenced similar production facilities to those operated by Qarmet as being planned in three other regions with the help of presumably foreign investors. “It is obvious that the benefits of such inappropriate decisions are questionable,” he said, without clarifying.
“It is obvious that the role of the government in this matter needs to be significantly strengthened.”
That may raise red flags for potential investors, as it suggests a heavy government hand in managing the pathways investments take. A 2025 report from the U.S. Department of State on Kazakhstan’s investment climate noted “significant progress,” but also pointed to ongoing restrictions on foreign ownership in certain sectors – notably “a 20 percent ceiling on foreign ownership of media outlets and a 49 percent limit on domestic and international air transportation services” – while also stating that “foreign companies sometimes experience difficulties with licensing, taxation, and legal disputes due to bureaucratic hurdles and inconsistent regulatory enforcement.”
Later in his speech, Tokayev pontificated on the necessity of attracting global and domestic companies, once again criticizing “individual departments and individuals” for taking “chaotic and uncoordinated” actions. “Therefore, investment policy management should be concentrated in a single center,” Tokayev said. Centralization has its benefits, but it also concentrates both wealth and risk. 
The speech went on to touch on subjects as varied as tax policy and education, ending with orders to reform the public administration system. “Civil servants must serve as models of competence,” Tokayev said. “Unfortunately, we are not seeing this yet.”

articles.title: The Evolution of Taiwan’s Military
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Eric Setzekorn – historian and author of “On the Brink: A Military History of Taiwan” (Naval Institute Press 2026) with over two dozen academic articles published in  Parameters, the Journal of American-East Asian Relations, and the Journal of Military and Strategic Studies – is the 532nd in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”  The views expressed in this publication are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the official policy or position of the Department of Defense or the U.S. government.
Identify the main milestones in the history of Taiwan’s military.
Since 1949, Taiwan’s military has undergone tremendous changes, but two pivotal moments are especially notable.
The 1958 Taiwan Strait Crisis demonstrated that a coherent and well-trained military in Taiwan was increasingly capable of a wide range of sophisticated operations. The poorly organized and equipped soldiers of 1949 would likely have been swept aside by PLA forces if there had been an invasion of Taiwan, but by the end of the 1950s Taiwan’s military had over a dozen well-trained divisions, hundreds of jet fighters, and professional officers. 
The enactment of a National Defense Act in 2002 was the culmination of a profound transformation during the 1990s from one-party KMT dominance into a non-partisan, civilian-led defense structure that reflected Taiwan’s democratic culture. The 2002 National Defense Act stipulated that the defense minister must be a civilian and required regular reports on military policies and combat readiness to the Legislative Yuan. The act also provided specific guidance regarding the political status of military personnel, noting, “The ROC Armed Forces shall remain neutral from individual, regional and party affiliations in accordance with the Act.” 
Explain how and why the institutional identity of Taiwan’s military moved away from a “party-army” conception.
After 1949, and well into the 1990s, Taiwan’s military was integrated into the KMT political party as a core element of the party’s authoritarian rule over Taiwan. During his nearly half-century as the leader of the KMT, Chiang Kai-shek kept close control over the military through stifling surveillance, required party membership for military officers, and incorporated KMT propaganda into military training. These political linkages meant that military roles often spilled over into numerous domestic functions, such as policing during the period of martial law from 1949 to 1987, often referred to as the White Terror. 
Beginning in the 1980s, and continuing into the 2000s, the military has become an apolitical institution that reflected the cultural sophistication and vibrant democracy of Taiwan. Despite this steady evolution, the legacies of Taiwan’s authoritarian past continue to influence the relationship between Taiwan’s military and society.
How did Taiwan’s military become more adaptable after the rise of Xi Jinping and China’s increasingly aggressive posture toward Taiwan?
Taiwan’s adaptation to the rise of Xi Jinping and increasing PLA aggressive behavior has taken two primary forms: increasing civil-military unity, and an operational shift in military planning.
Since 2020, there has been a significant increase in the negative attitudes of Taiwanese towards China, and this has led to increased public support for additional military spending and an extension of military service requirements. Public opinion polling conducted after the visit of U.S. Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi in August 2022, and subsequent Chinese exercises, revealed that 85 percent of respondents favored extending compulsory military service. Public concern is also reflected in steady increases to defense budget after 2016, with military spending more than tripling from 2016 to 2027. 
During Tsai Ing-wen’s first term (2016-2020), her administration promoted what became known as the Overall Defense Concept (ODC). The ODC emphasized what many Taiwanese and American defense analysts label “asymmetric warfare.” Supporters of the ODC argued that acquisitions should focus on fielding smaller, less expensive defense systems. For Taiwan’s Navy, for example, the ODC approach stressed fielding of smaller vessels, such as stealthy corvettes armed with short-range anti-ship missiles, and naval mines, rather than conventional surface ships such as frigates and destroyers. 
Describe two plausible scenarios for a potential Taiwan Strait conflict.
The massive expansion of the PLA Navy, with associated increases in air force and army capabilities, has enabled Chinese political leaders and PLA military planners to envision multiple scenarios for military action against Taiwan. 
A sudden Chinese attack on one of Taiwan’s outlying islands would force Taiwan’s military to respond in areas that would strain air and naval support. Taiping Island is 930 miles (1,500 km) from Taiwan’s main port of Kaohsiung, making it far outside the range of any Taiwanese combat aircraft. Taiwan faces a similar situation on Pratas Island, which is roughly 250 miles (415 km) southwest of Kaohsiung, and only 150 miles from the Chinese coast. 
In a blockade scenario, powerful PLA naval surface forces, likely including an aircraft carrier, could close shipping lanes near Taiwan. Submarines would provide Taiwan with a potent force to challenge PLA naval deployments and defend sea lanes of communication (SLOC). 
In December 2014, the Taiwan began a program to develop an Indigenous Defense Submarine (IDS), and in April 2018, the United States approved the export licenses needed for U.S. companies to sell naval technology to Taiwan for the submarine program. Construction of the first submarine, the Hai Kun, began in 2020, and by mid-2023 it was launched for testing and certification. In total, Taiwan plans to build eight IDS submarines by the mid-2030s.
Looking ahead, assess key factors that will likely shape the future development of Taiwan’s military and their impact on Taiwan-U.S. relations.
In the past 50 years, American support to Taiwan has often been measured in terms of arms sales, but Taiwan’s domestic arms industry has become increasingly sophisticated and efficient. In particular, the development of a wide range of anti-ship missiles and drones has decreased dependence on the United States and made Taiwan’s military more capable. For vital naval systems, Taiwan’s National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST), and Taiwan International Shipbuilding (CSBC) have become the primary suppliers of mines, missiles, drones, and warships for Taiwan. 
A second significant development is the shift from a primarily bilateral U.S.-Taiwan security relationship to a possible trilateral U.S.-Taiwan-Japan security relationship. Japan is heavily reliant on sea lanes that pass through both the South China Sea and Taiwan for roughly 90 percent of its energy imports and 40 percent of its maritime trade. Japanese political leaders have begun adjusting expectations about Japanese involvement in a Taiwan conflict. In November 2021, [former Prime Minister] Abe Shinzo made remarks that any contingency related to Taiwan would be an emergency for Japan and for the U.S.-Japan security alliance, and current Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has stated that a Taiwan conflict would be “a survival-threatening situation” for Japan.

articles.title: Can Singapore Help Europe Rethink Its Indo-Pacific Strategy?
articles.full_text:
Singapore has spent decades making itself indispensable to a global economy in which it has little control over the behavior of the major powers. Germany might be seeking to learn from that example.
Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong greets German Chancellor Friedrich Merz ahead of their joint press conference in Singapore, Oct. 27, 2026.
On October 27, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Singapore with a message that Europe needs closer partnerships in the Indo-Pacific. Trade, underwater infrastructure, and industrial artificial intelligence may seem like separate policy areas. In fact, they expose the same problem: Europe’s prosperity depends on networks that it cannot secure or shape alone. 
Singapore has spent decades making itself indispensable to a global economy in which it has little control over the behavior of the major powers. Germany might be seeking to learn from that example.
At his meeting with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, Merz proposed an interregional trade agreement between the European Union and the 12 members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP). Together, the two groups account for more than a third of global trade. Wong and Merz also agreed to deepen defense cooperation and industrial AI collaboration under an updated strategic partnership, building on their original agreement from 2024.
The EU already has trade agreements with CPTPP members Singapore and Vietnam in Southeast Asia, as well as with other CPTPP members, including Japan, Canada and New Zealand. Singapore specifically has had a free-trade agreement with the EU since 2019, followed by a digital trade agreement that took effect in February 2026. According to the European Commission, bilateral trade in goods between the EU and Singapore reached 47.8 billion euros in 2025. 
Merz’s proposal to link the EU more closely with the CPTPP would therefore need to do more than connect markets that already have bilateral FTAs. Its value would lie in addressing gaps between existing agreements, aligning trade rules where possible, and making it easier for businesses to operate across countries with different regulatory systems. But an interregional agreement would be politically difficult to negotiate.
In the realm of security, Merz and Wong focused on undersea cables, which carry more than 99 percent of international data traffic. These cables support financial transactions, cloud services and government communications, yet they are vulnerable to both accidental damage and purposeful sabotage. 
Singapore has taken a leading role in efforts to improve cooperation on critical underwater infrastructure. In May 2026, on the sidelines of the Singapore-hosted Shangri-La Dialogue, 17 countries launched the Guiding Principles for Underwater Infrastructure Defense Exchanges (GUIDE), a voluntary framework for sharing information and exploring practical defense cooperation. Singapore was one of the founding members; European countries, among them France and Italy, accounted for over half of the 17 states that joined at the launch. Germany joined GUIDE during Merz’s visit.

GUIDE provides a framework for countries to share information and improve their response to disruptions that cross national borders. The damage to five undersea cables in the Gulf of Finland in December 2024 illustrated the stakes. Such incidents can disrupt communications, incur substantial repair costs, and leave governments struggling to establish responsibility. For Singapore, a major hub for international data routes, and Germany, whose economy depends on secure digital connectivity, closer cooperation is therefore a practical necessity.

The National AI Strategy 2.0, launched in 2023, aims to make the city-state a leading center for AI solutions by 2030. It emphasizes adoption across industry, government and research.

articles.title: Will Pakistan Fight in Saudi Arabia’s Wars?
articles.full_text:
Questions have been raised over the strength of Pakistan’s security commitment to Saudi Arabia ever since the SMDA’s inception in September 2025.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohamed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif hold copies of the Mecca Agreement after its signing on August 7, 2026.
The past two years have been significant for Pakistan’s diplomatic revival in Middle Eastern politics. From the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) in September 2025, signed in the backdrop of the May 2025 conflict with India, to the August 2026 Mecca Agreement with Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, Islamabad has showcased its ability to navigate multifaceted strategic alignments. 
Historically, Pakistan-Saudi security cooperation began during the 1960s when Pakistan deployed its soldiers to train the Royal Saudi Air Force and ground forces. Moving beyond training, Pakistani pilots assisted Saudi pilots in its conflict against South Yemen forces in 1969. Within a decade, Islamabad was once again providing crucial security and advisory assistance to Riyadh countering the 1979 Mecca Grand Mosque seizure. 
In 1982, both sides signed a bilateral security agreement for the first time – thus formalizing security cooperation and large-scale deployment of Pakistani military personnel to Saudi Arabia as trainers and advisers. The agreement was put to the test during the 1990-91 Gulf war. Pakistan, taking a pre-emptive approach, stationed a large number of troops in the Kingdom. 
A major test of Saudi-Pakistan security ties came during the 2015 Saudi-Houthi war. Islamabad positioned itself as a neutral player and distanced its forces from any involvement in the conflict. The Saudi-Houthi war boiled over again in 2026. On October 5 Pakistan, along with Turkiye, agreed to join hands with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis under the Mecca Agreement. However, Islamabad has refrained from direct engagement, restricting its role to assisting Saudi forces without crossing the enemy border.
The Mecca Agreement was signed in the wake of rising Houthi attacks against both Yemeni state forces and Saudi Arabia. It is modelled on NATO’s Article 5 commitment: “an attack against one member is considered an attack against all.” In practice, this three-nation alliance is an expanded version of the Saudi-Pakistani SMDA, with the addition of Turkiye. 
The strategic weight of this new alliance stems from the three countries’ substantial combined capabilities. According to the 2026 Global Firepower Index, the alliance has a “combined strength of 1.4 million active troops, 3,400 military aircrafts, 6,000 tanks, and approximately 340 maritime assets.”
The blend of Saudi finance and capital, Turkish defense capabilities, and Pakistan’s military and nuclear posture make for a powerful combination. 
Once the Mecca Agreement was activated, Pakistan committed its armed forces to counter Houthi attacks against the Kingdom and Islam’s holy sites, while Turkiye, citing legislative restrictions, has limited its role to supplying technology and missiles. This distanced commitment by alliance members may undermine the basic idea of the security agreement. Pakistan and Turkiye are present in theory but are bringing a shield rather than a sword to the Saudi-Houthi conflict. 
The defensive nature of the contribution was acknowledged by Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif. “The forces of Turkiye and Pakistan are playing a supporting role,” he told Pakistan’s Geo News. “We are definitely involved in reconnaissance and such things, but the combat is practically being conducted by Saudi Arabia’s own forces.”
Questions have also been raised over the strength of Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia ever since the SMDA’s inception in September 2025. It took over a year for Islamabad to finally agree to send its troops to Saudi Arabia – that too only under the Mecca Agreement. Even now Pakistan has limited its participation to air attacks and has not committed to direct combat with the Houthis. Rawalpindi seems to be in no mood to sacrifice its forces in a conflict that will divert its attention from its northern and eastern border tensions with Afghanistan and India. 
The last time Pakistan fought along with the Kingdom against South Yemen was in 1969 during the Al-Wadiah War. Then too, Islamabad’s role was limited to air warfare, with Pakistan Air Force pilots flying Royal Saudi Air Force fighter jets. Close to half a century later the Saudi-led coalition waged war against the Houthis, but in April 2015, Pakistan’s parliament in a unanimous vote called for strict neutrality, barring Pakistan from engaging in the conflict in any form. 
Three years into the conflict, in 2018 Pakistan’s then-Army Chief General Javed Bajwa bypassed the 2015 resolution and sent a contingent of 1000 soldiers to the Kingdom, which he described as a “training and advisory mission.” During all these years Islamabad restricted itself to advisory and defensive deployments to protect Saudi interests within its territory. 
In the case of the Houthis – a Shia-dominated group with significant backing from Iran, with whom Pakistan shares close to 900 km of border – Islamabad faces a dual dilemma. First, followers of Shia Islam constitute 20 percent of Pakistan’s population, and this community has in the past stood in solidarity with Iran. Second, given Iran’s security concerns, any regional alignment working against its interest – in this case supporting Saudi Arabia against the Houthis – may be perceived as a direct challenge to Tehran’s interest in the region. Iranian displeasure with Pakistan could result in cross-border skirmishes along the rugged mountains and remote terrains bordering Baluchistan.  
How long can Pakistan distance itself from actual fighting? The answer hinges on Islamabad’s larger aspirations to leverage its military influence amid a post-U.S. security vacuum in the region. Another key factor is Saudi Arabia’s long-term financial assistance to Pakistan, which in the future may convince Islamabad to change its peripheral support posture toward a more robust involvement in the regional conflict. 
Pakistan’s realist approach to the Mecca Agreement seems to be shared by its partners. Both Riyad and Ankara offered little substantive backing to Islamabad during Pakistan’s recent conflict with Afghanistan. A similar response was received after the SMDA, when Saudi officials emphasized that the bilateral agreement was not against India. 
Pakistan may not be comfortable with the diplomatic and political silence from Riyadh following India’s 2019 abrogation of Article 370, which ended the special privileges to the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. Time and again Rawalpindi and Islamabad have drawn global attention to Kashmir by describing the issue as Pakistan’s jugular vein, but Saudi Arabia has offered only limited diplomatic support. That can be attributed to the growing economic ties between New Delhi and Riyadh. 
Such developments are a growing concern for Islamabad. Historically, Saudi Arabia sided with Pakistan during the 1965 and 1971 wars with India, and even assisted Islamabad financially in its nuclear program. But Pakistan cannot expect the same level of diplomatic or military support from the Kingdom in a future conflict with India.
Amid the changing contours of the Middle East, Pakistan is trying to balance its approach between war and peace. However, given its domestic security concerns, Pakistan is trying to thread the needle, fulfilling its commitments under the Mecca Agreement without further escalating the conflict.

articles.title: Why Are Russia and China Cooperating on ‘Patriotic Education’?
articles.full_text:
China has decades of experience in “patriotic education.” What it can learn from Russia is how to use education to support a war effort.
On October 21, China’s Premier Li Qiang traveled from Beijing to St. Petersburg to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin. The Li-Mishustin summit – the 31st such encounter between the Chinese and Russian heads of government – culminated in a long communiqué outlining a great number of collaborative initiatives in areas ranging from artificial intelligence to space exploration and nuclear energy.
Nestled among these, a commitment to “enhancing patriotic education for youth” toward the end of the communiqué could easily be overlooked. But this item deserves greater scrutiny. Often portrayed as simply a matter of convenience or unsentimental realpolitik, China and Russia’s collaboration on patriotic education helps to reveal how the two countries’ “no limits” friendship is, in reality, rooted in a shared obsession with revenging national humiliation and “Western influence.” 
The term “patriotic education” is used broadly across the post-Communist world, from Belarus to Vietnam, part of an inherited Leninist approach to “thought work” and propaganda. In all cases, it refers to top-down efforts to suppress criticism and promote loyalty to the state throughout the education system, drilling school children in correct “moral-ideological” standpoints. In many cases, the rollout of “patriotic education” measures is a direct response to a moment of political crisis. In Belarus, for example, a new patriotic education program was approved by the Council of Ministers as a response to the 2020 anti-government protest movement.
China is the archetype of this trend. The term “patriotic education” was first discussed by China’s leadership in June 1989, a mere two weeks after the massacre of student protesters in Tiananmen Square. Facing a serious legitimacy crisis, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) assumed the garb of patriotism to deflect overseas criticism. As part of the new “patriotic education campaign” rolled out across Chinese schools, students were exhorted to be loyal to the state and to distrust Western influences, with a dire reminder of Europe’s colonial exploitation of China during the 19th century. Schools held flag-raising ceremonies, instructed students in a new “patriotic” curriculum, and organized visits to historic sites, such as the remains of the Summer Palace razed by British and French forces in 1860. A new generation of Chinese students would be sternly exhorted, at every step, biewang guochi: “never forget national humiliation.” It worked: the Tiananmen crisis abated and the CCP recast itself as the righters of historical wrongs suffered by China. 
Both Putin and Xi Jinping appear to have taken this lesson to heart. In 2001, with Russia still reeling from the disintegration of the USSR, Putin – then newly-elected president – unveiled a new five-year plan for “the Patriotic Education of the Citizens of the Russian Federation.” Originally, Russian patriotic education stressed national pride in Russian culture and history, as well as instructing students in conservative moral teachings. However, successive iterations of patriotic education became more explicitly militaristic and resentful of foreign influence, particularly after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014. Patriotic education became a crucial medium through which to promulgate an image of Russia locked in an existential struggle against external threats, and to valorize military service for the glory of Russia. 
Under Xi’s rule, meanwhile, the Chinese state has elevated the patriotic education campaign into a whole-of-society effort to enforce ideological compliance with the CCP and combat “historical nihilism,” the party’s preferred term for public criticism of its record or skepticism about official historical narratives. 
This effort culminated in the 2023 Patriotic Education Law, which created a legal obligation for a wide range of institutions, not just schools and universities, to inculcate loyalty to the nation and the CCP. Professionals and organisations are expected to demonstrate “patriotic feelings and behavior that bring glory to the country.” The message – to be repeated continuously across Chinese society – is that under Xi, China has now overcome its historic humiliations and resumed its proper role as the regional superpower. 
Why the intensifying need for patriotic feelings among Chinese youth? China has keenly followed the developments of Russia’s patriotic education system, noting its success in cultivating nationalist feeling amongst Russia’s youth – and its role in boosting support for Putin’s military operations via military ceremonies and training sessions in Russian schools. Concerningly, patriotic education in China similarly appears to lay the groundwork for promoting the annexation of Taiwan, the self-governing island that the CCP claims as its territory. 
The Patriotic Education Law, which speaks of “the sacred duty to complete the great undertaking of uniting the motherland,” is explicitly aimed at increasing popular support for the forcible unification of Taiwan and China, including via covert influence operations in Taiwan itself. When CCP apparatchiks claim that the goal of patriotic education is to “gather the strength of the people for the great cause of building a strong country and national rejuvenation,” this is party-speak for Taiwanese unification, peaceful or otherwise. 
“Patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel,” observed Samuel Johnson, famously, in 1775. Just over 250 years later, having staked their legacies on grand promises of  expanded territory and renewed national pride, Putin and Xi alike find themselves under pressure to deliver or be exposed as weak and illegitimate in the eyes of the public. A commitment to boost cooperation on patriotic education suggests that these leaders are doubling down on a shared narrative of existential struggle against “the West.” The implications for the inhabitants of Eastern Europe and Taiwan, and for all of us, are sobering indeed.
