articles.title: China Wants Its AI to Go Global, on Its Own Terms
articles.full_text:
Beijing also wants tailored control over what technology leaves, who acquires it, and what remains in the hands of the Chinese government.
China wants its artificial intelligence (AI) to go global. But Beijing also wants tailored control over what leaves, who acquires it, and what remains in the hands of the Chinese government. That’s the tension behind proposed revisions to technology export measures, announced on October 16. Spurring international adoption while retaining authority over strategic technology creates room for China to exert leverage over those who use or build on Chinese AI abroad.
Announcement No. 48 from the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) proposed adding 23 AI technologies to its Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. Public comments are open until November 15; pre-export registration, however, took effect immediately, even though the classifications are not yet final. The formal scope looks narrow, with MOFCOM noting most AI technology will remain freely exportable.
The registration requirement will allow MOFCOM to see transactions before they happen, while the existing licensing requirements still apply. The need for registration is triggered by a transfer of ownership abroad, a license for overseas use, or a change of owner or actual controller to a foreign entity. The requirement applies to deals already underway. 
The listings reach the core technologies of qualifying advanced models, such as weights and source code, along with AI agents, AI chip design, and the interconnect and scheduling technologies for clusters of more than 10,000 accelerators. They do not cover the chips and other products made with AI technology. 
The accompanying MOFCOM explanation said that offering even restricted large models through APIs, apps or web interfaces, software-as-a-service applications, or lightweight on-device deployments falls outside the scope of large-model technology export controls. Under the proposed revisions, the AI listings also exclude technology already in the public domain through open-source release or academic publication. The first open-source release of restricted technology, however, is itself an export, though one eligible for automatic licensing. 
Deploying a restricted model on a customer’s servers abroad is also a technology export; it qualifies for automatic licensing when Chinese firms run it in their own overseas data centers. As under U.S. export controls, Chinese AI may go abroad as a service or an open release, but listed technology cannot be sold abroad without passing through Beijing.
China is trying to prevent another Manus controversy. Manus, an AI agent startup originally based in China that had moved its headquarters to Singapore, was acquired by the U.S. firm Meta – before the Chinese government moved to block the deal. On April 27, China’s foreign-investment security review office announced a prohibition decision requiring Meta’s acquisition of Manus to be unwound. 
In that case, Beijing intervened only after the deal had closed. Under the new rules, a Manus-style sale would have to register before closing, giving regulators notice before control changes hands. The rules also signal to founders and foreign acquirers that moving headquarters abroad will not, by itself, take listed technology beyond Beijing’s reach. 
Chinese authorities also reportedly barred two Manus co-founders from leaving China while the deal was under review. Separately, new State Council exit and entry rules in force since September allow exit bans on citizens whose breaches of export control or technology trade rules could endanger industrial or technological security.
Remote computing is harder to classify. When a Singapore company rents GPUs in Shanghai, the hardware stays in China, yet registration reaches any authorization of overseas use of listed technology. But MOFCOM’s carve-out for APIs and software says nothing about bare GPU rental. The rules leave this unsettled for now, and they do not rule out controls on remote access later. MOFCOM can require registration in other cases by notice. 
Washington is already weighing curbs on remote access to American chips, so Beijing could apply the same logic to its own compute once it has capacity to spare.
If control matters this much, why let Chinese AI be exported at all? 
Wide adoption of Chinese AI attracts developers, encourages complementary products, and sustains commercial relationships, above all in countries that cannot build competitive foundation models of their own. MOFCOM’s explanation explicitly supported AI capacity building in the Global South. It also promised additional facilitation for cooperation among members of the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO), a China-initiated body established in July by 29 founding governments. WAICO membership is not a condition of technology access, but could count in a partner’s favor when Chinese companies seek export licenses.
Automatic licensing would also cover chip designs sent abroad for fabrication and joint research using overseas resources. Because the fast track favors infrastructure Chinese firms build and operate abroad, the computing capacity and the models running on it can arrive as one package, both still owned by Chinese firms. 
The narrow prohibited tier – aimed at AI-driven malicious code, models trained on China’s data, agents for defense, critical infrastructure, and government use – gives Beijing room to frame its controls as keeping AI under human control, which in turn reinforces its bid to shape AI governance through WAICO.
In one respect, China’s approach seems to resemble Pax Silica, the U.S.-led supply chain compact launched last December that now has about two dozen signatories. Both are built to reward partnership with preferential treatment.
Pax Silica, however, is weighted toward the hardware layer, with secure supply chains for minerals, semiconductors, and AI infrastructure, and co-investment among trusted partners. WAICO centers on capacity building, technology sharing, and international AI governance. Beijing now promises to ease export licensing for its members. 
Indonesia, a WAICO founder still in talks over Pax Silica, said the two are “not necessarily at odds,” because WAICO focuses on AI as a tool and Pax Silica on broader digital development. 
AI adoption could lead to potential leverage. Users may come to rely on subsequent model releases, training and inference know-how, integration tools, or continuing technical support. That reliance can harden into path dependence, even for certain U.S. firms that have built on Chinese open models. Authority over future controlled transfers then becomes a bargaining chip. 
That leverage has limits, though. Weights already released cannot be recalled, and future open releases of restricted models would qualify for automatic licensing, which MOFCOM said would be largely filed and cleared at once. Running released weights locally, or switching to competing models, reduces reliance on Chinese providers. 
The model and hardware layers can also separate. Nvidia already optimizes its platform for leading Chinese open models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, and its own filings warn that open models deployed mainly on rival platforms could reduce demand for its products. Which model a user adopts does not necessarily settle whose hardware it runs on. That could change once Chinese chips are good enough for Beijing to bind Chinese models to them by policy. 
Commercial popularity does not automatically produce geopolitical control, and China’s tightened restrictions could push customers toward alternatives. Unclear rules could also lead future start-up founders to incorporate outside China from the start.
Governments and businesses that build on Chinese AI at the moment should keep the option to switch suppliers. Investors in China-origin AI firms should check for listed technology early and build registration into deal timetables. The question, now, is how far Beijing presses. If it ties its export licensing preferences more closely to WAICO endeavors, control over China’s AI stack could become a claim to lead AI governance across the Global South, possibly pushing governments in the non-Western world toward two rival stacks.
China wants its artificial intelligence (AI) to go global. But Beijing also wants tailored control over what leaves, who acquires it, and what remains in the hands of the Chinese government. That’s the tension behind proposed revisions to technology export measures, announced on October 16. Spurring international adoption while retaining authority over strategic technology creates room for China to exert leverage over those who use or build on Chinese AI abroad.
Announcement No. 48 from the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) proposed adding 23 AI technologies to its Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. Public comments are open until November 15; pre-export registration, however, took effect immediately, even though the classifications are not yet final. The formal scope looks narrow, with MOFCOM noting most AI technology will remain freely exportable.
The registration requirement will allow MOFCOM to see transactions before they happen, while the existing licensing requirements still apply. The need for registration is triggered by a transfer of ownership abroad, a license for overseas use, or a change of owner or actual controller to a foreign entity. The requirement applies to deals already underway. 
The listings reach the core technologies of qualifying advanced models, such as weights and source code, along with AI agents, AI chip design, and the interconnect and scheduling technologies for clusters of more than 10,000 accelerators. They do not cover the chips and other products made with AI technology. 
The accompanying MOFCOM explanation said that offering even restricted large models through APIs, apps or web interfaces, software-as-a-service applications, or lightweight on-device deployments falls outside the scope of large-model technology export controls. Under the proposed revisions, the AI listings also exclude technology already in the public domain through open-source release or academic publication. The first open-source release of restricted technology, however, is itself an export, though one eligible for automatic licensing. 
Deploying a restricted model on a customer’s servers abroad is also a technology export; it qualifies for automatic licensing when Chinese firms run it in their own overseas data centers. As under U.S. export controls, Chinese AI may go abroad as a service or an open release, but listed technology cannot be sold abroad without passing through Beijing.
articles.summary: Beijing also wants tailored control over what technology leaves, who acquires it, and what remains in the hands of the Chinese government.

articles.title: Kyrgyzstan Temporarily Bans Imports of Apples (and More)
articles.full_text:
The EU – which is the top exporter of apples to Kyrgyzstan – urged Bishkek against the ban, noting that WTO rules require “exceptional circumstances” to justify such measures.
In early October, Kyrgyzstan’s Cabinet of Ministers proposed imposing a temporary ban on the import of apples into the country until February 2027. The proposal was up for public discussion until October 23, with the European Union weighing in against the measure. On October 27 local media reported that Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Adylbek Kasymaliev had signed the resolution.
Kyrgyzstan’s Cabinet of Ministers explained the temporary import ban as necessary to support the country’s agricultural sector and ensure the “timely sale of the 2026 apple harvest.” 
Kyrgyzstan has more than 26,000 hectares of apple orchards, and expects a harvest of more than 179,000 tons this year. In justifying the temporary ban, the Cabinet of Ministers pointed to growing imports of foreign apples and declining exports of Kyrgyz apples. 
In 2024, the Cabinet stated, apple imports totaled more than 14,000 tons; in 2025 they amounted to just over 2,900 tons. But in the first eight months of 2026, from January to August, Kyrgyzstan had imported nearly 6,500 tons of apples, more than twice the 2025 total. These apples originated mostly in Poland (3,554 tons), China (1,696 tons), and Uzbekistan (860 tons).
At the same time, Kyrgyz apple exports were down 13 percent in the first eight months of 2026, over the 2025 data. “The decline in export shipments increases the importance of the domestic market for the sale of apples grown within the country,” the Cabinet argued in its justification for the resolution. “An influx of imported apples during the season when domestic supply is at its peak can intensify competition within the domestic market.”
The European Union submitted a comment on the resolution, expressing “serious concerns” regarding the proposed ban. “It is all the more concerning that the import ban appears to be intended as a measure to support the domestic producers during the harvest, whereas under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules such measures are to be invoked only in exceptional circumstances and subject to very strict criteria.”
Kyrgyzstan has been a member of the WTO since December 1998. It was the first Central Asian country to join, followed by Tajikistan in 2013 and Kazakhstan in 2015. Uzbekistan started down the WTO path in 1994 but dithered for decades before resuming talks in 2020. Last year Uzbek officials laid out 2026 as the target to finally accede, but a March 2026 goal post passed quietly by. Uzbek officials reaffirmed their goal to accede in 2026 during a Working Party meeting in July.
In its comment on the then-draft Kyrgyz resolution, the EU argued that “the sudden introduction of import restrictions would send a negative signal not only to EU apple exporters, but to all EU traders potentially interested in the market of the Kyrgyz Republic.” 
The EU noted that it is among Kyrgyzstan’s largest trade and investment partners, “with our Partnership and Cooperation Agreement (PCA) underpinning this relationship.” The PCA, the EU comment continued, “provides that goods originating in the EU shall be imported into the Kyrgyz Republic free of all quantitative restrictions…”
While apples hold special significant in Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan – the name of Kazakhstan’s largest city, Almaty, comes from the Kazakh word for apple, алма – it’s not just apples Bishkek is worried about. On October 16, First Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Daniyar Amangeldiev signed a resolution banning the import of potatoes for six months.
It’s not clear whether the EU will take its complaints to the WTO, though that threat certainly is conveyed by its comments on the apple ban.

articles.title: Toward a New ‘Normal’: The Recalibration of the Japan-US Alliance
articles.full_text:
Since the Cold War, Japan and the U.S. have both been seeking normalcy, but they define the term very differently.
U.S. President Donald Trump welcomes Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae to deliver remarks to Yokosuka Naval troops aboard the USS George Washington at Yokosuka Naval Base, Japan on Oct. 28, 2025.
The United States has never been a “normal country” – although it is difficult to find or define what that actually means – and has always, since its founding, been proud of its “exceptionalism.” The righteousness that has been one of the driving motivators of the republic has led it to take a moral stance on issues that are not directly related to its own material needs and to fight for values and principles rather than focusing purely on the defense of the homeland. However, if this way of behavioral instincts were to face a reckoning, the year 1991 provided the right opportunity to change course.
The Soviet Union, once an “evil empire,” and by then far less menacing, was gone, ending a half-century standoff between the two superpowers that had faced each other at the brink of nuclear Armageddon. The successful campaign and diplomatic coordination that defeated Iraqi aggression against Kuwait revived hopes for international governance and for multilateralism as a means of maintaining peace. The U.S. role of global policeman – a role Washington had concluded it needed to fill after Pearl Harbor in order to deter threats before they reached its shores – now seemed unnecessary, with the monsters abroad gone.
While triumphalism had taken hold in the United States, and Europe was still buoyed by German unification and held high hopes for the regional integration that proceeded during the decade, for Japan the 1990s were a different story. Many Americans saw Japan as the real victor of the Cold War and a graver threat than the Soviets had ever been. Among Japanese, there was dread, disappointment, and disbelief that the country’s cherished pacifism went unrecognized – and so did its contribution to the Gulf War. 
Japan had sent no troops but had given billions of dollars, including funds for humanitarian purposes. Yet many dismissed Japan’s contributions entirely – including the Kuwaiti government, which omitted Japan from a newspaper advertisement thanking the countries that had sent troops to liberate it. Economic prowess was one of Japan’s proudest post-war achievements, and the rejection of that power’s use deepened Japan’s disillusionment with its own altruism.
The experience of 1991 was vastly different for the United States and Japan. However, at the same time calls for normalcy in both countries began to gain momentum. In the United States, both mainstream and marginal figures began calling for the U.S. to become a “normal” country – one that does not feel required to right every international problem, regardless of the distance and resources at its disposal. 
The previous year, former U.S. ambassador to the U.N. Jeane Kirkpatrick, an archetype of Cold War foreign policy thinking, published an essay titled “A Normal Country in a Normal Time,” in which she urged the governing elites to adopt a foreign policy more attuned to domestic needs, with the end of the Cold War in sight.
“The time when Americans should bear such unusual burdens is past,” she wrote. “With a return to ‘normal’ times, we can again become a normal nation – and take care of pressing problems of education, family, industry, and technology. We can be an independent nation in a world of independent nations.”
On the other side of the spectrum, Pat Buchanan, who declared his bid to challenge the sitting president in December 1991, called for a reversal of the post-Cold War consensus, advocating trade protectionism and immigration restriction under the slogan “America First.”
However, for the vast majority of mainstream policy elites, a new world order was in sight, and the “unipolar moment” had arrived for the United States. In the following decades, U.S. foreign policy was guided by missionary zeal for exporting democracy and liberalized markets, ultimately leading to nation-building projects. Yet these prolonged, ambitious undertakings abroad gradually eroded the popular support that had initially sustained them, and the resulting frustration culminated in the rise of the anti-elite populist Donald Trump.
In contrast, while a debate over “normalcy” was ignited in Japan, 1991 turned out to be the moment when the country realized that it was not truly “normal” after all. The debate over troop deployment during the Gulf War highlighted the domestic nature of Japan’s definition of pacifism, as well as the lack of international understanding of how it put pacifism into practice. 
In 1993, Ozawa Ichiro, then a rising star in the Liberal Democratic Party, laid out the case for “normalcy” in his best-selling book “Nihon Kaizō Keikaku,” later translated into English as “Blueprint for a New Japan.” For Ozawa, being a “normal country” meant doing what is taken for granted in the international community, and cooperating to the fullest extent with “countries striving to build prosperous and stable lives for their citizens” and on the common challenges facing humanity. 
He also challenged what he saw as a “misunderstanding” of the so-called Yoshida Doctrine, a grand strategy, coined by scholars, that praised the genius of former Prime Minister Yoshida Shigeru’s decision to put the economy first and outsource the main burden of deterrence to the United States, which laid the foundation for postwar development. In Ozawa’s view, Yoshida’s decision was only tentative. In his book, he quoted at length from the former prime minister’s own 1963 writing, in which Yoshida argued that Japan should reduce its security dependence on the United States and instead bear responsibility for contributing to world peace.
Ozawa left the LDP shortly after the book’s publication, as it sold hundreds of thousands of copies. He remained an influential power broker in opposition politics for the rest of his career, with little direct influence on foreign policy. Nevertheless, his foreign policy vision largely defined the course the Japanese government charted over the following three decades. 
In 1992, Japan dispatched Self-Defense Forces personnel to Cambodia for a peacekeeping operation, the first such overseas deployment since the SDF’s founding. The SDF went on to participate in missions in other regions across the globe. In the following decades, Japan became an advocate for global issues such as “human security” and environmental action. In terms of international security, Japan has used its alliance with the United States as a platform for contributing to global security. Japan’s championing of free trade agreements that span the globe is also compatible with Ozawa’s vision of the dual pursuit of national and international interests.
At the present, Japan and the United States seem to hold different notions of what a “normalized” foreign policy entails. For the United States under Trump, it rests on the idea, similar to Kirkpatrick’s, that the national interest, narrowly and unambiguously defined, should be the guiding principle, and that the United States should not lecture other powers or dictate how they govern themselves, so long as they do not interfere with U.S. interests. For Japan, becoming a “normal country” means shouldering a greater burden for regional and international security and committing itself to being a facilitator of international cooperation. This resembles the “exceptional” path the United States took after 1991, albeit in a quieter and more modest fashion.
However, the two “normalcies” are converging. The United States is pursuing an offshore balancing approach that delegates primary responsibility for defense to allies, while Japan shows greater willingness to shoulder the burden, driven by an independent-minded prime minister, a public concerned about regional stability, and a coalition partner that wants to truly normalize the Japan-U.S. alliance by revising it into a mutual defense pact.

articles.title: What Type of Country Should India Be? The Debate Over the Sharjeel Imam Interview
articles.full_text:
Entrenching more group rights would permanently institutionalize the division of Indian society — already an issue — into a large number of groups with different privileges.
A 2020 photograph of jailed Indian Muslim activist Sharjeel Imam.
Sharjeel Imam, an Indian Muslim student activist who has been in jail since 2020 on charges relating to his alleged role in instigating communal riots in Delhi that year, recently gave an interview to The Quint news outlet.
Imam’s interview has sparked much debate in India, particularly because it presents a vision of India that is starkly at odds with the project of the modern Indian state and its constitution. Whatever one may think about the circumstances of his arrest — he has been both denied bail and trial — his ideas on India’s constitutional and political arrangement are problematic and deserving of criticism.
At the heart of Imam’s vision is the need for the Muslim community to have “community rights.” Community rights refer to group or corporate rights, which is the notion that groups can have certain rights particular to their group rather than those possessed by society — and all the individuals belonging to it — at large. This idea is necessary, as per Imam, because Muslims are a separate nation apart from, and distinct from, the larger mass of Indians, who are majority Hindu. Imam’s preference is for a “constitutional arrangement in which Muslims will have full autonomy to administer their affairs, carry out those reform programs, etc without fear of violence and interference from the majority community.”
The reason given for this proposal is the assertion that Muslims have faced discrimination within the modern Indian state, something that is true in some times and places. But his definition of discrimination goes beyond combating bigotry and guaranteeing constitutional rights so every citizen of India is treated with equal dignity. Rather, he alleges Muslims are discriminated against by the very circumstance of living under a constitution “which gave no statutory guarantees to Muslims.”
As the pseudonymous Muslim writer Ibn Khaldun Bharati noted in ThePrint news portal, Imam essentially rejects the framework of liberalism, rather than criticizing the Indian state for not living up to liberalism. According to Ibn Khaldun, Imam “dismisses liberalism as a ploy for majoritarianism… he contemptuously rejects any suggestion of a difference between liberals and Hindutvadis. For him, both are simply Hindus. In his essentialist worldview, all Hindus are the same, for they are unanimous in denying Muslims the political power they claim as a divine right….” In other words, the liberal promise of constitutionally protected individual rights is problematic by its very nature in denying groups their corporate rights. It privileges the group — and its desire to preserve its own distinctive traditions, laws, and customs — over the larger body of citizens which form the Indian nation.
Imam’s arguments are not new, nor are they exclusive to him or his community. In fact, India has long had a problem of groups demanding group rights, quotas on the basis of caste and gender, disproportionate regional representation, and various other schemes to privilege the rights of communities at the expense of individuals. In each instance, despite very different historical justifications, the logic is similar: a belief that a community’s needs or importance entitle it to a special dispensation, reserved seats, or legal privileges.
On the subject of needs, one of Imam’s defenders, Asim Ali, notes in The Telegraph that Imam’s proposals lie within the tradition of radical democratic politics, arguing that communities should organize around their own particular demands before negotiating with other communities. Imam holds that various underprivileged communities like Muslims and Dalits must work together and fight for decentralization, autonomous institutions, and proportional representation, making it more difficult for the majority to exercise power over minorities.
At the heart of this issue is a question: should India’s constitutional model be that of a country of individual citizens and individual rights or a country of corporate communities, including various religious groups, regional ethnicities, and jatis (castes)?
As Muslim leaders gathered at Simla in 1906 suggested to the British Viceroy of India, Lord Minto, “any kind of representation, direct or indirect, and in all other ways affecting their status and influence, should be commensurate not merely with the numerical strength but also with their political importance.” Subsequently, separate electorates were established for the Muslims of British India. A separate electorate is different from a quota or reserved seat in that only members of a specific group, who have their own voter roll, can elect their own representatives.
This led to demands for separate electorates for other groups, such as Dalits (formerly “Untouchables”). Negotiations between Indian independence leader Mohandas K. Gandhi and Dalit leader Bhimrao R. Ambedkar led to the Poona Pact in 1932, in which Dalits gave up their demand for a separate electorate but retained seats reserved for members of their community that the entire electorate could vote for. This compromise is enshrined in India’s post-independence constitution, which adopted the classical liberal propositions of one man, one vote, and a single electorate undivided by caste or religion (Article 325), while also making an allowance for some reserved seats.
The demand for group rights, laws specific to certain groups, quotas, and reservations, though rooted in a desire to remedy past injustices, has morphed into ways for groups to acquire privileges and entrench their power. They are not about protecting the constitutionally guaranteed rights of Indian citizens — only strict adherence to the constitution’s guarantee of individual equality under the law would accomplish that.
Entrenching more group rights would help permanently institutionalize the division of Indian society — already an issue — into a large number of groups with different privileges. It would also help justify majoritarianism as well, because if minorities have group rights, why not the majority?
Ultimately, this line of thinking could inhibit the true emergence of a modern state and society because it keeps a large number of people trapped in zero-sum, communal competition. For, if one group can have certain special rights in how they manage their personal relations, why not another group? If one group has its own electorate or a certain quota, why not another group — that would seem fair, after all. One group securing favorable representation is another group’s loss because it decreases the latter group’s percentage of representation.
Sharjeel Imam’s interview engendered debate because his ideas are so combustible. By seeking to define the Indian Muslim community as a distinct nation, by seeing oppression in the denial of specific group rights, and by alleging that India’s modern nation-building project is illegitimate and fake — an oppressive construct rather than an attempt to build a nation-state that guarantees all its citizens equal rights as individuals — he lays the groundwork for his solution: the fragmentation of the Indian social body itself. This would potentially lead to the Balkanization of citizenship and endless internecine domestic conflict. His logic points to a state seen not as one body of equal citizens, but as a negotiated compact among separate communities. It is hardly a formula for a functioning nation-state.
The alternative is a polity guided by an electorate that at least can aspire to vote on the basis of seeking solutions to economic, developmental, and national security issues, the very issues that a strong, modern nation-state is constituted to handle. This is, after all, the raison d’être of nation-building. In the 1940s, a key philosophical difference between the Indian National Congress (INC) and the All-India Muslim League was between their visions. The INC sought a stronger, more centralized government inhabited by a diverse but undivided Indian nation. But the Muslim League saw India as a land inhabited by separate nations, which necessitated proportional representation, devolution, and eventually, partition. In an era characterized by swift technological change, economic challenges, and geopolitical threats, India seems wise to have gone down the path that it did, not a path similar to the one Sharjeel Imam is advocating.

At the heart of Imam’s vision is the need for the Muslim community to have “community rights.” Community rights refer to group or corporate rights, which is the notion that groups can have certain rights particular to their group rather than those possessed by society — and all the individuals belonging to it — at large. This idea is necessary, as per Imam, because Muslims are a separate nation apart from, and distinct from, the larger mass of Indians, who are majority Hindu. Imam’s preference is for a “constitutional arrangement in which Muslims will have full autonomy to administer their affairs, carry out those reform programs, etc without fear of violence and interference from the majority community.”
The reason given for this proposal is the assertion that Muslims have faced discrimination within the modern Indian state, something that is true in some times and places. But his definition of discrimination goes beyond combating bigotry and guaranteeing constitutional rights so every citizen of India is treated with equal dignity. Rather, he alleges Muslims are discriminated against by the very circumstance of living under a constitution “which gave no statutory guarantees to Muslims.”
As the pseudonymous Muslim writer Ibn Khaldun Bharati noted in ThePrint news portal, Imam essentially rejects the framework of liberalism, rather than criticizing the Indian state for not living up to liberalism. According to Ibn Khaldun, Imam “dismisses liberalism as a ploy for majoritarianism… he contemptuously rejects any suggestion of a difference between liberals and Hindutvadis. For him, both are simply Hindus. In his essentialist worldview, all Hindus are the same, for they are unanimous in denying Muslims the political power they claim as a divine right….” In other words, the liberal promise of constitutionally protected individual rights is problematic by its very nature in denying groups their corporate rights. It privileges the group — and its desire to preserve its own distinctive traditions, laws, and customs — over the larger body of citizens which form the Indian nation.
Imam’s arguments are not new, nor are they exclusive to him or his community. In fact, India has long had a problem of groups demanding group rights, quotas on the basis of caste and gender, disproportionate regional representation, and various other schemes to privilege the rights of communities at the expense of individuals. In each instance, despite very different historical justifications, the logic is similar: a belief that a community’s needs or importance entitle it to a special dispensation, reserved seats, or legal privileges.
On the subject of needs, one of Imam’s defenders, Asim Ali, notes in The Telegraph that Imam’s proposals lie within the tradition of radical democratic politics, arguing that communities should organize around their own particular demands before negotiating with other communities. Imam holds that various underprivileged communities like Muslims and Dalits must work together and fight for decentralization, autonomous institutions, and proportional representation, making it more difficult for the majority to exercise power over minorities.
At the heart of this issue is a question: should India’s constitutional model be that of a country of individual citizens and individual rights or a country of corporate communities, including various religious groups, regional ethnicities, and jatis (castes)?
As Muslim leaders gathered at Simla in 1906 suggested to the British Viceroy of India, Lord Minto, “any kind of representation, direct or indirect, and in all other ways affecting their status and influence, should be commensurate not merely with the numerical strength but also with their political importance.” Subsequently, separate electorates were established for the Muslims of British India. A separate electorate is different from a quota or reserved seat in that only members of a specific group, who have their own voter roll, can elect their own representatives.
This led to demands for separate electorates for other groups, such as Dalits (formerly “Untouchables”). Negotiations between Indian independence leader Mohandas K. Gandhi and Dalit leader Bhimrao R. Ambedkar led to the Poona Pact in 1932, in which Dalits gave up their demand for a separate electorate but retained seats reserved for members of their community that the entire electorate could vote for. This compromise is enshrined in India’s post-independence constitution, which adopted the classical liberal propositions of one man, one vote, and a single electorate undivided by caste or religion (Article 325), while also making an allowance for some reserved seats.
The demand for group rights, laws specific to certain groups, quotas, and reservations, though rooted in a desire to remedy past injustices, has morphed into ways for groups to acquire privileges and entrench their power. They are not about protecting the constitutionally guaranteed rights of Indian citizens — only strict adherence to the constitution’s guarantee of individual equality under the law would accomplish that.
Entrenching more group rights would help permanently institutionalize the division of Indian society — already an issue — into a large number of groups with different privileges. It would also help justify majoritarianism as well, because if minorities have group rights, why not the majority?
Ultimately, this line of thinking could inhibit the true emergence of a modern state and society because it keeps a large number of people trapped in zero-sum, communal competition. For, if one group can have certain special rights in how they manage their personal relations, why not another group? If one group has its own electorate or a certain quota, why not another group — that would seem fair, after all. One group securing favorable representation is another group’s loss because it decreases the latter group’s percentage of representation.
articles.summary: Entrenching more group rights would permanently institutionalize the division of Indian society — already an issue — into a large number of groups with different privileges.

articles.title: Bangladesh’s Persisting Mob Violence
articles.full_text:
Are law enforcement agencies responding swiftly when someone is beaten on the street, or when a mob vandalizes an institution?
The headquarters of the Daily Prothom Alo newspaper in Dhaka, which was vandalized and burnt by mobs on the night of December 18, 2025.
Since the fall of the Sheikh Hasina government on August 5, 2024, mob violence has assumed serious proportions in Bangladesh. Incidents range from individuals being beaten to death over allegations of religious blasphemy to attacks driven by personal vendettas or attempts to seize property. Mobs have indulged in vandalism and attacked shrines, newspaper offices and cultural organizations, national monuments, and memorials related to the 1971 liberation war, even exhuming bodies from graves.
The recent killing of 38-year-old Wahiduzzaman Shamim in Satkhira in southwest Bangladesh on allegations of blasphemy and attacks on a charitable maternity clinic in the capital, Dhaka, have only deepened these concerns.
After the exit of the Awami League government, the interim administration under Dr. Mohammad Yunus (August 2024-February 2026) failed to act effectively amid the deteriorating law and order situation.  Since February, Bangladesh has an elected government led by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP). However, mob violence persists.
According to data from the Human Rights Culture Foundation, 537 incidents of mob violence occurred in Bangladesh between January 1 and October 17 this year, resulting in 256 deaths and 575 injuries, compared to 428 incidents in 2025 and 169 in 2024. Data from Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK), a rights organization, indicates that 171 people were killed in mob violence from January 1 to September 30 this year; the figures for 2024 and 2025 were 128 and 198, respectively.
While methodologies for data collection and calculation may vary across different organizations, the data points to a similar scenario — mob violence has become a grave public security crisis for Bangladesh. And it is not stopping.
There are allegations that leaders and activists from the ruling BNP are involved in incidents related to the seizure of property. The most significant BNP-related incident in the past eight months was the attack on a 50-year-old government-run maternity center in Dhaka, the sole medical facility serving local slum women. A group of local shopkeepers allegedly carried out the attack with the intent to seize the hospital’s land. The BNP has expelled several local leaders in this incident and forced a parliamentarian to resign.
Meanwhile, questions have been raised about the role of the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami, Bangladesh’s largest Islamist party, and its associates in mob violence linked to religious issues. The killing of 38-year-old Shamim in the name of protecting Islam is just one example.
Shamim, who suffered from a mental illness, was beaten to death by a mob. The violence was triggered by audio clips that allegedly contained derogatory remarks about Islam. Although the police initially rescued Shamim and admitted him to a local hospital, a frenzied mob of approximately 250 people attacked the hospital that same night. He subsequently died. The family members of the deceased have alleged that members of the Jamaat were involved in the incident.
Jamaat-e-Islami has denied these allegations, claiming that it is a political organization that believes in the rule of law, justice, and democratic values.
Determining the veracity of allegations requires impartial investigations and concrete evidence. It is as unjust to treat mere allegations as proven facts as it is dangerous to exempt individuals from investigation simply because of their political affiliation.
Hence, if allegations are levelled, it is the police’s duty to register complaints and the courts’ responsibility to try the alleged perpetrators under the law. But this isn’t happening in Bangladesh today.
Leaders of the ruling BNP and the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami routinely blame each other in incidents of mob violence. Neither party is committed to putting an end to such mob actions.
Over the past two years in Bangladesh, most instances of mob violence have occurred in the name of the “Tawhidi Janata“ (the devout masses).
Prior to the incident at Satkhira, a Jamaat activist and its student wing leader in Kushtia were involved in attacking a shrine and exhuming the body of a deceased “pir” (spiritual leader) from his grave and burning it. Jamaat activists were also accused of similar actions at a major shrine in Dhaka. Yet, the Jamaat has not expelled any of them. They simply dismissed allegations of the party’s involvement.
When members of any political party face such allegations, it is not enough for the party in question to simply evade responsibility; they must cooperate with impartial investigations and take necessary organizational action against those accused. This responsibility applies equally to all political parties, whether they are in power or in the opposition.
The BNP government has repeatedly claimed that it is dealing firmly with mob violence. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said that since the BNP took office, mob violence has declined. Regarding allegations of political involvement, he said that these must be verified through investigation.
Whether the number of violent incidents is down or not, the bigger question is whether the law enforcement agencies responded swiftly when someone was beaten on the streets, or a mob vandalized an institution. If they did not arrest perpetrators, launch an impartial investigation, and punish them under the law, warnings from authorities would be seen as empty rhetoric. It is important that justice is done on the basis of the crime committed, and not the identity of the person committing the crime.
Bangladesh police are still not fully operational since the July-August 2024 protests. According to the U.N. OHCHR Fact-Finding Report, 450 out of the 639 police stations across Bangladesh were destroyed or damaged during the protests and the subsequent retaliatory attacks. Hundreds of police personnel were forced into retirement. Many police officials say they hesitate to make decisions that could later become politically controversial.
Importantly, mob violence cannot be addressed unless political parties allow the police to do their work and politicians rein in their supporters

articles.title: How Would China Actually Govern Taiwan?
articles.full_text:
A recent academic symposium offers new insights into China’s vision of a “Taiwan Special Administrative Region.”
On September 12, the University of Hong Kong’s Beijing Center held a low-profile symposium at which Chinese scholars discussed the institutional design and governance arrangements that would follow unification with Taiwan. The participants reached 12 points of consensus on how the “One Country, Two Systems” principle should be implemented in Taiwan.
All of Taiwan’s power would derive from authorization by Beijing; Taiwan’s armed forces would be disbanded and People’s Liberation Army (PLA) troops stationed on the island. All this while still upholding the central government’s policy on Taiwan: “peaceful reunification.” The blueprint, however, also accounts for the scenario of achieving “reunification through non-peaceful means,” which would involve a transition period of “quasi-military governance for a duration of three to five years.”
The symposium built on Xi Jinping’s 2019 speech marking the 40th anniversary of the “Message to Compatriots in Taiwan,” in which he called for exploring a “Two Systems” solution for Taiwan. The symposium was not an isolated event. Chinese scholars regularly debate and publish on how Beijing should approach unification. 
This article puts the 12-point consensus in context and compares it with the 2022 white paper “The Taiwan Question and China’s Reunification in the New Era,” to assess how part of China’s scholarly community envisions governing Taiwan after unification, and where that vision departs from the contemporary official line.
More than 20 Chinese scholars who participated in the symposium drew on the post-handover experience Beijing has from Hong Kong and Macao, both Special Administrative Regions (SARs) that operate under the principle of “One Country, Two Systems.” 
Hong Kong was transferred from British to Chinese sovereignty on July 1, 1997, after more than 150 years of British rule following the First Opium War (1839-1842). During the negotiations, Beijing promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and pledged to maintain its capitalist system and way of life unchanged for 50 years. Macao, where Portuguese traders settled in the 1550s, was handed over to Beijing on December 20, 1999, becoming China’s second SAR.
The “One Country, Two Systems” principle was initially designed with Taiwan in mind. In September 1981, Ye Jianying, a top military leader and chairman of the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, set out a nine-point proposal for peaceful unification, which became known as “Ye’s Nine Points.” At that point, it was proposed that Taiwan would maintain a “high degree of autonomy” as an SAR. 
In 1982, Deng Xiaoping, China’s paramount leader after Mao’s death, developed these ideas into the “One Country, Two Systems” formula. The principle was first applied to Hong Kong and later to Macao. The recent symposium attempted to spell out what a Taiwan version would involve.
According to the 12-point consensus, the “One Country, Two Systems” principle would be implemented whether the unification came by peacefully or via “non-peaceful means.” In a “non-peaceful” scenario, the scholars envisioned a post-conflict transition period of “quasi-military governance,” which could be implemented for a duration of three to five years, during which the central government would crack down on “Taiwan independence elements,” or (in Beijing’s terminology) “Taiwan independence separatists.” China uses the term to refer to anyone who advocates or promotes the de jure independence of Taiwan. 
The symposium’s direct discussion of the use of force against Taiwan – and what would follow – is an outlier. “Peaceful reunification” remains Beijing’s official discursive approach to Taiwan, reflected in many official documents of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Force is left as a last resort aimed at external interference and a “very small number of separatists,” as stated in the 2022 white paper.
The possibility of a military conflict across the Taiwan Strait is widely regarded as one of the most serious geopolitical flashpoints today. In the last decade, China has been steadily intensifying military pressure on Taiwan through a combination of large-scale military exercises and gray-zone operations around the island. 
However, many analysts argue that a large-scale military conflict across the Taiwan Strait – particularly if the United States, Japan, or other regional actors were drawn in – would carry serious risks for the CCP’s primary goal: maintaining its monopoly on political power and ensuring the regime’s survival. As a professor at MIT and China researcher M. Taylor Fravel argued, China is even more aware of such a risk since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Following the “reunification,” all existing Taiwanese armed forces would be disbanded, their weapons “collected and turned over” to the central government, and the island’s defense would become Beijing’s responsibility. The central government would station troops in Taiwan, following the practice in Hong Kong and Macao, where PLA garrisons have been present since 1997 and 1999, respectively. The 2022 white paper did not mention anything about the future of Taiwan’s military, but the 1993 white paper on “reunification” stated that Taiwan would keep its own military and the mainland would not send troops or administrative personnel to Taiwan.
According to the symposium’s 12-point plan, Taiwanese people would also be allowed to voluntarily enlist in the PLA. The PLA is the armed force of the CCP, which commands it through the Central Military Commission, chaired by Xi Jinping, following the principle that “the party commands the gun.” Taiwan’s armed forces, by contrast, are constitutionally required to stand above party affiliation, as stated in Article 138 of the Constitution of the Republic of China (ROC). 
Matters of security, defense, and foreign affairs involving Taiwan are expected to be the sole responsibility of the central government in Beijing following unification.
In terms of law, the Chinese scholars proposed a “de-nationalization” and “de-centralization” of the old legal system, transferring the whole body of law to the SAR regulations. They called for ensuring that “patriots govern Taiwan,” while the existing political parties could be retained under the new constitution. This diverges from the 2022 white paper, which was silent on this topic.
Taiwan is a fully functioning democracy with a pluralistic, multiparty electoral system. Since the democratization in the 1990s, the two dominant parties at the national level have been the Kuomintang (KMT) and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), both holding the presidency and controlling parliament at different times. The KMT generally favors closer cross-strait relations and engagement with China, while the DPP generally emphasizes Taiwan’s distinct identity and supports maintaining Taiwan’s de facto independence and autonomy, while officially calling for the preservation of the status quo in the Taiwan Strait. 
China, on the other hand, is a one-party state with the leadership of the Communist Party embedded in the PRC Constitution. Alongside the CCP, however, exist eight other legally recognized political parties, all of which accept the CCP’s leadership. While China holds no elections these parties can contest, they participate in the state advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.
The 12-point consensus also covers a complete reorganization of Taiwan’s administrative divisions and electoral system. The scholars also called for a thorough reform of Taiwanese textbooks to align with the “patriotic and national” education of China.
Post-unification, Taiwan and the mainland are expected to undergo deeper economic integration. Commerce and cultural ties would continue as usual. Taiwan is expected to become a key economic node in the new “Zhejiang-Fujian-Taiwan Greater Bay Area,” which would serve as an Asia-Pacific economic operations center and high-tech industrial base. 
From a geopolitical perspective, the scholars envision Taiwan becoming an “eastern bulwark of national security.” Taiwan has a pivotal position in the First Island Chain, a strategic line of islands from Japan, through Taiwan to the Philippines, that limit China’s direct and uninterrupted access to the Western Pacific. Taiwan is geopolitically perceived as both the gateway for China’s expansion into the Pacific and as a frontline for external interference in China’s mainland.
According to commentary on the symposium, no participants from Taiwan took part, including Taiwanese figures who favor closer cross-strait ties or eventual unification. One online commentary offered two explanations. First, it claimed that Taiwanese scholars were not invited out of concern for their safety. Due to the sensitivity of the topics discussed – especially unification through “non-peaceful means” – the article argued that attendance could expose pro-unification figures to repercussions at home. Separately, however, the author bluntly stated that Taiwan’s interests should not constrain China’s national interests. The absence of any Taiwanese voices at the symposium nonetheless raises the question of how much decision-making power Beijing would be willing to grant to Taiwanese people post-unification.
In late August 2026, shortly before the symposium took place, Ci-Ze Li, an associate professor at Taiwan’s National Changhua University of Education, published three essays on what a Taiwan-specific version of “One Country, Two Systems” might involve. His proposal, according to his words, was a conditional exercise, not a claim that Taiwanese society had accepted unification. 
Assuming a single sovereign state for the sake of discussion, Li argued that Taiwan should retain democratic elections, judicial authority, financial autonomy, and locally controlled defense forces. He also proposed constitutional safeguards that would make it harder for Beijing to withdraw these guarantees unilaterally. Specifically, he called for a Taiwan-specific chapter in the PRC Constitution, a Basic Law, and a charter endorsed by Taiwan’s voters. 
His proposals differed sharply from the symposium’s consensus. Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office nonetheless welcomed discussion of such proposals in Taiwan, with spokesperson Zhu Fenglian stating that engaging earlier and more broadly would bring Taiwan greater benefits.
In response to these discussions, Liang Wen-chieh, the deputy minister of Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council (MAC), stated that Beijing would not accept Li’s conditions, since China’s approach to “One Country, Two Systems” amounts to replicating the Hong Kong model in Taiwan. Liang added that as long as the CCP retains absolute leadership, any guarantees offered by Beijing would lack credibility, and that Taiwan would not accept the formula on any terms. These statements reflect the position of the government in Taipei.
The latest public opinion survey commissioned by Taiwan’s MAC and conducted by National Chengchi University in August 2026 found that 81.2 percent of respondents opposed Beijing’s “One Country, Two Systems” proposal, while 83.9 percent agreed that Taiwan’s future should be decided by its 23 million citizens. Furthermore, 65.8 percent of respondents considered Beijing’s attitude toward the Taiwanese government unfriendly, and 51.1 percent expressed the same view regarding its attitude toward the Taiwanese people. 
Support for eventual or immediate unification dropped among Taiwanese respondents from 23.2 percent to 7.8 percent between 2000 and 2026. The decline in support for unification is consistent with a stronger, distinct Taiwanese identity and with a growing share of people who see Taiwan as their primary political community and democracy as a defining feature of that community.
The unification of Taiwan with China is portrayed by Xi as nothing less than an “inevitable requirement for the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.” The CCP today holds that Taiwan has been part of China since antiquity, that it was ceded to Japan in 1895 during what official Chinese narratives call the “century of humiliation,” and that it was returned in 1945 under the Cairo and Potsdam declarations. It also holds that the PRC, as the successor to the ROC in 1949, holds sovereignty over the island.
articles.summary: A recent academic symposium offers new insights into China’s vision of a “Taiwan Special Administrative Region.”

articles.title: Mongolia Eyes a Non-Permanent Seat on the UNSC – in 2048
articles.full_text:
To make good on Khurelsukh’s announcement, Mongolia’s foreign policy will require more than two decades of sustained continuity.
Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa addresses the general debate of the General Assembly’s 81st session at the U.N. headquarters in New York, Sep. 22, 2026.
In September, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), the Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa announced Mongolia’s official candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for the 2048-2049 term. With Mongolia’s track record in contribution to the U.N. global missions and its growing commitment, Ulaanbaatar believes that it may have the qualification to gain such an opportunity. That’s not unusual; what’s odd is the lengthy timeline involved.
During his speech to the UNGA, Khurelsukh reflected on and reiterated Mongolia’s multipilared foreign policy objectives. He noted that Mongolia supports United Nations reform, peacekeeping operations, sustainable development goals, and has a special interest in landlocked developing countries. 
This year, Mongolia’s Permanent Representative to the U.N. Ambassador Ankhbayar Nyamdorj served as one of the vice presidents of the 81st UNGA. Mongolia also chaired the Asia-Pacific States Group this June for the election of the General Assembly. 
Despite Mongolia’s many contributions to the United Nations, as Khurelsukh pointed out, the country is “one of the 58 states that have never served as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council.”
At first glance, announcing Mongolia’s candidacy for a seat more than two decades away may seem unusually distant. But the announcement serves to promulgate Mongolia’s deeper commitment to international engagement as an active and responsible player on the world stage. The goal of serving on the UNSC in 2048-2049 cements Mongolia’s longstanding multilateral diplomacy as a concrete, long-term objective. 
Mongolia’s contributions to the United Nations have been growing since gaining membership status in 1961. Mongolia’s engagement with the U.N. and U.N.-led missions have diversified and expanded over time, making Ulaanbaatar an unquestionably active member of the global organization. 
Since 2002, Mongolian “Blue Helmets” – U.N. peacekeepers, including both military, and police contingents – have served in diverse conflict zones around the world: Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUC), South Sudan (UNMISS), Abyei Region (UNISFA), Western Sahara (MINURSO), Lebanon (UNIFIL), Central African Republic (MINUSCA), and Cyprus (UNFICYP). In total, Mongolia has deployed 21,000 peacekeepers. 
As of July 2026, the latest data update from the U.N., Mongolia had 548 active military and police personnel deployed to U.N. peacekeeping operations. That makes Mongolia the 24th largest contributor of peacekeepers in the world. It’s even more impressive given Mongolia’s relatively small population. On a per capita basis, Mongolia is the third largest contributor, behind only Rwanda and Uruguay.  
In June, Mongolian peacekeepers and contingents received U.N. medals for their contribution in civilian protection and safety in conflict zones. Mongolia is planning to host international conference on women in UN peacekeeping in 2027. 
In recent years, Mongolia has also adopted and actively promoted the U.N. Sustainable Development Goals. With issues of climate change taking center stage in the U.N., Mongolia stepped up its game and hosted COP17 to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) this summer. 
Moreover, Mongolia’s continued commitment to its nuclear-weapon-free status has received recognition through the U.N. General Assembly. Mongolia’s Ulaanbaatar Dialogue on Northeast Asian Security serves as a recognized platform for regional and global actors to discuss nuclearization and proliferation issues. 
Taken individually, none of these initiatives would guarantee Mongolia a Security Council seat. Taken together, with Mongolia’s track record of U.N. contributions, they form the foundation of the case. These active engagements within the U.N. framework serve as an important element for Mongolia’s multilateral diplomacy, opening diverse cooperation mechanisms that are supported by Mongolia’s multi-pillared foreign policy. 
The choice of 2048-2049 as a target date may appear unusually distant, but UNSC candidacies are often planned far in advance. Mongolia will compete for one of the seats allocated to the Asia-Pacific Group, which holds two of the Council’s 10 rotating non-permanent seats. One Asia-Pacific seat normally comes up for election each year. 
Unlike some regional groups, however, the Asia-Pacific Group does not have a formally established rotation system for its Security Council seats. Therefore, countries have to plan their candidacies around other declared and anticipated candidates. Each would-be UNSC member must make an assessment of when they have the highest chance of being selected.
For Mongolia, 2048-2049 emerged as the first viable opening in that longer-term regional calendar. The distant date thus illustrates how far ahead states must think when seeking representation on one of the U.N.’s most consequential bodies. Even so, Mongolia’s attempt to “reserve” a seat may not work. The competitive landscape could change considerably over the next two decades, as any country could throw its hat into the ring. 
Under the U.N. Charter, non-permanent Security Council members are elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms, with attention given both to contributions to international peace and security and to equitable geographical distribution. Election requires a two-thirds majority of members present and voting. To reach that goal, Mongolia must continue building the substance behind its candidacy. 
As of now, it’s not clear what agenda Mongolia would like to highlight in its candidacy. For comparison, Kyrgyzstan was elected to its first non-permanent stint on the UNSC in July. Its campaign, as Oliver Fisk noted for The Diplomat at the time, “prioritized four key areas of focus: conflict prevention; promoting the sustainable development of mountainous, less developed, and small-island states; nuclear disarmament; and support for U.N. reform.”
The basis for a Mongolian campaign can already be guessed at. Its consistent support for U.N. peacekeeping missions and its call for nuclear disarmament will likely bolster Mongolia’s diplomatic identity. In addition, Mongolia can be expected to highlight issues that already form the focal points for its U.N.  engagement, such as advocacy for landlocked countries; issues related to the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda; climate and desertification issues; and regional dialogue. Mongolia’s track record on these issues will bolster Ulaanbaatar’s bid to gain a non-permanent seat at the UNSC in 2048-2049. 
There are risks involved with a seat on the U.N.’s most powerful body. Mongolia has spent much of its post-Cold War foreign policy attempting to preserve room for maneuver between its two large neighbors while expanding relations with “third neighbors” and multilateral institutions. A seat on the Security Council would place Mongolia directly inside difficult debates over wars, sanctions, and geopolitical disputes involving major powers. 
If elected to the UNSC, Ulaanbaatar could face pressure to take visible positions on issues concerning Russia, China, the United States, or their respective partners. The same membership that would expand Mongolia’s international influence could therefore make its traditional balancing act considerably more challenging.
Khurelsukh launched Mongolia’s candidacy, but he will be long out of office when the election takes place more than 20 years later. That said, Mongolia’s approach to the United Nations is not dependent on changing governments but rather a foreign policy strategy that is approved by Mongolia’s legislative branch and executed at the government and agency level. Since Mongolia jointed the U.N. in 1961, its relationship with the U.N. has moved on the same trajectory, toward deeper contributions and engagement. The long-term test will be whether Mongolia can convert its international initiatives into sustained institutional influence and durable partnerships across successive governments.
Mongolia will have more than two decades to build support and strengthen its diplomatic record, but the campaign will also have to survive several presidents, governments, and foreign ministers, as well as shifting geopolitics and competing domestic interests. 
As a relatively small, landlocked state situated between Russia and China, Mongolia has limited ability to shape the strategic environment around it through hard power. International institutions, a diverse set of diplomatic partners, and participation in multilateral initiatives have provided Ulaanbaatar with additional political space beyond the constraints of its geographic location. The bid for a Security Council seat fits naturally within this approach. 
In September, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), the Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa announced Mongolia’s official candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for the 2048-2049 term. With Mongolia’s track record in contribution to the U.N. global missions and its growing commitment, Ulaanbaatar believes that it may have the qualification to gain such an opportunity. That’s not unusual; what’s odd is the lengthy timeline involved.
During his speech to the UNGA, Khurelsukh reflected on and reiterated Mongolia’s multipilared foreign policy objectives. He noted that Mongolia supports United Nations reform, peacekeeping operations, sustainable development goals, and has a special interest in landlocked developing countries. 
This year, Mongolia’s Permanent Representative to the U.N. Ambassador Ankhbayar Nyamdorj served as one of the vice presidents of the 81st UNGA. Mongolia also chaired the Asia-Pacific States Group this June for the election of the General Assembly. 
Despite Mongolia’s many contributions to the United Nations, as Khurelsukh pointed out, the country is “one of the 58 states that have never served as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council.”
At first glance, announcing Mongolia’s candidacy for a seat more than two decades away may seem unusually distant. But the announcement serves to promulgate Mongolia’s deeper commitment to international engagement as an active and responsible player on the world stage. The goal of serving on the UNSC in 2048-2049 cements Mongolia’s longstanding multilateral diplomacy as a concrete, long-term objective.
articles.summary: To make good on Khurelsukh’s announcement, Mongolia’s foreign policy will require more than two decades of sustained continuity.

articles.title: Japan Confirms Dispatch to India to Explore Anti-Ship Missile Drills
articles.full_text:
Discussions highlight the training challenges posed by Japan’s expanding arsenal and opportunities for closer defense cooperation with New Delhi.
A Japan Ground Self-Defense Force (GSDF) Type 88 surface-to-ship missile is launched during a live-fire exercise.
Japan has dispatched personnel to India to explore possible live-fire training involving Ground Self-Defense Force (GSDF) surface-to-ship missiles and small attack drones, GSDF Chief of Staff General Arai Masayoshi confirmed at a press conference on October 27.
“It is true that we dispatched personnel to coordinate various matters with India,” the head of the GSDF said.
The confirmation followed an October 21 report by public broadcaster NHK that Defense Ministry officials had traveled to India in mid-October and spent about one week inspecting test facilities and firing ranges. 
The missile system for any prospective exercise has not been selected, and no decision has been made to conduct the training. But the exploratory talks attempt to solve a new problem for Japan.
“When operating relatively long-range missiles, such as surface-to-ship missiles, how to conduct training that makes use of their range is a major challenge,” Arai said.
The service is examining how to secure suitable training environments in Japan while also considering overseas facilities, he added.
The issue is becoming increasingly important as Japan expands its stand-off defense capabilities. Acquiring missiles capable of reaching targets hundreds of kilometers away is only part of the challenge. Personnel must also be trained to deploy and operate these weapons effectively.
Japan’s newly deployed Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missile illustrates the growing training requirements.
The GSDF deployed the missile to Camp Kengun in Kumamoto Prefecture in March 2026. Its range is believed to be around 1,000 kilometers, compared with around 200 kilometers for the earlier Type 12 surface-to-ship missile.
On October 25, during Keen Sword 27, a large-scale Japan-U.S. joint exercise running from October 19 to 29, the GSDF demonstrated the Type 25 to reporters at a training area spanning Nagasaki and Saga prefectures. Personnel demonstrated procedures for deploying a mobile launcher and preparing it for firing, but no missile was launched.
Such exercises help troops practice operating the system, but live-fire training that makes full use of its range presents additional challenges involving safety, airspace, maritime areas, and coordination with relevant authorities. 
There is no confirmation that the Type 25 specifically would be used in India.
Japan has previously conducted surface-to-ship missile firing exercises in the United States and Australia. During the Philippine-U.S. Balikatan exercise in April and May 2026, the GSDF conducted such training in the Philippines for the first time, firing its Type 88 surface-to-ship missile.
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro later told the Asahi Shimbun that the Type 88 was one of the leading candidates for acquisition by Manila.
Access to training facilities in India could further expand Japan’s overseas options while creating opportunities for closer cooperation with New Delhi.
“India is an important partner in the Indo-Pacific region, and we recognize the importance of promoting various forms of defense cooperation and exchanges amid an increasingly severe and complex security environment,” Arai, the GSDF chief, said.
Japan and India already conduct bilateral military exercises and cooperate with the United States and Australia through the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, or Quad, against the backdrop of growing concerns over China’s maritime activities.
However, the latest discussions concern possible bilateral arrangements, not an announced Quad military exercise. Potential Japanese missile training in India would add a practical dimension to bilateral defense cooperation. 
Asked specifically about small attack drones, Arai confirmed that training involving such systems was also among the possibilities being explored.
He identified several challenges associated with training involving these systems, including radio frequencies, training content, suitable locations, operational conditions, and safety management.
Training arrangements must also reflect when, where, and how the GSDF expects to employ the drones, Arai explained. The service is considering both domestic training environments and possible overseas alternatives.
The general said no decision had been made on whether overseas training would precede domestic exercises or proceed alongside them. Conducting live-fire training in Japan would require coordination with relevant local governments and other authorities, taking account of the training activities and safety requirements.
For now, the India discussions remain exploratory. Neither the location nor the timing of any prospective exercise has been announced.
