articles.title: The Future of India-Israel Ties After Israel’s Election
articles.full_text:
The election may change the political setting in which India-Israel relations operate, but it is unlikely to erase the interests and institutional links that sustain them.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu greets Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on his arrival at Ben Gurion Airport in Israel, Feb. 26, 2026.
Israel’s parliamentary election on October 27 posed a consequential test of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership – and a moment for India to consider how resilient its expanding relationship with Israel is to political change. 
The election was the first national vote since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack. Since then, public debate has centered on the government’s security failures, the wars that followed, and questions of accountability. Netanyahu also faces an ongoing corruption trial; the charges remain allegations, not findings of guilt. The election’s outcome will depend not only on which party wins the most votes, but also on who can assemble a governing coalition – a defining feature of Israeli politics for decades.
For New Delhi, the central question is whether the interests and institutions underpinning bilateral cooperation are strong enough to sustain momentum under a different Israeli government. The close personal rapport between Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has given the partnership visibility, but it is not its sole foundation. Since establishing full diplomatic relations in January 1992, India and Israel have expanded cooperation across defense, agriculture, water management, technology, and trade. These accumulated ties give both countries practical reasons to continue working together beyond the political fortunes of their current leaders.
Defense cooperation is a particularly clear example of the relationship’s depth. The Barak-8 air-defense system, jointly developed by India’s Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO)and Israel Aerospace Industries, illustrates how collaboration has moved beyond a simple buyer-seller relationship. Both sides are also exploring the possibility of co-producing Israeli-manufactured defense items such as Iron Dome air defense systems and Tamir interceptor missiles in India. 
Between 2021 and 2025, India was Israel’s largest destination for arms exports, accounting for 29 percent of Israel’s sales worldwide. Such engagement is likely to continue despite India’s push for defense indigenization. In June 2026, Amir Baram, director general of Israel’s Ministry of Defense visited India and met senior Indian officials to discuss strengthening defense-industrial cooperation, including technology sharing and joint projects. Earlier, in November 2025, the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding on defense cooperation. 
These developments do not guarantee that every project or initiative will proceed unchanged under a new government. They do, however, create established channels and a record of cooperation on which future leaders can build.
A change of government in Israel should therefore not make it a herculean task to take the relationship forward. Both countries have developed bilateral mechanisms and ongoing engagement in areas including trade and commerce as well as military and defense cooperation. These working relationships can help preserve continuity through a political transition, even if a new Israeli administration reviews particular priorities, timelines, or agreements. The policy challenge for both sides will be to turn that institutional continuity into practical results, rather than relying only on personal rapport or broad declarations.
Economic ties offer an important opportunity to maintain and expand the relationship. During Modi’s February 2026 visit to Israel, the two governments discussed expanding cooperation in defense technology, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity, while pursuing a free trade agreement. Negotiations are at an advanced stage. The India-Israel Bilateral Investment Agreement, signed in September 2025 as a precursor to the anticipated FTA, entered into force in July 2026. To facilitate trade, the State Bank of India also raised the possibility of using the rupee for trade with Israel in January 2026. 
Bilateral trade between the countries reached approximately $3.93 billion in 2025-26. A breakthrough in FTA talks could provide a stronger framework for trade and investment and help lift economic ties to a new level. It should therefore be in the interest of any future Israeli government to bring the negotiations to a successful conclusion and sign a mutually beneficial agreement at an opportune moment. 
A new Israeli government under a different leader could bring a change in diplomatic style and emphasis. It might seek to repair Israel’s international standing or place renewed weight on improving relations with traditional Western partners, particularly the United States and European countries whose ties with Israel have been strained by the Gaza war and deteriorating security in the West Bank. These possibilities would not necessarily imply a retreat from engagement with India. Israel has reason to maintain partnerships beyond its established relationships, while India values Israeli expertise and technology in areas relevant to its security and development. Any new leadership would need to establish its own working relationship with New Delhi, but the existing bilateral agenda offers a basis on which to do so.
India’s approach will also be shaped by the wider regional environment. New Delhi has important interests across West Asia, including energy security, trade and maritime routes, and the welfare of nearly 10 million Indian citizens in the Gulf. It also maintains relationships with the Arab Gulf states and Iran, a longstanding partner. Escalation involving Israel and its neighbors, as witnessed this year, could put these interests under pressure and make India’s balancing act more difficult. Regional instability could also hamper connectivity and economic cooperation initiatives such as the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEEC) and the India, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States (I2U2) framework. Both these projects have made no progress due to regional tensions, though neither has been completely shelved by the countries involved.
This context makes diplomatic calibration essential. India can deepen practical cooperation with Israel while continuing to support dialogue, regional stability and a political horizon for Palestinians, including a two-state solution. Such an approach reflects the need to protect Indian interests across a diverse region; it does not require New Delhi to treat bilateral cooperation as a substitute for wider diplomacy. For Israel, sustaining ties with India is valuable because the relationship spans several sectors and retains scope for further growth.
The likely trajectory is continuity, though not without qualifications. Netanyahu’s return as prime minister would preserve a familiar political channel, while a new government could bring different priorities and require a period of relationship building. In either case, established defense cooperation, the prospect of closer economic ties, and the growing convergence of interests in areas such as agriculture, water management, AI, renewable energy, cybersecurity, people-to-people ties, educational partnerships, and science and technology provide a foundation for continued engagement. 
The election may change the political setting in which India-Israel relations operate, but it is unlikely by itself to erase the interests and institutional links that sustain them. India’s task will be to translate continuity into concrete cooperation while retaining the diplomatic flexibility needed to navigate a volatile region.

articles.title: China Is Learning to Sell Japanese Culture Better Than Japan
articles.full_text:
In much of the world, Chinese firms introduced local consumers to Japanese aesthetics. Now, they are ready to sell Japanese culture back to Japan itself.
What would Japanese youngsters respond when asked about Chinese culture? Chances are that they will point to the neon-lit streets of Yokohama Chinatown, the culinary tradition that invented gyoza and mapo tofu, and perhaps something they overheard from friends, classmates, and coworkers who are part of the 900,000-strong Chinese diaspora in Japan. 
But what about Genshin Impact, the role-playing video game created by Shanghai-based miHoYo?
It certainly is wildly popular. After launching in 2020, it earned $10 billion in revenue by the end of 2025, becoming the fastest mobile game ever to reach that milestone. In Japan, it was ranked first in popularity as late as 2024, and remains within the top 20 for new downloads, more than six years after launch. 
While created by a Chinese firm, Genshin Impact draws heavily from Japanese pop culture. Its graphics use the typical nijigen visuals perfected through the country’s anime and manga industries, while the gameplay features gacha mechanics of obtaining mystery items, so culturally rooted in Japan’s gachapon capsule toy vending machines.
MiHoYo, branded internationally as Cognosphere, had been publishing games for China’s otaku community since its founding in 2011. The co-founders stated that their inspiration for creating games came from personal love for Japanese anime and technology. However, their business has expanded far beyond those roots. Only 5 percent of Genshin’s total downloads come from Japan despite the game’s popularity in the country. And as miHoYo increasingly expands globally, its games now mix Japanese, Chinese, and Western elements to attract a more diverse audience, as the transnational visuals of its successful Honkai series attest. 
Translating Japanese cultural vocabulary for the global audience has become a source of success for other Chinese firms too. Toymaker PopMart manufactured a global fad for its Labubu dolls by applying that same gacha mechanics to its blind boxes, compelling fans to buy more to chase those rare varieties. Consumer goods retailer Miniso – much derided in Japan as “(Daiso + Muji) / 2” – has become an international promoter of Japanese characters such as Chiikawa and Hello Kitty through licensing agreements.
Notably, Miniso has more than 8,000 stores in 110 countries. With Japanese firms largely absent from large swathes of Africa and South America, Chinese firms have become the first point of contact local consumers have with Japanese aesthetics.
Now, these Chinese firms are ready to sell Japanese culture back to Japan. If miHoYo’s success in Japan through Genshin was accidental, the next wave of Japanified Chinese products will be anything but. 
Following PopMart’s entry into the Japanese market in 2022, Miniso-owned toymaker TopToy entered Japan in 2025 using the same formula. Mellojoy, leveraging Japan’s love for punipuni, engineered a craze among young Japanese women for its own handmade squishies. Even Miniso itself is making a return to Japan through a pop-up shop in collaboration with renowned idol Lisa. 
Japanese firms will now be in an unusual situation of competing for Japanese consumers in products they have long believed to be idiosyncratically Japanese. The case of the BYD Racco is illustrative. The Chinese electric vehicle giant became the first foreign company to ever launch a dedicated Japanese kei car, a class of ultra-compact cars found only in Japan. Japanese carmakers long considered the kei class to have a technological, cultural, and regulatory moat deep enough to deter foreigners. After the Racco sold more than 1,000 two weeks after its launch, domestic rivals were driven out of their complacency and compelled to respond. Suzuki’s recent launch of the e SKY, an electric kei car using BYD-made batteries, will surely ignite more competition in the previously insular market.
As that competition heats up, Japanese firms may come to discover that consumers no longer really care what it means for a product to be culturally Japanese. A coordinated effort to promote the country abroad through the Cool Japan Fund’s investments in media and retail proved a costly failure, while Miniso plans 900-1,000 new stores every year and BYD is readying the Racco for the international market. 
As Genshin Impact showed us, people are interested in a Japanese aesthetic that anyone can access affordably. That means commercialized and scalable products, rather than ones completely made by Japan.

articles.title: China Pulls Out of Logistics Hub Project at Colombo Port
articles.full_text:
Given international developments, geopolitical rivalries, and the expertise needed to develop a logistics center, finding a replacement investor will be difficult.
Last week, China Merchants Port Holdings (CMPH) pulled out of an agreement to build a $392 million South Asia Commercial and Logistics (SACL) hub at the Colombo port. The Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) agreed to pay $21.9 million to settle investments. This should not have come as a surprise given that the project was rife with delays from the start.
When the project was announced in April 2023, it was expected to be completed by the end of 2025. The SLPA and private sector firm Access Engineering were the other parties to the agreement and each holds a 15 percent stake in the project. The logistics hub was to be an eight-story, 5-million-square-foot facility with a storage capacity of 530,000 cubic meters (CBM). The SACL project was expected to provide direct employment to at least 1,800 people and create 10,500 other indirect jobs.
China has been a major financier and builder of Sri Lanka’s infrastructure. Chinese loans helped finance infrastructure projects, while Chinese companies made substantial investments in port operations. China Merchants developed the $500 million Colombo International Container Terminals facility, in which it holds an 85 percent stake, and secured a 99-year concession to operate Hambantota Port through a $1.12 billion agreement in 2017. Separately, China Harbor Engineering undertook the Colombo Port City development on reclaimed land adjoining the capital’s harbor. The proposed logistics hub would have expanded China Merchants’ existing maritime business into a larger warehousing and distribution operation, further linking Chinese investment to Sri Lanka’s ambitions to become a regional logistics center.
There were allegations against the SACL project from the beginning, including claims that the Ranil Wickremesinghe administration signed the agreement without following tender processes. The unions insisted that Sri Lanka would lose 2.8 billion Sri Lankan rupees annually (around $8.4 million) and that the agreement prevented the SLPA from granting other port logistics or warehousing operators royalty terms below those payable by this project, raising questions about the SLPA’s freedom to attract competing investment.
In March 2024, almost a year after the agreement was signed, it was revealed that the project had not yet commenced due to delays in approval for concessions. Almost another year later, the SLPA said the project was scheduled to commence in 2025 after the attorney general’s approval for the proposed concession agreement.
SLPA Chairman Admiral (Retd) Sirimevan Ranasinghe told the media that the delays in the project were due to difficulties in reaching an agreement on the concessions applicable to the project. When the agreement was signed, it was expected to enjoy concessions as a Strategic Development Project (SDP). However, this facility was withdrawn due to the objections of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which had long insisted that Sri Lanka suspend SDP concessions. Ranasinghe also said that the logistics center project would take around 42 to 45 months to be completed, which would have pushed the project’s completion to around 2029, four years after the original completion deadline of 2025.
In October this year, leader of the house Bimal Rathnayake told parliament that the deal was called off because the two sides could not see eye to eye on the agreement. He said the agreement allocated 10 acres between the East and West Container Terminals at the Colombo port. The agreement’s clauses were highly problematic, and despite several rounds of discussions, the two sides could not reach an agreement, Rathnayake said.
This falling out between CMPH and the SLPA raises a number of issues. The Colombo Port could have benefitted greatly from a logistics center. Had it been completed as scheduled in late 2025, it could have allowed Sri Lanka to earn more from cargo passing through.
The World Bank’s latest reports show both the strength of Colombo’s position and the danger of allowing it to weaken. The Connecting to Compete 2025 report said Sri Lanka is among the developing economies whose emergence as shipping hubs have given them unusually strong international connectivity. Yet the Container Port Performance Index 2025 placed Colombo 95th for vessel turnaround, behind Jawaharlal Nehru Port and Mundra, both in India, at 22nd and 30th places, respectively. Colombo’s performance scores also deteriorated sharply in 2024 and 2025.
The World Bank reports showed that while Sri Lanka has valuable shipping connections, it faces growing pressure to provide better service. The reports recommended that Colombo must earn more from the cargo those connections bring. Much of Colombo’s transshipment work involves transferring unopened containers between ships. A logistics center would have allowed operators to unpack selected shipments and prepare their contents for onward distribution.
There could also have been operational benefits. The Container Port Performance Index 2025 report said that inadequate storage and slow movement of cargo fill terminal yards, disrupt handling, and lengthen ships’ stays. A well-integrated logistics center could help by providing suitable space for cargo processing and storage, supported by efficient transfers and customs procedures.
In response to CMPH’s pullout, the SLPA has decided to call for tenders to develop a new logistics hub at Colombo port, under a public-private partnership (PPP) model. Colombo port is a busy place, and some believe that it will not be difficult to attract new investors to build the logistics center.
However, given international developments, geopolitical rivalries, and the expertise needed to develop a logistics center, finding a replacement investor will be difficult and time-consuming. The conflicts in West Asia have disrupted shipping routes, raised transport costs, and made future cargo flows harder to predict. Then, there are alternative ports for Colombo that are modernizing rapidly.
The falling out with CMPH, which already operates a major Colombo terminal and has obvious commercial interests in making the proposed center work, would be another obstacle in attracting a new investor. A replacement investor will want to know why that venture failed and whether the same difficulties could affect its own investment.
And if indeed the deal didn’t go through because the initial agreement of April 2023 did not follow due process and ignored IMF dictates about SDPs, prospective investors will wonder whether an agreement signed with the Sri Lankan government is a dependable basis for committing significant funds for long-term projects. Sri Lanka’s IMF program was approved on March 20, 2023, a month before the logistics hub agreements were signed on April 21. Negotiations with the IMF had begun much earlier, with a staff-level agreement reached on September 1, 2022. In December 2023, Sri Lanka committed to stop approving new SDP projects.  
The Wickremesinghe administration was responsible for negotiating both the IMF program and the logistics investment. It can’t say that the IMF demands were unforeseen, as the government knew the fiscal commitments it had accepted from the IMF and the concessions the developer wanted.
CMPH is expected to recover approximately $20.83 million under the settlement, before winding-up costs. But it also spent time pursuing a project that never became operational. Returning most of the capital does not compensate for the forgone opportunities. So, a prospective investor may require a higher expected return, stronger compensation provisions, or more approvals completed before committing money.
A business that commits hundreds of millions of dollars to a long-term investment project like the SACL looks for stability and clarity. No investor would like to spend months agreeing on terms of a project, invest substantial time and resources, and then be compelled to leave because opportunity costs are great, especially at a time when the world is in flux. In recent years, successive Sri Lankan governments have shown international partners that they were unreliable. One of the National People’s Power (NPP) government’s main challenges is to change that perception. However, there has not been much to write home about in the past two years.
Last week, China Merchants Port Holdings (CMPH) pulled out of an agreement to build a $392 million South Asia Commercial and Logistics (SACL) hub at the Colombo port. The Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) agreed to pay $21.9 million to settle investments. This should not have come as a surprise given that the project was rife with delays from the start.
When the project was announced in April 2023, it was expected to be completed by the end of 2025. The SLPA and private sector firm Access Engineering were the other parties to the agreement and each holds a 15 percent stake in the project. The logistics hub was to be an eight-story, 5-million-square-foot facility with a storage capacity of 530,000 cubic meters (CBM). The SACL project was expected to provide direct employment to at least 1,800 people and create 10,500 other indirect jobs.
China has been a major financier and builder of Sri Lanka’s infrastructure. Chinese loans helped finance infrastructure projects, while Chinese companies made substantial investments in port operations. China Merchants developed the $500 million Colombo International Container Terminals facility, in which it holds an 85 percent stake, and secured a 99-year concession to operate Hambantota Port through a $1.12 billion agreement in 2017. Separately, China Harbor Engineering undertook the Colombo Port City development on reclaimed land adjoining the capital’s harbor. The proposed logistics hub would have expanded China Merchants’ existing maritime business into a larger warehousing and distribution operation, further linking Chinese investment to Sri Lanka’s ambitions to become a regional logistics center.
There were allegations against the SACL project from the beginning, including claims that the Ranil Wickremesinghe administration signed the agreement without following tender processes. The unions insisted that Sri Lanka would lose 2.8 billion Sri Lankan rupees annually (around $8.4 million) and that the agreement prevented the SLPA from granting other port logistics or warehousing operators royalty terms below those payable by this project, raising questions about the SLPA’s freedom to attract competing investment.
In March 2024, almost a year after the agreement was signed, it was revealed that the project had not yet commenced due to delays in approval for concessions. Almost another year later, the SLPA said the project was scheduled to commence in 2025 after the attorney general’s approval for the proposed concession agreement.
SLPA Chairman Admiral (Retd) Sirimevan Ranasinghe told the media that the delays in the project were due to difficulties in reaching an agreement on the concessions applicable to the project. When the agreement was signed, it was expected to enjoy concessions as a Strategic Development Project (SDP). However, this facility was withdrawn due to the objections of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which had long insisted that Sri Lanka suspend SDP concessions. Ranasinghe also said that the logistics center project would take around 42 to 45 months to be completed, which would have pushed the project’s completion to around 2029, four years after the original completion deadline of 2025.
In October this year, leader of the house Bimal Rathnayake told parliament that the deal was called off because the two sides could not see eye to eye on the agreement. He said the agreement allocated 10 acres between the East and West Container Terminals at the Colombo port. The agreement’s clauses were highly problematic, and despite several rounds of discussions, the two sides could not reach an agreement, Rathnayake said.
This falling out between CMPH and the SLPA raises a number of issues. The Colombo Port could have benefitted greatly from a logistics center. Had it been completed as scheduled in late 2025, it could have allowed Sri Lanka to earn more from cargo passing through.
The World Bank’s latest reports show both the strength of Colombo’s position and the danger of allowing it to weaken. The Connecting to Compete 2025 report said Sri Lanka is among the developing economies whose emergence as shipping hubs have given them unusually strong international connectivity. Yet the Container Port Performance Index 2025 placed Colombo 95th for vessel turnaround, behind Jawaharlal Nehru Port and Mundra, both in India, at 22nd and 30th places, respectively. Colombo’s performance scores also deteriorated sharply in 2024 and 2025.
The World Bank reports showed that while Sri Lanka has valuable shipping connections, it faces growing pressure to provide better service. The reports recommended that Colombo must earn more from the cargo those connections bring. Much of Colombo’s transshipment work involves transferring unopened containers between ships. A logistics center would have allowed operators to unpack selected shipments and prepare their contents for onward distribution.
There could also have been operational benefits. The Container Port Performance Index 2025 report said that inadequate storage and slow movement of cargo fill terminal yards, disrupt handling, and lengthen ships’ stays. A well-integrated logistics center could help by providing suitable space for cargo processing and storage, supported by efficient transfers and customs procedures.
articles.summary: Given international developments, geopolitical rivalries, and the expertise needed to develop a logistics center, finding a replacement investor will be difficult.

articles.title: The ASEAN-India Trade Agreement and Its Discontents
articles.full_text:
The myth of the ASEAN FTA as a bad deal is costing India diplomatically.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and leaders of ASEAN member countries pose for a group photograph at the 21st India-ASEAN summit at Vientiane, Laos, Oct. 10, 2024.
Even as India has embraced a renewed fervor for free trade agreements, one trade deal remains disfavored in Indian memory. The 2009 ASEAN-India Goods in Trade Agreement (AITIGA) is one of the oldest trade agreements signed by post-liberalization India as well as one of its most controversial. Atypically for an establishment that prefers to settle diplomatic disputes behind the scenes, Indian diplomats and trade officials are publicly trenchant in their criticism of AITIGA.
An oft-repeated narrative has emerged around the agreement: in the early 2000s, inexperienced Indian negotiators walked into an asymmetric deal, opening up their markets while getting little in return. Consequently, India’s trade deficit with ASEAN ballooned. Moreover, China exploited the AITIGA to route its goods into India through Southeast Asia.  
This narrative stems from misremembering history. Rather than a powerful tool for ASEAN and China to penetrate the Indian market, the AITIGA is, in fact, a shallow and weak instrument. Moreover, it is shallow precisely because India preferred it that way. By repeatedly telling itself an alternative story, New Delhi has developed irrational fears over economic cooperation with Southeast Asia and injected unnecessary acrimony in the relationship. The myth of AITIGA as a bad deal is costing India diplomatically. 
India started running a trade deficit with ASEAN in 1996, 13 years before the AITIGA was signed. The deficit stemmed from Southeast Asia’s shift from agrarian to manufacturing-led economies. The currency devaluations triggered by the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis further boosted the deficit. While the absolute figure of the trade deficit has ballooned over the last three decades, the India-ASEAN imports-to-exports ratio remains broadly similar to what it was in the 1990s.
After the 1997 crisis, ASEAN was looking to economically integrate itself with its East Asian neighbors. In the early 2000s, it began pursuing ASEAN+1 FTAs with its six immediate neighbors: China, India, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand. India had been excluded from the first wave of post-1997 regional integration – the ASEAN Plus Three, Asian Bond Markets Initiative, and Chiang Mai Initiative for currency swap. Eager not to miss out on another wave of regional integration, India agreed to negotiate the FTA. 
Contrary to the myth, Indian officials were tough negotiators. After all, India had decades of experience negotiating economic deals in the GATT, WTO, and elsewhere. The negotiations were tortuous and took much longer than the other ASEAN+1 FTAs. 
Moreover, there was a mismatch of approach. On the one hand, eager to gain access to the Indian market, ASEAN wanted to widen the FTA’s scope. On the other hand, India looked to protect its domestic industry by limiting the scope of the agreement. Indian businesses were lukewarm about seeking out greater market access in Southeast Asia.
India’s tough negotiating ensured that the AITIGA was the shallowest of the ASEAN+1 FTAs. Whereas all other agreements committed parties to tariff elimination coverage of more than 90 percent, the AITIGA’s promised coverage hovered around 79 percent. ASEAN mirrored India’s reluctance to open its markets. For instance, Indian critics of the AITIGA often point to the fact that Indonesia promised only 48.7 percent tariff elimination coverage to India. Notably, Indonesia offered above 91 percent coverage to all other ASEAN+1 partners, including Australia, with which it ran a trade deficit at the time.
AITIGA also ended up with the most stringent Rules of Origin among all the ASEAN+1 FTAs. It is the only agreement that demands dual compliance (35 percent local content and change in tariff subheading) for goods to qualify for preferential treatment. Its complex compliance rules and lower scope resulted in exporters avoiding using the AITIGA.  
In AITIGA, India got what it wanted – an agreement that signaled India’s commitment to its Look East policy without exposing its domestic industry to excessive international competition. While economists may argue over whether Indian protectionism is good economic policy, the debate is irrelevant from a diplomatic standpoint. For whatever reasons, Indian economic managers prefer shielding the Indian market. The AITIGA was a natural outcome of such preference. 
However, to then construct a narrative of the agreement as a bad deal in which India got duped is diplomatically damaging. To begin with, it erodes India’s credibility in the region as a reliable and competent partner. India began criticizing the AITIGA almost as soon as it was signed. The two sides agreed to open a review of the agreement in 2015 but still haven’t concluded it. Such long-drawn, dangling processes chip away at India’s image.
AITIGA’s beleaguered state becomes a particularly bad look when contrasted with other ASEAN+1 FTAs, especially the one with China. Beijing began negotiating its FTA with ASEAN around the same time as New Delhi. However, it not only concluded the negotiations fairly quickly, but China and ASEAN have since upgraded the agreement twice. Today, the ASEAN-China FTA is a powerful instrument that deals with a range of issues from digital trade to green technology.
The narrative of AITIGA as a loss for India has made New Delhi a less confident economic actor in Southeast Asia. The resultant hesitation has been evident in India’s exit from the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership as well as its reluctance to conclude bilateral FTAs with Southeast Asian countries such as Thailand and Indonesia. Today, even as India seeks out FTAs in the Middle East and Europe, it is too unsure of itself to look for a trade deal in Southeast Asia.
Tellingly, the acrimony over AITIGA has spilled over into other aspects of ASEAN-India economic cooperation, even the ones which are in India’s interests. For instance, the 2014 ASEAN-India Trade in Services Agreement needs urgent upgradation to account for all the advancements in the digital economy. Given that India enjoys a services surplus with Southeast Asia, New Delhi should be eagerly driving the process. However, so far the two sides have not even begun discussing the issue.
The self-created myths around AITIGA have cast a shadow on India’s Look/Act East policy. New Delhi needs to shed them to become a more confident, credible and engaged actor in the region.

articles.title: Togo’s China Pivot: Building a Strategic Gateway to the Sahel
articles.full_text:
Lomé’s maritime ambitions, deepening ties with Beijing, and growing coordination with the AES could reshape West Africa’s trade and geopolitical architecture
President of the Council of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, Oct. 13, 2026.
As Togo’s President of the Council of Ministers Faure Gnassingbé concluded his eight-day visit to China on October 16, much of the geopolitical attention surrounding the deepening relationship between Lomé and Beijing naturally centered on China’s expanding commercial and strategic influence in West Africa. Yet an equally important question deserves attention: What does Togo stand to gain from its growing partnership with China?
For Togo – a relatively small coastal country with significant maritime assets and ambitions to become a regional economic hub – China offers opportunities that extend beyond conventional bilateral cooperation. Togo is seeking to leverage its geographic position, particularly the strategic Port of Lomé, to strengthen domestic development while expanding its commercial influence across West Africa, including the landlocked countries of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).
During the visit, both countries elevated their bilateral relations to a “China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era,” alongside agreements spanning agriculture, industry, infrastructure, finance, and security.
From Togo’s perspective, three strategic opportunities stand out: building domestic productive capacity, consolidating its position as a maritime gateway to the Sahel, and expanding financial and strategic optionality.
One of the most important opportunities for Togo lies in leveraging Chinese investments, technology, and market access to accelerate domestic industrialization. The composition of Togo’s exports to China illustrates the challenge. According to U.N. Comtrade data reported by Togo, the country exported approximately $18.1 million in merchandise to China in 2025, compared with $14.8 million in 2024. Leading products included sesame seeds, unwrought aluminum alloys, cocoa beans, copper scraps, and manganese ores. 
These figures reveal an export relationship still heavily concentrated in primary commodities, metals, and limited processing activities. They also illustrate the considerable scope for Togo to capture economic value domestically. During this visit, Gnassingbé toured a smart farming park in Shaanxi, and the Third Institute of Oceanography in the coastal city of Xiamen. He further expressed that Togo will learn from China’s comprehensive production ecosystems as it pursues a sustainable blue economy. 
The significance of these engagements becomes clearer when considered alongside Togo’s existing industrial ambitions. At the Adétikopé Industrial Platform, a major industrial and logistics zone near Lomé, Chinese manufacturer Vivace Group inaugurated a building-materials factory in April 2025 following an investment of about $13.6 million. The facility has a reported annual production capacity of 10,000 tonnes and is intended to supply Togo and neighboring markets. 
These developments suggest that Chinese engagement could complement Togo’s efforts to establish a broader industrial production ecosystem rather than remain predominantly a channel for merchandise imports. China’s zero-tariff access arrangements for eligible African exports and the newly signed phytosanitary protocol for Togolese soybeans could further expand export opportunities.
The second opportunity concerns Togo’s maritime geography and its potential to becomes an increasingly important commercial intermediary between China and the landlocked economies of the Sahel. The Port of Lomé is central to Togo’s development strategy. Its maritime facilities and the connections to inland transport corridors give the country a structural advantage in serving neighboring economies without direct access to the Atlantic Ocean. For the AES countries of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, reliable access to coastal infrastructure remains essential for international commerce, industrial supplies, and economic development. 
Togo’s ambition is to convert this geographic advantage into a durable regional logistic position. During his China visit, Gnassingbé emphasized maritime security, technological capacity, and the need to capture greater economic value from port activities. He spoke highly of China’s record in terms of global maritime governance. The China–Togo joint declaration similarly identified port cooperation, logistics infrastructure, and the development of Lomé as a West African commercial gateway as areas for further engagement. 
The timing is particularly significant because Togo and the AES have been pursuing closer customs and trade coordination to harmonize their customs and trade frameworks. Experts from the four nations met in Ouagadougou between October 12 and 14, while Gnassingbé was in China. Their objectives revolved around defining the interconnection of custom IT systems, the adoption of community regulations, and boosting capacity for customs administrations. The strategic benefits of these developments cause a multiplier effect especially in coordination with China.
For Togo, the benefits could extend beyond port traffic to include warehousing, freight services, customs administration, logistics employment, industrial distribution, and greater regional diplomatic influence.
However, Togo must compete with alternative coastal corridors through Benin, Ghana, and Côte d’Ivoire. Its advantage will ultimately depend on transport costs, customs efficiency, infrastructure reliability, and the security of inland routes. This is where Togo’s relationship with China could become strategically consequential. Chinese capabilities in logistics infrastructure, industrial system, and transport technology could complement domestic and regional investments, helping Togo strengthen its competitiveness as a gateway economy.
Diversifying Togo’s Strategic and Economic Partnerships
The third opportunity concerns Togo’s ability to use its relations with China to diversify development financing, strengthen financial connectivity, and expand its room for strategic maneuver. Chinese financing has already played a role in Togo’s infrastructure development.
Research on China’s overseas lending estimated that Togo’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors reached approximately $740 million in 2021. This figure demonstrates the scale of earlier financing relationships, although it does not represent Togo’s current outstanding obligations. During Gnassingbé’s visit, the Togolese government also announced an agreement providing partial cancellation of debt owed to China.
Beyond conventional lending, the most significant new development concerns financial infrastructure. On October 10, the pan-African banking group Ecobank, headquartered in Lomé, signed a memorandum of understanding with China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) to strengthen renminbi-denominated payment connectivity between China and African markets. With operations across 34 African countries, Ecobank provides a potentially important institutional bridge between Chinese financial infrastructure and African commercial networks.
Gnassingbé reaffirmed Togo’s support for the One China principle, and both leaders spoke on the importance of connecting immediate security conditions to long-term development planning. The wider implications of these connections were expressed in the joint declaration on October 15 where Gnassingbé and Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivered five main points as the foundation of the China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era. First was to undertake joint contribution towards the promotion of an orderly and equal multipolar world. Second was to work together to implement the Global Development Initiative. Third was to implement the Global Security Initiative. Fourth was to collaborate toward implementing the World Civilization Initiative and finally, to establish the Global Governance Initiative.
By maintaining economic connectivity with the landlocked Sahel while deepening its engagement with China, Togo is positioning itself as an increasingly important intermediary in the region’s evolving economic architecture. However, the success of this strategy will ultimately depend on Togo’s ability to convert diplomatic agreements into financed projects, domestic technical capabilities, efficient institutions and productive economic activity.

articles.title: Arakan Army Firms Up Relocation Plan For Villages on Bangladesh-Myanmar Border
articles.full_text:
Under pressure from ARSA and the Myanmar military, the AA is looking to simply move vulnerable villagers to new locations.
People from the border villages of Pyar Re and Kyauk Lone that lie near Myanmar’s border with Bangladesh are constructing huts after relocating to Maungdaw in Myanmar’s Rakhine State.
The Arakan Army (AA) is preparing to relocate some villages from the restive Bangladesh-Myanmar border at a time when the outfit is also deeply engaged in fierce battles against the Myanmar military’s renewed attempts to reclaim territories in Rakhine State.
The plan being fine-tuned will move residents of select villages from the border to areas in different parts of Maungdaw district in Myanmar’s Rakhine State that are well connected by roads and rivers.
In an interview on March 2, Arakan Army (AA) chief Twan Mrat Naing told this correspondent about the relocation plan, which would focus on “remote villages” along the border, many of which are inhabited by the Buddhist Mro community.
Twan Mrat Naing explained that concern for “better security arrangements” for the residents was the primary reason for the decision to shift residents of a few villages to other zones. “Many villages are isolated and scattered. We will have to ensure that this isolation comes to an end.  We will have to relocate them and move them to a place where we can provide security and keep an eye on them,” he said.
The AA chief did not spell out any deadline for completion or details of the project.  But the concerns he expressed over the security of some villages has multilayered connotations for the current situation along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border and AA’s plan to take control of it.
The 271 km-long Myanmar-Bangladesh border includes a riverine border of 64 km, where the Naf River serves as the boundary between the two countries. In Myanmar, the border runs along the districts of Maungdaw in Rakhine State and Paletwa in Chin State, contiguous to Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh.
The two districts are both under AA’s control, but the focus of the relocation is on the border villages in Maungdaw, where the population of Rohingya Muslims is over 90 percent.
There is no clarity on how many villages there are along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border. Observers believe there were more Rohingya-inhabited villages before the ”clearance operations” of 2017, when many settlements were destroyed and ceased to exist. Currently, there are over a hundred villages, mostly inhabited by non-Rohingya communities such as Rakhine Buddhists, Mro, Khami, and Chakma.
Underlying the AA’s decision to relocate border villages is its inability to establish absolute control along the border, unlike other parts of Rakhine State that it captured from the military two years ago.
Besides, the AA has to contend with the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), a Rohingya Muslim militant group, which is seeking to carve out a distinct region for the community in northern Rakhine State.
In 2016-17, ARSA carried out a series of attacks on police and military outposts in northern Rakhine State. The military retaliated with the “clearance operations,” resulting in the death of thousands of Rohingya and the displacement of over 700,000 people, now lodged at refugee camps in Bangladesh.
The situation changed in late 2023 when the Myanmar military joined hands with Rohingya rebel outfits, including ARSA and the Rohingya Solidarity Organization (RSO), to stall the AA’s campaign to capture Maungdaw. While the military could not prevent the AA from taking control of Maungdaw, the violence resulted in more Rohingya and rebel functionaries crossing over to Bangladesh.
ARSA has support in the Rohingya villages in north Maungdaw. It mounts operations intermittently against the AA and residents of non-Rohingya villages. Its functionaries also frequent the Mayu mountains, which cut across the townships of Buthidaung, Maungdaw, and Rathedaung.
ARSA has clashed with the AA often. It has also abducted and murdered non-Rohingya residents from villages located either near the border or the Mayu mountains. Its victims were mostly from the Rakhine Buddhist, Mro, Khami, Thet, and Chakma communities.
On November 12 last year, ARSA abducted and killed three people, including a 10-year-old girl from Kone Chaung village in Maungdaw. “They were in a group of six people.  Three men managed to escape with injuries,” Soe May, a resident of the village, whose daughter was killed, told The Diplomat.
Possibility of Battles on Multiple Fronts
Currently, the AA is engaged in a fierce battle against the Myanmar military in Sittwe and the adjoining region. The Myanmar military unleashed a renewed offensive codenamed Operation 4926 to claw back territories it had lost to the AA in Rakhine State.
However, so far, the military has met with little success. Functionaries of the AA and its political wing, the United League of Arakan, who spoke to this correspondent, were of the view that the military might equip ARSA with weapons to launch more attacks against the AA in north Rakhine State. Reports have emerged of ARSA stepping up its campaign along the border even as the military offensive in Rakhine State deepens.
The AA is concerned about the vulnerability of non-Rohingya border villages to ARSA attacks. Residents of these villages often visit Bangladesh to purchase essential commodities and for medical treatment; this could cease if ARSA trains its guns on them.
A senior ULA functionary pointed out that the most vulnerable to ARSA attacks are about 20 villages located between border pillars 50 and 57, most of which are inhabited by the Mro and Rakhine Buddhist communities.
ARSA, along with the RSO, could target the AA and border villages from camps it has established on the Bangladesh side of the border. Traders from Maungdaw town who frequent the border, including some Rohingya, told The Diplomat that they have seen ARSA and RSO camps at Bandarban in Bangladesh’s Chittagong Hill Tracts.
“Some of these camps are not far from the outposts established by the Bangladesh Border Battalion. The border around Tombru in Bangladesh is the area where the ARSA is most active,” said Kyaw Aye Than, a trader based in the border village of Waylartaung, who occasionally lives in Maungdaw town.
The AA has diverted most of its resources to fight the military for control of Sittwe, the capital of Rakhine State. In addition, it has cadres stationed in the Bamar heartland such as Sagaing Region, Magwe, and Ayeyarwady, where it has teamed up with the local People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) in the movement against the military. The outfit would be overstretched if it were to divert more resources to confront ARSA along the border.
Two months ago, the AA launched its second compulsory recruitment drive under a special law called the National Emergency Defense Provision to increase its cadre strength.
The AA has reportedly learned of the “intimate ties” between ARSA and a section among the non-Rohingya villages, Twan Mrat Naing told me. A sustained collaboration between them could extend to information sharing, which would weaken the AA further in the border areas.
In addition to relocating villages, the AA plans to use technology to surveil the border areas. Drones, camera, and other equipment are being actively considered, the AA chief said.
Some non-Rohingya households from the border villages have started relocating to safe areas in Maungdaw, even as the AA is giving final shape to its relocation plans.
On February 10, I saw four huts being constructed near Kine Gree village, located about 20 km north of Maungdaw town. The residents, who belonged to the Mro community, hailed from Don Nyou village near pillar 52 on the border.
articles.summary: Under pressure from ARSA and the Myanmar military, the AA is looking to simply move vulnerable villagers to new locations.

articles.title: Laos Expected to Scuttle ASEAN’s South China Sea Code of Conduct
articles.full_text:
Sources say Vientiane is poised to replace Phnom Penh as China’s spoiler in ASEAN.
Throughout its year as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Philippines has aggressively sought to push the China-ASEAN Code of Conduct (CoC) for the South China Sea to the top of the regional agenda and end the long and drawn out diplomatic saga, which dates back more than two decades.
The CoC is part of a long (and thus far inconclusive) quest to find peaceful resolutions to the many maritime and territorial disputes that persistently plague the sea lines of communications across a waterway that accounts for almost a quarter of world trade. A CoC would enable ASEAN to negotiate with China as a united entity, and after all that is what ASEAN is supposed to be all about: a centrist political and trade bloc that can represent the interests of 11 Southeast Asian states on the world stage through a rules based order.
It’s a process that does not suit China, which has done its best to belittle and intimidate Manila and specifically Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, who has demanded respect for international law while juggling heated diplomatic tensions and the ASEAN chair. Publicly, Beijing maintains its policy of non-interference and at times even espouses the virtues of potentially resolving maritime issues with Southeast Asian states through ASEAN. But behind the public spotlight, China has persistently used its proxies to obstruct and scuttle the CoC.
Cambodia was particularly useful in this regard. At the 2012 ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, hosted by Phnom Penh, Prime Minister Hun Sen was signaling a significant shift in foreign policy toward China and the CoC was topping the agenda. The Philippines and Vietnam pushed to explicitly mention the ongoing Scarborough Shoal standoff and Chinese maritime encroachment in their Exclusive Economic Zones, but Hun Sen and his Foreign Minister Hor Namhong balked and declared that such disputes should be handled bilaterally.
For the first time in ASEAN history, no joint communique was issued at the end of the meeting. It was a major embarrassment for the Cambodians.
The CoC was effectively frozen, delays amid the COVID-19 pandemic followed, and whenever necessary Cambodia could be relied upon to do China’s bidding and scuttle the process.
That is what China wants; bilateral negotiations between individual states that enable it to reject international verdicts like the 2016 arbitral ruling on the South China Sea while protecting its expansive unilateral claims and military bases on artificial reefs.
China has also secured its state, military, and civilian investments along Cambodia’s limited coastline, but times have changed with the roaring days of the Belt and Road Initiative disappearing into the vacuum of history.
Given the colossal damage caused by online scam compounds, Beijing would prefer to exact penance out of Phnom Penh than scout for new investments, and the Cambodians, sources in ASEAN are saying, are not prepared to weather the diplomatic heat from blocking another effort to resolve the CoC.
Thus Beijing has considered and pressed its alternatives ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit, to be held in Manila on November 16–18 and chaired by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Myanmar could work, but it remains barred from ASEAN summits in retaliation for the ousting of Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government in early 2021 by a junta led by current regime president Min Aung Hlaing. That could change next year.
Timor-Leste, ASEAN sources say, is moving rapidly into China’s orbit, but as the newest member remains unwilling to upset Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, or Singapore on the CoC, nor to offend Cambodia after it shepherded Dili into the trade bloc.
That leaves landlocked Laos, an economic basket case in a region struggling for growth, and an absolute dependent on Chinese largesse. There are shades of the Khmer-Sino relationship from a decade ago now emerging between Vientiane and Beijing.

“Cambodia does not have the appetite for this,” said a Western source privy to CoC negotiations between ASEAN states over the last 12 months.
“It’s overwhelmed by the mess created by organized crime, the scam compounds and the conflict with Thailand. Phnom Penh is now moving closer to the United States and it just can’t deal with any more pressure. Myanmar, not yet; Timor-Leste, watch this space.
“Laos? Laos has been tapped by China and will have to defend its interests, and it’s the only country in ASEAN that Beijing can lean on, and it has been doing precisely that. Laos is going to shatter the Philippine dream of using the chair to pass the Code of Conduct. It’s as simple as that.”

articles.title: Myanmar Using Fake Paperwork to Conceal Shipments of Iranian Jet Fuel, Reports Claim
articles.full_text:
Over the past few years, the country’s military has received hundreds of thousands of barrels of aviation fuel from Iran’s large tanker “shadow fleet.”
Myanmar’s military authorities have imported Iranian jet fuel using “sham paperwork” designed to circumvent the U.S. sanctions on both nations, according to reports published by Reuters and a local activist group yesterday.
The reports, which were based on shipping records, satellite imagery, and documents from Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator and Ministry of Commerce, show how both the origin and content of the shipments were falsified. These shipments of jet fuel, which were disguised as diesel, have allowed the Myanmar Air Force to sustain its brutal air campaign against those opposing its coup d’etat in February 2021.
It has been clear for some time that Myanmar’s military was receiving fuel shipments from Iran’s large tanker “shadow fleet” – both Reuters and the rights group Amnesty International have reported on the issue – but the exact mechanism by which the shipments were being concealed was previously unknown.
The Reuters report traced the journey of a particular vessel, the U.S.-sanctioned tanker Reef, which arrived in Myanmar waters in December of last year with some 113,000 barrels of fuel aboard. As the report detailed, the shipment was ordered by Myanmar-based energy broker Dynamic Wave, which signed a $15.8 million sales ​contract with Thailand’s Tawan-Oil Trading “to supposedly take delivery of a similar amount of South African diesel.”
But the vessel really contained jet fuel from Iran, which Reuters verified both via documentary evidence and satellite images and analysis provided by SynMax Intelligence, “which tracked the tanker’s journey from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas to Southeast Asia.”
Myanmar’s military junta, which in April pupated into a quasi-civilian government under coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, was involved in concealing the origin and nature of the shipment. Days before the Reef arrived, Reuters stated, Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator told the client of Dynamic Wave that it would issue import documentation that labeled the delivery as diesel “instead of ⁠jet fuel,” according to a copy of a November 30 letter seen by the news agency.
Reuters said that it received the document from the local activist group Justice for Myanmar (JFM), which also published a report yesterday providing more detailed evidence of how Myanmar and Iran had concealed the shipments. In its report, JFM stated that leaked import documentation “reveals a network of junta-linked businesses in Myanmar, Thailand, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), for fuel declared as originating in or transiting through Singapore and South Africa.”
Between December 2024 and November 2025, JFM said that it identified records from the Myanmar Commerce Ministry for six shipments of jet fuel that included more than 843,000 barrels of aviation fuel, valued at $109.5 million. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that shipments of jet fuel between Iran and Myanmar have continued into 2026, stating that a tanker reached Myanmar in September.
According to previous reports, Iranian “shadow tankers” have also used a number of other methods to conceal their shipments. They have “gone dark” and switched off their location signals when onloading or offloading aviation fuel. Fuel shipments have also been resold and transshipped multiple times in order to hide the source.
All of this demonstrates the lengths to which Myanmar’s military is prepared to go to ensure a continued supply of jet fuel, as well as the porous nature of U.S. sanctions against both Iran and Myanmar.
In March 2023, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions on two individuals and six entities linked to Myanmar’s jet-fuel industry, citing its deadly bombing campaign against civilian targets. In a statement at the time, Treasury said that the U.S. government “remains steadfast in its commitment to the people of Burma, and will continue to deny the military the materiel it uses to commit these atrocities.” Similar sanctions have also been imposed by the United Kingdom, European Union, Canada, and Australia.
These shipments from Iran have allowed the military to sustain its fierce air campaign against resistance groups and civilian populations that are believed to harbor them. As it has lost territory in various parts of the country, the Myanmar military has relied ever more heavily on its air force, one of its main advantages over the welter of rebel groups and civilian militias that oppose it.
According to the U.N. Human Rights Office, civilian deaths from airstrikes rose by more than 50 percent in 2025. The figure increased from 641 in 2024 to 982 last year. The latter figure included 232 children, which, as JFM noted, is more children than were killed by airstrikes in the previous four years combined.
The past several months have been marked by fierce bombing attacks in Rakhine State, where the military is battling to retake territory from the Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist group that has conquered most of the state since late 2023. Airstrikes on two camps for internally displaced people in AA-controlled Ponnagyun township earlier this month killed at least eight people. These came after a major aerial attack in neighboring Kyauktaw township on September 28, which killed 50 people and wounded at least ​58, according to the AA and other local sources.

However, the fact that fuel continues to flow between Iran and Myanmar, despite extensive sanctions, demonstrates how difficult it can be for the United States and its partners to establish firm control over complex and attenuated global fuel supply chains.
JFM yesterday concluded its report by urging like-minded governments to close the gaps that have permitted the Myanmar military access to jet fuel. It called on the Thai, Singaporean, and Emirati authorities “to urgently investigate the junta’s trade fraud and use of companies in their territory to source aviation fuel.” It also said that the U.S. and other Western powers should “sanction the junta’s whole aviation fuel supply chain network, including the companies and individuals identified in this investigation.”

articles.title: Malaysia’s 2027 Budget: Fiscal Consolidation Continues Apace
articles.full_text:
Unlike most of its ASEAN counterparts, Malaysia can look forward to strong growth, increased state revenue, and shrinking deficits in 2027.
The Malaysian economy is coasting these days. Growth for 2026 will be around 5 percent, with similar levels projected for 2027. Investment in manufacturing and digital services is flowing in, and the current account and trade balance are running large surpluses thanks to booming exports. The deficit is shrinking, even as fuel subsidies rise to cushion consumers from spiking energy prices. Inflation is stable, and fiscal reforms have succeeded in widening and diversifying the tax base, reducing exposure to volatile petroleum rents. For Malaysian fiscal planners, 2027 is coming up roses.
This kind of stable, sustained economic growth is music to the ears of fiscal forecasters because it means tax revenue will continue to grow in proportion to GDP. Not only that, but it will grow in a largely predictable manner. This is obviously important when making a budget because decisions about future spending and borrowing depend on how well you forecast revenue and growth. If growth misses the forecast, revenue comes in below target and the deficit widens. This has been a recurring theme in the Philippines in recent years.
It seems unlikely Malaysia will have a similar issue. Steady, predictable growth means more accurate revenue forecasts, making it easier to control spending and trim the deficit, something Malaysian fiscal planners are particularly fond of. Government expenditures mostly focus on maintaining and upgrading systems and services, and it is unusual to see big budget-busting social or infrastructure programs. As soon as the economy stabilized after the pandemic, Malaysia pivoted toward fiscal consolidation and sought to get the deficit under control through a combination of spending cuts and tax hikes.
This has continued apace in recent budgets, and it is working. The deficit in 2026 is projected at 3.6 percent of GDP, a steep decline from the high of 6.4 percent in 2021. Fiscal consolidation continues in 2027, with the deficit shrinking to 3.3 percent of GDP. That would be the lowest level since 2017. This is expected to happen even as approved government spending for 2027 rises to 458 billion ringgit ($112 billion), a 3.7 percent increase year over year.
Such is the power of tax reform. Historically, Malaysia has been highly dependent on dividends and taxes derived from extracting, refining, and selling petroleum products such as natural gas and oil. In 2019, dividends from state-owned oil and gas firm Petronas and excise and other taxes on petroleum-related activities accounted for 32 percent of government revenue. By 2026, it had fallen to 15 percent, and is expected to remain around that level in the 2027 budget. More than 80 percent of government revenue now reliably comes from non-petroleum sources, mainly taxes.
This is good news because while rents from natural resources like oil and gas can be an important contributor to government operations, they are unpredictable. Prices go up and down, and as the world pivots toward cleaner energy, any government that relies excessively on exploiting fossil fuels to shore up its revenue could be left holding the bag in a couple of decades when renewables are more dominant. By then, it will be too late.
Tax reforms, particularly a recent hike in the sales and service tax, have shifted revenue toward a more sustainable and diversified tax base. Revenue from this tax is set to increase from 10.5 percent of the total in 2019 to 19.2 percent in 2027. The sales and service tax is expected to contribute 73 billion ringgit in 2027, around $18 billion. Few people are happy to pay higher taxes, but during disruptive and uncertain transitional periods, such as the one we are currently living through, expanding the tax base and shoring up the country’s fiscal health is boring but sound medicine.
Evidence of this can be found in the one major line item where Malaysia continues to spend big: subsidies. Malaysia spent around $18 billion on subsidies in 2026, and is targeting roughly the same amount for 2027. A lot of this will go toward cushioning consumers from spiking energy prices. Fiscal planners would prefer to see subsidies go in the opposite direction. Indeed, they started cutting subsidies soon after the post-pandemic economy began stabilizing.
But with an unexpected shock to global energy prices that most rational people would not have seen coming, tax reforms and prudent fiscal management give Malaysia sufficient policy space to increase spending and shell out $18 billion in subsidies in successive years while still narrowing the deficit. That is the kind of fiscal math finance ministers in some neighboring countries can only dream about.

articles.title: Indonesia Announces New Measures to Improve Stock Market Transparency
articles.full_text:
The global index provider MSCI has threatened to downgrade the country to “standalone market” status, potentially triggering billions of dollars in capital outflows.
Indonesia yesterday introduced a host of additional measures to address stock market manipulation, in order to stave off a potential downgrade of the country’s investment status by the global index provider MSCI.
On October 16, MSCI announced that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status” due to its lack of action to increase the transparency of its stock market. The announcement led to an immediate plunge in the Indonesian stock market, which shed 15 percent of its value over two days of trading.
Amid a defiant response from President Prabowo Subianto, who last week accused MSCI of trying to “intimidate” Indonesia, Indonesian officials have promised action to address the index provider’s concerns. Last week, the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) said that it would exclude stocks with high shareholding concentrations from its main Jakarta index starting on November 2.
At a press conference yesterday, IDX chief Jeffrey Hendrik said it plans to expand the membership of a committee that will come up with a list of stocks with high shareholder concentration to include independent parties, Reuters reported. These could include a number of Indonesian academics as well as F. Taylor Chapman, an American businessman currently serving on the board of the new Indonesian state investment fund Danantara, who will act as a representative of foreign investors.
Hendrik said that the IDX also plans to launch investigations when it detects possible coordinated trading aimed at manipulating share prices. It will also freeze suspicious investor accounts.
“We encourage the IDX to strengthen the mechanism and methodology of trading supervision, including its capacity to identify patterns of irregular transactions, detect coordinated trading and strengthen the mechanism to respond to such events,” said Hasan Fawzi, the financial regulator’s capital market supervisor, according to Reuters.
The Indonesian announcements reflect the seriousness of MSCI’s threat to recategorize Indonesia as a “standalone” market. Given its status as the primary benchmark for institutional investors, such a downgrade could potentially trigger billions of dollars in capital outflows.
MSCI initially threatened to downgrade Indonesia in January, but only to “frontier market” status, which is a rung above the “standalone market” category. At the time, it expressed concerns with a host of issues, including coordinated share purchases, the high concentration of ownership in certain companies, and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.
Whether these measures are enough to stave off a downgrade when MSCI makes its determination next June remains to be seen. After MSCI’s January announcement, Indonesia announced a long list of reforms to address MSCI’s concerns, including a doubling of the ​minimum free float for listed companies to 15 percent. Top executives of the exchange and regulatory body also ​stepped down.
However, in its October 16 announcement, MSCI said that despite these promised reforms, “significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement.” For this reason, it said, “a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.”

Indonesia yesterday introduced a host of additional measures to address stock market manipulation, in order to stave off a potential downgrade of the country’s investment status by the global index provider MSCI.
On October 16, MSCI announced that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status” due to its lack of action to increase the transparency of its stock market. At a press conference yesterday, IDX chief Jeffrey Hendrik said it plans to expand the membership of a committee that will come up with a list of stocks with high shareholder concentration to include independent parties, Reuters reported. These could include a number of Indonesian academics as well as F. Taylor Chapman, an American businessman currently serving on the board of the new Indonesian state investment fund Danantara, who will act as a representative of foreign investors.
Hendrik said that the IDX also plans to launch investigations when it detects possible coordinated trading aimed at manipulating share prices. It will also freeze suspicious investor accounts.
