articles.title: ‘We Have Friends, No Enemies’: Timor-Leste’s First Year in ASEAN
articles.full_text:
Dili will seek to “ensure that ASEAN’s principles work together in support of peace and the well-being of its peoples,” says the country’s vice minister for ASEAN affairs.
Timor-Leste’s Prime Minister Xanana Gusmão addresses the 47th ASEAN Summit following a ceremony marking Timor-Leste’s accession to the Southeast Asian bloc in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Oct. 26, 2025.
On October 26, Timor-Leste marks the first anniversary of its admission to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), a milestone that followed 14 years of efforts and a much longer history of struggle for independence. Its accession as the bloc’s 11th member was celebrated as the completion of Southeast Asia’s regional family. Yet behind the diplomatic celebrations lies a more complicated reality. Timor-Leste is entering an organization whose political traditions and practices do not always sit comfortably with the principles that have shaped its own foreign policy.
While Timor-Leste’s resistance against Indonesian occupation is well known, considerably less attention has been paid to its foreign policy and relations with major powers. Dili has occasionally taken positions that have unsettled its neighbors. Myanmar’s military authorities expelled Timorese diplomats twice, first in 2023 following Dili’s engagement with the opposition National Unity Government (NUG), and again in February 2026, following the filing of a criminal complaint in Timor-Leste against senior Myanmar military officials over alleged atrocities. The second expulsion came barely four months after ASEAN accession, exposing the tensions between Dili’s commitment to international justice and the bloc’s longstanding principle of non-interference.
These tensions extend beyond Myanmar. Timor-Leste’s relationship with Indonesia remains shadowed by unresolved questions of justice, accountability, and reparations, while its relationships with China, the United States, and Australia require careful navigation amid intensifying geopolitical competition. At home, ASEAN membership brings demanding economic and institutional obligations, growing concerns over transnational crime and the responsibility of chairing ASEAN in 2029. For a small state whose independence depended heavily on international solidarity, membership offers greater diplomatic influence, but also new pressures to compromise. How Dili manages these competing pressures will reveal much about the kind of regional actor it intends to become.
In this inaugural interview for Conversations on Southeast Asia, a new Diplomat interview series hosted by Khoo Ying Hooi, Timor-Leste’s Vice Minister for ASEAN Affairs, Milena Maria da Costa Rangel, speaks about the country’s first year in ASEAN and the political and practical choices confronting Dili.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Timor-Leste joined ASEAN on October 26, 2025, with substantial legal and institutional commitments under its accession roadmap and access to development assistance through the Initiative for ASEAN Integration (IAI). One year on, how far has Dili progressed in fulfilling these commitments, and how much of the promised assistance has actually materialized? Beyond the diplomatic achievement of accession, what tangible benefits can ordinary Timorese, particularly businesses and young people, expect? 
We remain grateful for the welcome and solidarity extended to Timor-Leste by ASEAN member states. But becoming a member is only the beginning of a much longer process.
Our first year of membership has focused on translating the achievement of accession into coordinated implementation across government. On the legal instruments, Timor-Leste had acceded to most of the 66 instruments under Priority 1 of the accession roadmap [the Roadmap for Timor-Leste’s Full Membership in ASEAN] before joining ASEAN. Two instruments relating to the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement and the ASEAN Comprehensive Investment Agreement remain under discussion, particularly regarding the common legal framework and domestic procedures required by member states.
We are also working with the ASEAN Secretariat to review the economic agreements under the remaining priorities. Some agreements have expired, have not entered into force, or have been replaced. As a result, the number under Priority 2 has been reduced from 48 to 35, and under Priority 3 from 106 to 62. The review has also identified 45 additional agreements that Timor-Leste will need to address. Domestic preparations for accession to the remaining economic agreements are under way.
In terms of assistance, Timor-Leste has benefited from the IAI since May 2024, even before becoming a full member. We are now covered by IAI Work Plan V for 2026–2030, which offers technical assistance and capacity-building in trade, agriculture, education, skills development, and institutional strengthening.
We have established a national task force with focal points in relevant ministries to identify priorities and develop proposals. So far, we have developed six initial project concepts, three of which have been finalized and submitted to the ASEAN Secretariat. They cover areas including sustainable tourism, youth capacity-building, digital skills for primary school teachers, and more resilient coffee production. The challenge now is to turn these proposals into funded projects that produce practical results.
For businesses and young people, ASEAN membership opens access to a much larger market and new opportunities in trade, investment, education, and skills development. But these benefits will not come automatically. Our businesses still face challenges in production capacity, competitiveness, and meeting regional standards. We also need to improve young people’s skills and qualifications so they can make use of these opportunities.
We recognize that many of the obligations require action now, while some of the economic benefits will take longer to emerge. That is why we are taking a phased approach, based on national priorities, institutional capacity, and the timelines agreed with ASEAN.
On October 21, the Council of Ministers approved the National Roadmap for the Implementation of ASEAN Economic Commitments for 2026–2030, accompanied by 19 sectoral strategic action plans and 19 sectoral work plans. These set out the reforms and responsibilities across government. Our focus is not simply to meet legal requirements, but to use membership to support economic diversification, stronger institutions, private sector development, and better opportunities for our people.
Turning to relations with Indonesia, the two countries often present their relationship as a model of post-conflict reconciliation. Yet the 2008 Commission of Truth and Friendship (CTF) acknowledged the serious violations committed during the 1999 violence, while justice and reparations remain unresolved for many victims. Has political reconciliation moved ahead at the expense of justice? Now that both countries sit together in ASEAN, is this chapter effectively closed?
Timor-Leste and Indonesia share a difficult and bitter history. Over the years, however, we have made significant progress in building a peaceful and constructive relationship based on mutual respect, dialogue, and cooperation. This reconciliation is something both countries can be proud of.
At the same time, reconciliation does not mean forgetting the past. We recognize the suffering of victims and their families, and we understand that justice, accountability, and reparations remain important. The CTF helped acknowledge what happened in 1999. At the national level, the Commission for Reception, Truth, and Reconciliation documented past human rights violations in its Chega! report and made important recommendations.
We need to continue preserving historical memory, supporting victims, and advancing a national reparations policy. Membership of ASEAN does not close this chapter. It provides an additional setting for cooperation between two sovereign neighbors, while the needs and dignity of victims remain important in their own rights.
Indonesia is one of our closest neighbors and an important partner in trade, investment, education, security, and regional cooperation. For us, reconciliation means acknowledging the past, addressing its consequences, and building a better relationship for the future. But there is still work to be done on the recommendations of the Chega! report. In that sense, reconciliation remains an ongoing process.
One of ASEAN’s most contentious issues is Myanmar. Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s military-backed leader, has visited five ASEAN member states, most recently Malaysia. These developments raise concerns about the gradual normalization of Myanmar’s military-backed leadership, despite the lack of meaningful progress on ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus. How does Timor-Leste view these developments? What is Dili’s position on engagement with the NUG, and how should Myanmar’s representation in ASEAN relate to progress on the Five-Point Consensus?
Timor-Leste’s position on Myanmar is guided by our commitment to peace, democracy, and international law. These principles remain central to our foreign policy as we engage with other ASEAN member states.
We recognize that the situation in Myanmar is complex, and we are deeply concerned about the continued violence, humanitarian suffering, and its impact on civilians. We believe inclusive dialogue is essential.
Engagement with all relevant stakeholders, including different political groups, should contribute to ending the violence, facilitating political dialogue, and achieving meaningful reconciliation and lasting peace.
Regarding the NUG and other stakeholders, our position is that an inclusive process is indispensable to a peaceful and sustainable solution. We should not focus on only one group while excluding others. At the same time, we respect Myanmar’s sovereignty and recognize its importance in addressing the crisis.
ASEAN membership does not require Timor-Leste to abandon its principles. It provides another platform through which we can advance them collectively. We continue to support the full and effective implementation of ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus as the principal framework for addressing the crisis, and we support ASEAN’s established position concerning Myanmar’s representation at high-level meetings. Engagement should help reduce violence, improve humanitarian access, and create conditions for an inclusive, Myanmar-owned political process.
We take note of the engagement by some ASEAN member states with the Myanmar authorities and will continue to follow developments closely. One thing is certain: Myanmar remains an integral part of the ASEAN family.
Timor-Leste has long emphasized democracy and human rights in its foreign policy, reflecting its own struggle for independence. ASEAN, however, places considerable weight on non-interference. How does Dili reconcile these competing commitments?
We do not see respect for sovereignty and the promotion of human rights as mutually exclusive. Timor-Leste’s approach is to uphold these commitments together. Respect for non-interference is essential to relations among sovereign states, while dialogue, humanitarian cooperation, and collectively agreed ASEAN action can also address matters of shared concern.
articles.summary: Dili will seek to "ensure that ASEAN’s principles work together in support of peace and the well-being of its peoples," says the country's vice minister for ASEAN affairs.

articles.title: The 2026 US Midterm Elections: Ramifications for Australia
articles.full_text:
From AUKUS to trade, the implications of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections for Australia are likely to be profound.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese show members of the media a signed agreement on critical minerals after a bilateral meeting in the Cabinet Room, Oct. 20, 2025.
The 2026 midterm elections in the United States represent a consequential juncture in the evolution of the U.S.-led international order and, by extension, Australia’s strategic environment. Their significance lies not merely in the redistribution of legislative power in Washington, but in what the electoral outcome may reveal about the durability of President Donald Trump’s political mandate, the institutional constraints on executive authority, and the future trajectory of U.S. engagement with its allies.
For Australia, the implications are particularly profound. Its post-war strategic posture has rested on the assumption that U.S. military predominance, institutional continuity, and alliance commitments will provide an enduring foundation for national security. However, as the last two years reveal, the contemporary United States presents a more complex proposition. It remains inextricably linked to Australian security, while its domestic political polarization, transactional approach to alliances, and increasingly protectionist economic orientation have introduced significant uncertainty into the strategic calculus of middle powers.
The consequences of the midterms must therefore be assessed through three interrelated dimensions: the domestic institutional constraints they may impose on the Trump administration, the implications for the credibility of U.S. strategic commitments in the Indo-Pacific, and the extent to which changes in U.S. trade and industrial policy may affect Australia’s economic sovereignty.
The Congressional Balance of Power and U.S. Policy Continuity
The U.S. midterm elections determine the composition of the House of Representatives and a portion of the Senate, thereby influencing the legislative environment within which a president exercises executive authority. Their effects, however, extend beyond the immediate capacity to enact legislation. They can alter congressional oversight, appropriations, appointments, policy implementation, and the political incentives governing presidential conduct. A strengthened Republican congressional majority would potentially consolidate Trump’s capacity to pursue an agenda centered on economic nationalism, immigration enforcement, industrial protection, and a more explicitly transactional conception of international relations. 
For Australia, the implications would be ambiguous. Greater legislative alignment could facilitate the implementation of U.S. defense and industrial initiatives, but at the same time could equally reinforce policies that subordinate alliance management to narrowly defined domestic economic interests.
In particular, a congressional majority sympathetic to protectionism could legitimize further restrictions on international trade, including measures affecting allied economies. Canberra’s diplomatic relationship with Washington would not necessarily insulate it from such pressures. Indeed, the fundamental tension between strategic partnership and economic nationalism may become more pronounced precisely because Australia is both a close security ally and an independent trading nation.
On the other hand, a Democratic victory in either chamber would produce a different, although not necessarily more predictable, policy environment. Legislative resistance and intensified oversight could constrain the administration’s capacity to enact its domestic program. Nevertheless, congressional opposition would not automatically reverse executive trade measures, eliminate presidential discretion in foreign affairs, or restore the policy assumptions associated with earlier administrations. Here, a divided government may generate policy instability rather than moderation, particularly where disputes over appropriations, executive authority, and national security priorities impede coherent long-term planning.
For Canberra, the critical variable is therefore not simply which party controls Congress, but whether the electoral outcome increases or diminishes the predictability of U.S. statecraft. In this regard, Australia should not merely equate Republican control with strategic reliability or Democratic control with international engagement. Both parties operate within a political environment increasingly shaped by strategic competition with China, an overstretched U.S. foreign policy, concerns about domestic industrial capacity, and demands for a more equitable distribution of alliance costs. These structural pressures will only persist beyond the 2026 electoral cycle.
AUKUS and the Problem of Strategic Continuity
As has been well documented, the AUKUS partnership represents perhaps the clearest expression of Australia’s dependence on sustained American strategic commitment. Its submarine pathway and its Pillar II advanced technology initiatives are designed to strengthen deterrence, improve interoperability, and reinforce the capacity of the United States and its partners to respond to an increasingly contested Indo-Pacific.
At the same time, however, AUKUS also exposes an inherent asymmetry in Australia’s strategic position. The program requires decades of investment, complex industrial coordination, technological integration, and political continuity, whereas the U.S. political system operates through short electoral cycles and increasingly polarized partisan competition. The durability and cogency of the partnership therefore depends not simply on presidential support, but on sustained congressional appropriations, industrial capacity, and institutional commitment across successive administrations.
A change in congressional control could have vast material consequences even if formal support for AUKUS remains intact. Congressional scrutiny of submarine production schedules, shipyard capacity, workforce availability, technology transfers, and the allocation of U.S. defense resources could affect the program’s implementation. Such scrutiny would not necessarily constitute opposition to Australia; it might instead reflect legitimate concerns about whether the United States possesses the industrial capacity, not to mention political will, to fulfill its commitments while meeting its own naval requirements.
The broader implication is that Australia must distinguish between the durability of the alliance as a strategic concept and the reliability of particular programs as instruments of policy. Canberra should pursue bipartisan institutional engagement, demonstrating that AUKUS strengthens U.S. security, supports defense sector employment, and contributes to regional stability. 
Equally important is the development of domestic defense-industrial capacity and capabilities that reduce Australia’s vulnerability to delays in U.S. production. The objective should not be strategic self-sufficiency, which is neither feasible nor necessarily desirable, but greater strategic resilience.
Trade Protectionism and Australia’s Economic Vulnerability
The economic reverberations of the midterms may also prove as consequential as their strategic implications. The defining tension in the Australia-U.S. relationship is the coexistence of deep security integration with an increasingly contested economic relationship. Whereas the alliance is premised on mutual strategic advantage, U.S. trade policy under Trump 2.0 has increasingly reflected the proposition that international economic relationships should be evaluated through their contribution to domestic production, employment, and national bargaining power.
For Australia, this creates a structural vulnerability. The United States is concurrently a security guarantor, a major source of investment and technology, and an economy whose trade policies can impose costs on close partners. Australian exporters may therefore find themselves exposed to policy decisions driven less by bilateral diplomatic considerations than by U.S. domestic political imperatives.
A Republican electoral victory could strengthen the political legitimacy of protectionist measures, although it would not necessarily produce a uniform escalation of tariffs. Conversely, Democratic gains could increase scrutiny of the administration’s economic policies without fundamentally displacing the bipartisan turn toward industrial protection and strategic supply chain security. The U.S. emphasis on domestic manufacturing, technological sovereignty, and reducing dependence on Chinese supply chains is not exclusively a Trump phenomenon; it reflects a broader reassessment of the relationship between economic interdependence and national security.
Australia must consequently resist the assumption that favorable diplomatic relations will reliably translate into preferential economic treatment. In this regard, critical minerals, energy, advanced materials, and defense-related technologies offer opportunities for cooperation, provided that agreements deliver commercially sustainable outcomes rather than merely political symbolism. Equally, diversification should not be understood as a retreat from the U.S. relationship. It is a means of reducing the economic costs associated with policy volatility and strengthening Australia’s bargaining position within the alliance.
China and the Strategic Balance in the Indo-Pacific
The regional outcomes of the midterms extend beyond the bilateral alliance. Australia’s strategic domain is defined by the interface between U.S. power, Chinese ambitions, and the calculations of regional states seeking to preserve autonomy amid intensifying great power competition.
A politically strengthened Trump administration might adopt a more assertive posture toward China, particularly in areas involving military deterrence, technological competition, and economic security. Such an approach could align with Australia’s concern about coercion and the deterioration of the regional balance of power. 
Nonetheless, greater rhetorical or economic confrontation should not automatically be interpreted as a strengthening of regional security. As has already been evident across the last two years, a more transactional U.S. foreign policy has engendered uncertainty about the circumstances in which Washington is willing to support its partners, the conditions attached to that support, and the relative priority assigned to different theaters.
Alternatively, a Democratic-controlled Congress might seek greater oversight of the administration’s foreign policy, potentially reinforcing institutional scrutiny, and encouraging more deliberate consultation with allies. Still, partisan conflict could also undermine the coherence of U.S. external engagement, particularly if disputes over appropriations or executive authority hinder policy implementation.
For Australia, the central issue is credibility rather than electoral ideology. Deterrence depends not only on military capabilities but also on an adversary’s assessment of political resolve, alliance cohesion, and the likelihood that commitments will be honored under pressure. Canberra must therefore evaluate concrete indicators, including defense appropriations, force posture, operational coordination, diplomatic consultation, and the implementation of agreed commitments, rather than treating U.S. domestic politics as a reliable proxy for strategic behavior.
At the same time, Canberra must recognize that its interests are not identical to Washington’s. Its prosperity and security depend on maintaining a stable regional order, functioning economic relationships, and effective diplomatic channels. An escalation in China-U.S. confrontation could impose substantial costs on Australia even where the underlying U.S. objective is strategically defensible. The appropriate response is neither unconditional alignment nor strategic equidistance, but calibrated alliance management that combines credible defense cooperation with independent assessment of Australian interests and sustained regional diplomacy.
Strategic Autonomy and Australia’s Policy Response
articles.summary: From AUKUS to trade, the implications of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections for Australia are likely to be profound.

articles.title: Taiwan-Vatican Ties: The Dynamic Interplay Under Pope Leo XIV
articles.full_text:
Regardless of the Sino-Vatican agreement, the practical, multifaceted ties between Taiwan and the Holy See have deepened over the past year.
Chen Chien-Jen, former vice president of Taiwan and current president of Academia Sinica, meets with Pope Leo XIV while attending the Pontifical Academy of Sciences (PAS) meeting in the Vatican, Sep. 27, 2026.
Pope Leo XIV succeeded Pope Francis in May 2025, becoming the 267th Pontiff of the global Catholic Church. According to academic and media analyses, Pope Leo XIV’s diplomatic strategy continues Pope Francis’ approach of “engagement” and “openness,” placing a particular emphasis on “peace” and the “de-escalation of potential armed conflicts.” 
For Taiwan, the most closely watched diplomatic development during Pope Francis’ tenure was the 2018 provisional agreement on appointing bishops, signed between the Holy See and the People’s Republic of China (PRC). This agreement led the Chinese government to formally recognize the Pope as the Catholic Church’s supreme religious leader, facilitating the joint appointment of multiple bishops by Beijing and the Vatican under its framework. Since taking office, Pope Leo XIV has not altered the Sino-Vatican agreement; instead, he has accelerated the bishop-appointment process, ushering in a “rejuvenated” roster of Chinese bishops.
The Holy See remains the Republic of China (Taiwan)’s sole diplomatic ally in Europe. Since 2000, public discourse has frequently debated whether the Holy See might sever formal diplomatic ties with Taipei in favor of establishing relations with Beijing. Pope Leo XIV’s continuation of his predecessor’s approach to China implies a further deepening of Sino-Vatican relations. However, from Taiwan’s perspective, society should not underestimate its own standing. In fact, since Pope Leo XIV assumed the papacy, the Pontiff has received numerous Taiwanese organizations and individuals. 
Furthermore, Pope Leo XIV has not shied away from being photographed alongside the Taiwan national flag. These gestures show that the Chicago-born Pope is friendly toward Taiwan, understands Taiwan’s significance to the global community, and recognizes the distinct differences between Taiwan and the PRC.
When discussing Taiwan-Vatican relations, the analytical lens must not be restricted solely to the continuation of the Sino-Vatican agreement or ongoing negotiations. Instead, one must examine whether the practical, multifaceted ties between Taiwan and the Holy See have correspondingly deepened. From Taipei’s perspective, the answer is a resounding yes.
From September 23 to 26, 2026, Chen Chien-Jen, former vice president of Taiwan and current president of Academia Sinica, attended the Pontifical Academy of Sciences (PAS) meeting and its biennial plenary session at the Vatican. Chen presided over the seventh session, titled “Medicine, Neuroscience, and Human Well-being.” Following the meeting, Chen and the PAS issued a joint statement titled “The Future of Science in a Changing World,” serving as an action plan for the international scientific community. Through the Holy See’s global platform, Taiwan once again showcased its scientific prowess to the world.
Shortly after, from October 7 to 15, Bishop John Lee Keh-mien, president of the Chinese Regional Bishops’ Conference in Taiwan, along with Professor Chou Te-yu and Consultor Yeh Chia-yen – members of the Holy See’s Dicastery for the Laity, Family and Life – attended a major conference at the Vatican. Hosted by Pope Leo XIV, the event marked the 10th anniversary of Pope Francis’ apostolic exhortation, Amoris Laetitia. The grand-scale conference welcomed 187 invited guests, including 111 presidents of episcopal conferences from around the globe. Taiwan was not only present, but Taiwanese scholars attended in their official capacities as members of the Vatican’s Dicastery, underscoring Taiwan’s deep engagement with the Holy See.
Furthermore, on October 19, Pope Leo XIV appointed new members to the Holy See’s International Theological Commission. Sister Hu Shu-qin, an associate professor at the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine, was appointed as a new member of the Commission for the 2026-2031 term. Sister Hu is the first ethnic Chinese theologian to be appointed to the Commission since Archbishop Savio Hon Tai-Fai, S.D.B., who served from 2004 to 2014. Her long-standing dedication to theological education and academic research in Taiwan has deepened Taiwan’s participation in global Catholic theology, further demonstrating the Vatican’s high regard for theological development in Taiwan.
Immediately following, from October 22 to 24, the Vatican’s Dicastery for Evangelization hosted the “The Church of the Sheaves” international conference in Rome. Under the theme “A Church for All: Synodal in Method, Missionary in Spirit, Credible in Love,” the event gathered over a hundred scholars worldwide. Grounded in the spirit and method of synodality, the conference emphasized mutual listening and sharing, signaling a shift in the Catholic Church’s approach to evangelization from the traditional model of missionaries transmitting and teaching, to local churches sharing and receiving each other’s gifts to enrich one another. 
Professor Tan Liang-chen, an assistant professor and well-known public Catholic theologian at the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine, was selected to attend the Rome conference. He brought Taiwan’s voice – and the voice of the Taiwanese Catholic Church – to the West and the Vatican, sharing it with the universal Church.
The relationship between Taiwan and the Holy See is concretely built upon these small yet monumental steps. Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been advancing an “Integrated Diplomacy” strategy, using “Values,” “Alliances,” and “Trade” to expand Taiwan’s friendships – a deeper diplomatic approach increasingly evident in Europe. The good that Taiwan can bring to the world extends beyond high-tech industries like semiconductors and AI; it also includes the vibrant space for religious faith nurtured within Taiwan’s free society. 
The stable, deepening relationship between Taiwan and the Holy See is the fruitful result of joint efforts by Taiwanese civil society, the local Catholic Church, and the government. These rich fruits stem from the relentless educational and research dedication of the Fu Jen Faculty of Theology of St. Robert Bellarmine and Fu Jen Catholic University. More importantly, they rely on tireless diplomats on the front lines in Rome and on Ketagalan Boulevard in Taipei. Even when the road ahead is fraught with challenges, they keep working diligently, paving bridges for the present and the future, which is why Taiwan-Vatican ties remain so steadfast. 
In the face of shifting Sino-Vatican dynamics, Taiwan has no reason to worry; in the eyes of the Holy See, Taiwan remains an undeniably “precious” presence.

In fact, since Pope Leo XIV assumed the papacy, the Pontiff has received numerous Taiwanese organizations and individuals.

articles.title: Uzbekistan Wants Out of the Iran-US Social Media War
articles.full_text:
Tashkent summoned the Iranian ambassador to lodge a protest regarding social media posts by Iranian diplomatic missions.
U.S. Secretary Marco Rubio, with Jeanette Rubio, receives a tour of Registan Square in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, Oct. 19, 2026. At left is Uzbekistan Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Odilovich Saidov and at right is Head of the Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva.
On October 23, Uzbekistan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Iranian ambassador in Tashkent in order to hand over a note of protest related to a recent slate of social media postings made by several Iranian diplomatic missions. The posts sniped at U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, using his recent visit to Samarkand as a touchstone.
“It’s great that you’re learning history! The place where you are standing is part of the Persian civilization and architecture. The same civilization you were babbling nonsense about last week at the Acropolis!” read a since-removed post on X from the Iranian embassy in Armenia. 
In early October, Rubio delivered remarks during a visit to Greece that set off a history-based social media war that has now spilled over to Uzbekistan. With the ancient Acropolis as his backdrop, he mused on the meaning of Western civilization. Early in the speech he recounted the destruction of the Acropolis in 480 BCE by a Persian army. 
“The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood. And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon,” Rubio said before jumping ahead a 25 centuries to the modern era and the American obsession with antiquity. 
Later in the speech, Rubio got the point: a rhetorical attack to match the physical war ongoing between the U.S. and Iran.
“It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country… This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.”
When Rubio landed in Uzbekistan two weeks later, Iran’s keyboard warriors were ready. 
“At the Acropolis, you invoked civilizations. Samarkand invites you to a deeper conversation with history, in a city whose heritage is deeply interwoven with Iranian civilization,” the Iranian Permanent Mission to the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) stated in its post, which remains available as of publication. 
On October 24, the Uzbek Foreign Ministry reported that it had summoned the Iranian ambassador,  Mohammad Ali Eskandari, to complain about the posts, which it said in its own social media post, “interpret the historical and cultural heritage of the city of Samarkand for unilateral political purposes.”
“During the meeting,” the ministry said, “it was noted that the heritage of Samarkand, Bukhara, Khiva, and other historical cities of Uzbekistan is an integral part of the rich and multifaceted historical and cultural development formed over many centuries.”  The ministry demanded that the offending posts be taken down, and those posted the Iranian embassies in Armenia, China, and Zimbabwe have been.
“Uzbekistan values ​​relations with Iran based on mutual respect and trust,” the Foreign Ministry stated. “At the same time, it maintains its principled position against one-sided interpretation of the historical and cultural heritage of our country.”
Of note: While a post regarding Tashkent’s summoning of the Iranian ambassador remains available on Instagram as of publication, there’s no trace of an earlier post on the Foreign Ministry’s website regarding the meeting – although a relic remains on Facebook.
Without recounting the entire history of Samarkand, it’s fair to say that the city’s history and culture is multilayered, with many empires having risen and fallen across (and from within) its territory. It has existed, in some form, since the 8th century BCE. In 329 BCE, Marakanda – as it was then known – was captured by Alexander the Great. It had been one of the most important cities for the Sogdian civilization; by the time of Alexander, Sogdiana was part of the greater Achaemenid Persian Empire. 
The importance of Persian civilization to Central Asia is indisputable. What Tashkent took umbrage over, however, is the operationalization of the past into a weapon (albeit an online one) in a very modern, and very difficult, conflict.
To put it bluntly: Uzbekistan does not want to be invoked in the Iran-U.S. conflict, certainly not while it has tried to deepen relations with Washington while also maintaining ties with Iran.

articles.title: Beyond the Pukpuk Treaty, Australia’s Strategic Footprint in PNG Grows
articles.full_text:
In the wake of the Pukpuk Treaty, Australia and PNG continued to deepen relations with a new rotation planned, defense infrastructure investment, and expanded ADF recruitment.
Last week Australia’s foreign and defense ministers, Penny Wong and Richard Marles, travelled to Port Moresby in Papua New Guinea (PNG) to lead Australia’s delegation to the 32nd Australia-Papua New Guinea Ministerial Forum. The meeting was the first since the Pukpuk Treaty, which established PNG’s first formal defense alliance with another country, entered into force in July. The forum focused on turning the treaty’s commitments into practical initiatives for defense cooperation, infrastructure, recruitment, and new technologies.
The headline agreement was a new rotation of Australian defense personnel to PNG. A new combat group of 130 Australian Defense Force (ADF) personnel will be based in PNG on three month rotations. The deployment, known as the Magani Rotation, is intended to deepen military cooperation and increase familiarity between the two forces.
A rotation offers greater advantages over occasional military exercises. It allows personnel to develop more consistent working relationships, become familiar with how each defense force works, and be able to coordinate activities over longer periods. For PNG, it provides greater access to Australian military expertise, while for Australia, it strengthens its ability to operate alongside a neighbor whose geography makes it important to the defense of Australia’s northern approaches.
Alongside this, the two governments also announced a $77 million infrastructure investment fund for the PNG Defense Force. This funding is intended to upgrade PNG’s military facilities to be better able to house, train, and sustain additional personnel.
While the Magani Rotation may be a significant step in advancing the integration of the two defense forces, the more radical idea is the opening up of Australian military recruitment to eligible Papua New Guineans. Applications for the first intake will open on November 16, with an initial pilot program starting in 2027. The first two cohorts will comprise roughly 50 recruits each, with candidates initially sought from the University of Papua New Guinea, Pacific Adventist University, and the University of Technology in Lae. The program is intended to expand over time, although the initial recruitment numbers are modest.
In order to address recruitment shortages, Australia has already expanded ADF recruitment to Australian permanent residents from New Zealand, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada who are on the pathway to citizenship. However, the new PNG recruitment is different – it has been established under the Pukpuk Treaty and will allow eligible PNG citizens living in PNG to apply directly.
The initial rationale is similar – to overcome persistent personnel shortages – but it comes with a broader strategic goal. These recruits will train and serve alongside Australians, creating personal, cultural and institutional links as part of a longer-term alliance-building objective. Australia citizenship will be an eventual requirement, but this will come via the conventional permanent residency and citizenship application processes.
At the ministerial forum, Australia and PNG also formalized a partnership covering digital governance, network security, and emerging technologies. The agreement builds on a Telecommunications Blueprint designed to improve PNG’s connectivity and digital infrastructure. For Australia, the partnership has strategic as well as economic significance: secure telecommunications networks are essential to military coordination, government resilience, and the protection of critical infrastructure. It also gives Canberra a greater role in shaping the systems connecting PNG to the outside world, while helping the country strengthen its own digital capabilities.
Australia’s alliance with PNG builds on an existing security program. Since 2023, Canberra has committed AU$200 million under the bilateral security agreement to support PNG’s police and justice institutions, including upgraded training facilities, police helicopters, and a National Forensic Science Center. A second phase of support is planned after the current program ends in 2027. Though separate from the Pukpuk Treaty, this work strengthens PNG’s capacity to maintain internal security and exercise authority across its territory.
The challenge for both Australia and PNG is to turn these commitments into lasting capabilities. Australia is investing serious capital in PNG – including across issues like health and other social infrastructure – and hopes to gain a return for its investment. This return for Australia is PNG’s ability to develop its defense, economic, and social capabilities, and to be better equipped to contribute to its own security and regional stability. This also comes with the caveat that it keeps PNG within Australia’s orbit of influence. For Port Moresby, the objective will be whether its alliance with Australia actually increases PNG sovereign capabilities and improves its development objectives, rather than simply accommodating Australia’s strategic priorities.

articles.title: A US Pivot Toward Commercial Espionage?
articles.full_text:
However justified or inevitable it might be, this represents a major shift in how the U.S. has thought about intellectual property for the last three decades.
Washington has spent three decades lecturing the world about intellectual property protection. Now it looks as if the United States wants to start stealing economic secrets from China and elsewhere. 
According to the Washington Post, the Pentagon is standing up an intelligence unit geared toward the acquisition of economic secrets from foreign companies to benefit American companies. Although details remain hazy, the unit is expected to use operatives disguised as private business persons in order to infiltrate foreign companies and appropriate their commercial secrets. This shift was presaged in a Foreign Affairs article by David Cohen, former deputy director of the CIA. 
This represents a significant, if not necessarily unwarranted, change in U.S. commercial espionage policy. In its recent history the United States has refrained from direct theft of economic secrets. During the Obama administration the United States attempted to establish norms of commercial espionage that rejected thefts of intellectual property that would award private firms with stolen secrets. The theft of information in order to improve the strategic position of the U.S. was fine; handing stolen goods to an American firm was across the line. This was in accord with a broader U.S. diplomatic effort to improve intellectual property protection across the world.
That the Trump administration would reject such norm-building efforts is unsurprising. The administration has made it clear that it does not believe that anything approaching a “fair” system of global trade exists; the United States has leverage over its trading partners and should use that leverage in order to generate favorable trade arrangements. It is also clear that while Chinese trade policy and practice has become more complex, especially with respect to intellectual property protection, Beijing never accepted anti-espionage norms. China would of course be a primary target for such espionage, especially in fields such as artificial intelligence.
But the effort also suggests that the Pentagon has no confidence that U.S. firms will remain ahead of Chinese and other foreign firms on the innovation curve. The Obama administration’s policy reflected the convenient reality that U.S. companies were, by and large, well ahead of most of their international competitors. Playing “fair” thus benefitted the United States more than it benefitted anyone else. The Pentagon now believes (probably correctly) that America’s technological advantage is not as secure as it would like. 
While aggressive industrial espionage is obviously in contrast with some of the norms of the liberal international order, it is not exactly unprecedented for liberal democratic states to play hardball on technology theft. France, for example, has long conducted espionage to benefit French firms, to the endless frustration of French partners. South Korea and Japan have long made light technology appropriation a key part of their industrial strategies. And at its inception, even the United States undertook aggressive steps to steal foreign intellectual property, a practice that paused only when the US achieved a dominant technological position. 
In any eventuality, this change in U.S. espionage policy, however justified or inevitable it might be, represents a major shift in how the United States has thought about intellectual property for the last three decades. Moreover, given the technological challenge that China represents to the United States, it seems unlikely that a future administration will reverse this effort.

articles.title: Face-Offs at India-China Border Are Continuing at Multiple Points, ITBP Chief Confirms
articles.full_text:
Since June, civil society groups and local media warned of PLA encroachments into Arunachal Pradesh. Hitherto, Delhi’s response was to deny and dismiss their claims.
Taksing, a border village in the Upper Subansiri district in Arunachal Pradesh.
Claims by civil society groups and media in India’s northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh that Chinese troops have been crossing into Indian territory, which the Narendra Modi government has repeatedly denied, were confirmed by a top Indian official last week.
At an event in Alwar, Rajasthan, on October 22, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur said that face-offs are happening between Indian and Chinese forces “at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues.”
Kapur’s remarks on Thursday about the face-offs are hardly a revelation. Civil society groups and media in the northeast Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China, have been drawing attention to the fragile, even alarming situation along the frontier since June-July.
In a letter dated June 26, 2026, to the deputy commissioner of Upper Subansiri, the Nah Welfare Society (NWS) said that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) had occupied Indian territory in and around Taksing, including Oying in the Asaphila area, Paniar in the Chujarta area, Marpan in Marnafe, Portrang Lake, and Tingdingtang. In addition to establishing a military camp in the area, the PLA has also built roads, bridges, and military camps in several locations traditionally used by local communities for grazing, hunting, and collecting forest produce. A Taksing-based tribal organization, the NWS expressed “deep grief” over the PLA’s gradual occupation of ancestral lands, which it said, has intensified since 2020.
Soon after the contents of the NWS’ memorandum became public, the Indian Army categorically dismissed the “reports” as “incorrect and without any basis.” Then came videos claiming the PLA had advanced 50-60 km into Indian territory. The Indian government’s Press Information Bureau Fact Check unit dismissed the reports as ” fake;” the videos did not pertain to the India-China border, it said. This was followed by reports and videos of “skirmishes” in the Taksing Circle on July 25-26. The “confrontation” reportedly “continued for nearly a week before the situation was brought under control following intervention by senior commanders from both sides.” However, Arunachal Pradesh’s Home Minister Mama Natung dismissed the reports of Chinese encroachment as “just rumors.”
Now, for the first time, there is official confirmation of confrontations at multiple locations along the India-China border in Arunachal Pradesh. And this confirmation has come from the head of the ITBP, the force that guards the India-China border.
The entire India-China border is disputed. The two countries not only have differing perceptions of where the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border, runs, but they also claim swathes of territory under the other’s control. China claims 90,000 sq km of territory that roughly coincides with Arunachal Pradesh. India claims 38,000 sq km of territory in Aksai Chin that China occupied during the 1962 border war, and another 5,300 sq km in the Shaksgam Valley of Jammu and Kashmir that Pakistan occupied in 1947-48 and gifted to China in 1963.
Besides the war in 1962, which China won, the two sides have engaged in skirmishes and standoffs several times over the decades, including at Samdurong Chu in Arunachal in 1986-87, at the Doklam trijunction of China, India and Bhutan in 2017, and at Galwan in Ladakh in June 2020, which resulted in the death of 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers.
Interestingly, China’s interest in Arunachal Pradesh has waxed and waned over time. After occupying Arunachal, then known as the North East Frontier Agency, for several weeks during the 1962 war, the PLA pulled out. Indeed, it did not seem interested in pressing any claims here, and under a swap proposal, was willing to give up claims in the eastern sector, in return for India accepting its control over Aksai Chin in the western sector.
It was only from the mid-1980s that China began reasserting claims over what it calls “Zangnan” or “South Tibet,” at bilateral talks, through military intrusions, by pushing back Indian patrol teams, objecting to visits of Indian leaders to Arunachal Pradesh, refusing to issue visas to Indian passport holders from the state on the argument that they are not Indian, and announcing “standardized” or Chinese names for places and geographical features in the state. According to a 2025 Pentagon report, Arunachal Pradesh is among China’s “core interests.”
In recent months, India and China have engaged in a slew of talks. On August 6, the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs was held in New Delhi. Then on August 26, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval met with China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the Boundary Question in Beijing. On September 6, the Indian Army and the PLA held their first Corps Commander-level meeting in the Eastern Sector at the Vacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting Point in Arunachal Pradesh.
India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping shook hands and chatted at the SCO Summit at Bishkek on August 31, and held a meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in Delhi on September 12.
If the India-China face-offs are continuing, as the ITBP Director General Kapur said they are, it is clear the talks have had little impact in deterring the PLA.
One obvious reason is that Prime Minister Modi’s China strategy is guided more by his interest in beefing up his image among his supporters than taking a strong position against China. His government has repeatedly denied PLA encroachment into Indian controlled territory. “Neither is anyone inside our territory nor is any of our post captured,” Modi grandly declared at an all-party meeting days after the Galwan clashes. The recent spate of denials by the government over PLA’s encroachments in Arunachal is part of the same short-sighted vision. It has weakened India’s hand at talks.
Even more baffling is the Modi government’s withdrawal of ITBP companies from the border. Since June-July, massive anti-government protests in the capital have rattled the Modi government. In response, it has pulled out ITBP personnel from the India-China border and redeployed them in Delhi at a time when the border situation is volatile. Clearly, using the ITBP to crush unarmed civilian protestors in Delhi is more important to Modi than using the force to push back PLA advances at the Arunachal border.
Under the BJP government, almost every Indian state/union territory bordering China is roiled in unrest. Arunachal’s civil society has strongly opposed a mega dam being constructed in the state’s Upper Siang district. The state’s inept handling of public concerns raised over displacement, environmental impact, and loss of livelihoods, and its use of force to deal with protests have resulted in the escalation of the conflict. On October 23, Upper Siang witnessed unprecedented scenes of violence.
Already, Arunachalis are upset with the government for not acting on their apprehensions over PLA encroachment into their traditional lands and hunting grounds. Delhi’s use of the iron fist now to put down their protests will fuel further anger. This will only add to India’s troubles in a sensitive border region.
Claims by civil society groups and media in India’s northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh that Chinese troops have been crossing into Indian territory, which the Narendra Modi government has repeatedly denied, were confirmed by a top Indian official last week.
At an event in Alwar, Rajasthan, on October 22, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur said that face-offs are happening between Indian and Chinese forces “at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues.”
Kapur’s remarks on Thursday about the face-offs are hardly a revelation. Civil society groups and media in the northeast Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China, have been drawing attention to the fragile, even alarming situation along the frontier since June-July.

articles.title: The Debate Over the Maldives’ Deal with Eagle Hills
articles.full_text:
Handing over prime land in a land-scarce country, on an island pitched as a lasting solution to an acute housing crisis, warrants deeper scrutiny.
Emirati businessman Mohamed Alabbar addresses attendees at a luncheon meeting in the Maldives, on Oct. 8, 2026, to share his plans for the Maldives Waterfront and Marina Project.
A proposed deal between the Maldivian government and Abu Dhabi-based developer Eagle Hills to build a waterfront and marina has dominated Maldives’ news cycle in recent weeks.
Founded in 2014 by Emirati businessman Mohamed Alabbar, who also founded Emaar Properties, the developer behind Dubai’s Burj Khalifa, the Eagle Hills project is planned for Ras Malé, an artificial island being reclaimed from the Fushi Dhiggaru lagoon, south of the capital, Malé. The project is being championed by President Mohamed Muizzu as one of his flagship initiatives.
Originally conceived as the Indian Ocean’s first “eco-city,” Ras Malé was meant to ease the housing crisis in the Maldives, a country where dry land makes up less than 1 percent of its territory.
Although the agreement signed in Abu Dhabi on September 21 is a letter of intent rather than a final contract, the project, if realized, would alter that original vision substantially. Under the reported terms, Eagle Hills would receive 500 of the 1,009 hectares earmarked for reclamation, on a 99-year lease, without paying an acquisition fee or rent, to develop resorts, commercial facilities, and residential properties marketed to foreign buyers.
That would leave only the remainder for other development, including housing for the Maldivians originally intended to be its primary beneficiaries.
In partial compensation, Eagle Hills has offered to finance 5,000 housing units in nearby Hulhumalé, though their cost would be recovered from the government’s share of project revenue.
Arguably, there is an economic case for the project. An investment of this scale could bring in much-needed dollars, create jobs, and generate revenue. Infrastructure and Housing Minister Abdulla Muththalib, who signed the agreement, also argues that the project could establish “a structured, world-class real estate sector,” helping diversify an economy heavily dependent on tourism.
Yet the opacity surrounding the deal makes assessing its economic merits challenging. The exact agreement itself has not been made public. Meanwhile, the numbers conflict. The government valued the project at $20 billion, while Eagle Hills reportedly envisaged a $12 billion development. Neither figure is a binding investment commitment. Nor did the developer repeat the government’s projection of more than 54,000 jobs. How these figures were calculated is unclear.
Critics have also questioned why the land is effectively being offered for free.
The government argues that its 10 percent share of the developer’s gross revenue, which it projects at around $3.1 billion over ten years, would earn it more than an upfront fee, and touts the added advantage of requiring no government loans or sovereign guarantees. Yet the project was never put out to competitive tender, and no independent valuation of the land has been made public. Without one, it is difficult to gauge whether the expected returns justify proceeding on the reported terms, especially given the hundreds of millions of dollars already spent on reclaiming Ras Malé.
Beyond price, the deal has also revived concerns over foreign land ownership. Article 251 of the constitution prohibits foreign ownership and limits leases to non-citizens to 99 years. An amendment allowing foreign ownership in return for large financial investments was introduced by President Abdulla Yameen in 2015, but repealed in 2019 by his successor, Ibrahim Solih.
Eagle Hills’ original announcement stated that a fresh 99-year lease would begin each time a property changed hands. Critics argue that this circumvents the constitutional limit, effectively allowing foreigners to retain control of the land indefinitely. The company has since revised the wording, and the government rejects this interpretation, insisting that the land would remain state-owned and that every transfer would require its approval. It also maintains that buying property would not automatically confer residency, even as Eagle Hills’ sales website advertises a renewable residency visa.
Much of the public opposition has played out on social media under the hashtag #EagleHillsOut, centering on the deal’s opacity and the prospect of foreign control of land. Alabbar has also drawn scrutiny over his past projects. In Serbia, his Belgrade Waterfront development, pushed through with little transparency under a special law favoring the developer, sparked mass protests.
Alabbar’s links with Israel have further fueled opposition in the Maldives, where support for Palestine runs deep, and entry on Israeli passports has been banned since April 2025 in response to the war in Gaza. In 2005, as Emaar’s chairman, Alabbar discussed purchasing homes Israeli settlers would vacate during Israel’s planned withdrawal from Gaza, as well as reconstruction with Palestinian leaders. In 2020, after the UAE normalized relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords, he publicly advocated closer Emirati-Israeli ties. Amid concerns that the development could enable Israelis to acquire property in the Maldives despite existing restrictions, Alabbar has insisted that Eagle Hills will comply with Maldivian law, including the passport ban.
Organized political opposition, however, has been divided, particularly within the main opposition Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP). In an official statement, the party demanded full disclosure of the agreement’s terms and a referendum on the project, while opposing any arrangement that would permit foreign ownership of land. Yet its chairperson, former President Mohamed Nasheed, supports the project in principle. After MDP lawmakers denounced Alabbar in parliament as a supporter of Zionism, Nasheed warned that such attacks could jeopardize investment from the UAE.
Nevertheless, nationalist opposition to foreign-backed megaprojects has been a recurring theme in Maldivian politics since the country transitioned to democracy in 2008. This time, the most strident criticism has come from Muizzu’s erstwhile mentor, Yameen, who has remained embittered against him since the 2023 presidential election. When a since-overturned corruption conviction barred Yameen from running, Muizzu, who had until then been campaigning for the former, stepped in at short notice as the opposition candidate and won. Yameen eventually endorsed him but has since publicly regretted it.
Yameen’s strategy appears to be to undermine the nationalist credentials central to Muizzu’s “pro-Maldives” platform, while challenging the government’s claim to champion the Palestinian cause. To this end, he has exploited public sympathy for Palestine to stir up opposition to Eagle Hills in openly antisemitic terms. In a characteristically bizarre post on X, he denounced the developer as a “depraved bunch” exploiting a “morally bankrupt regime” and claimed, without evidence, that the project would establish a Jewish settlement in the Maldives.
For all the public criticism, both genuine and opportunistic, Muizzu faces few legislative barriers to proceeding. No date has been set for a final agreement, but the president says a real estate bill underpinning the project will go to Parliament “very soon,” where his People’s National Congress has held a supermajority since 2024.
Yet the debate over Eagle Hills raises broader questions about how the Maldives balances its need for foreign investment with the public interest.
A small, import-dependent economy can ill afford to shun large investors whenever objections are raised on nationalist grounds, particularly when those objections are cynically motivated. For instance, scrapping Indian firm GMR’s airport contract in 2012 eventually cost the state $271 million. At the same time, handing over prime land in a land-scarce country, on an island pitched as a lasting solution to an acute housing crisis, warrants deeper scrutiny. That scrutiny cannot occur until the government publishes the full agreement.
