articles.title: What Does Durga Puja Tell Us About Minorities in Bangladesh?
articles.full_text:
The largest Hindu religious festival went off smoothly – a credit to the new BNP government.
Bangladeshi Prime Minster Tarique Rahman poses for a selfie with celebrants during a visit to the historic Dharmasabha Puja Mandap in Rangpur, northern Bangladesh, on the occasion of Maha Navami of Durga Puja, Oct. 20, 2026.
Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of Bengali Hindus, ended on October 21, and Hindus celebrated the festival peacefully in the Muslim-majority country without any major incidents. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government passed its first major test of communal harmony since taking office in early 2026. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman also drew attention by visiting puja pandals in several divisional cities outside Dhaka, becoming the first Bangladeshi prime minister to do so. 
Beyond the celebrations, this year’s Durga Puja highlighted a significant shift in Bangladesh’s political landscape. The long-held perception that religious minorities are safer under the Awami League now appears to be on the verge of breaking down.
Durga Puja is celebrated on a large scale in both Bangladesh and the neighboring Indian state of West Bengal. West Bengal has around 70 million Hindus among its population of roughly 100 million, and nearly 58,000 puja pandals were set up across the state this year. Bangladesh, meanwhile, has about 13.1 million Hindus but hosted 33,851 puja pandals, around 1,500 more than last year. This means Bangladesh had more puja pandals relative to its Hindu population than West Bengal.
This was the first Durga Puja celebrated under the BNP government, which came to power in February this year. As a result, the festival carried significance beyond that of a religious celebration. In particular, it represented a test of the new government’s ability, political will, and commitment to ensure the security of religious minorities.
Some untoward incidents have occurred during the festival over the years. This year was no exception in the period leading up to the formal commencement of the festivities, with several incidents reported in different parts of the country. Given the precarious law and order situation, there were concerns that such incidents might escalate. 
Nevertheless, the BNP government successfully met the challenge of ensuring that Durga Puja was celebrated peacefully. 
Representatives of the Hindu community had long demanded three days of public holidays for Durga Puja. During the Awami League’s rule, there was one public holiday on Bijaya Dashami. Following the political transition in 2024, the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus increased the holiday to two days.
This year, the BNP government extended it to three days. With public holidays from October 20 to 22 followed by the weekly holidays on October 23 and 24, people enjoyed a continuous five-day break.
The government also allocated more financial assistance than requested to encourage a festive atmosphere during the celebrations. While the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust sought 40 million Bangladesh taka for Durga Puja, the government allocated 50 million. Similarly, for the Buddhist community’s Kathina Civara Dana, the government allocated 30 million taka against a request for 20 million. The significance lay not in the amount of money but in the message conveyed by the government.
Netizens described this year’s Durga Puja as having been celebrated with unprecedented security arrangements and a festive atmosphere.
On October 20, during Durga Puja, Rahman visited puja pandals in the capital, Dhaka, and three other divisional cities: Rangpur, Rajshahi, and Chittagong. Rahman exchanged greetings with members of the Hindu community and listened to their concerns. 
Earlier, in his Durga Puja greetings message on October 16, Rahman urged Hindus to celebrate the festival with joy and confidence, free from fear. He emphasized religious harmony, mutual respect, and equal rights for all citizens, regardless of their faith. “Religion belongs to individuals, while the state belongs to all,” Rahman said, stressing that ensuring everyone’s security is a responsibility of the state. He also spoke of building a safe and inclusive Bangladesh where people of all religions and communities can live with dignity.
These comments were significant in Bangladesh’s political context. Many have historically viewed a large section of the Hindu community as supporters of the Awami League. In contrast, there have long been attempts to portray the BNP as a relatively conservative political party, which has previously formed alliances with Jamaat-e-Islami, though the BNP, as a party, believes in liberal democracy.
On October 16, while visiting a puja pandal in Dhaka’s Banani area, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told members of the Hindu community, “You do not need to be anyone’s vote bank.” He urged them to make political decisions based on their civil rights, religious freedom, and constitutional entitlements. Ahmed also remarked that various political parties had exploited the Hindu community for political gain in the past.
His statement carries considerable significance in Bangladesh’s political landscape. Although the Awami League has been perceived as a relatively safe political refuge for minorities, numerous instances of attacks and discrimination against minority communities occurred during the party’s long tenure in power. These include the attacks on the Buddhist community in Ramu, Cox’s Bazar, in 2012; the attacks on Hindu homes and temples in Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, in 2016; and the communal violence that spread from Cumilla during Durga Puja in 2021. According to the U.S. State Department’s human rights report, six people were killed in the 2021 violence. These incidents demonstrated that the Awami League was not necessarily effective in protecting religious minorities.
According to the 2022 Population and Housing Census, Hindus accounted for 7.96 percent of Bangladesh’s total population, down from 8.54 percent in the 2011 census. The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) identified migration, alongside a lower fertility rate, as a factor behind the declining proportion of Hindus in the population. 
Following the fall of the Awami League government in August 2024, allegations emerged of attacks on minorities, vandalism of homes and businesses, and assaults on places of worship in different parts of the country. Although the fact-finding team of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) found political rather than communal motives behind most of these incidents, neighboring India has continued to express concern over the situation.
According to the OHCHR’s 2025 fact-finding report, the violence was driven by several factors, including religious and ethnic discrimination, political revenge against people seen as Awami League supporters, land disputes and personal conflicts. The report also found that some local BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami leaders and activists were involved in the attacks. However, it found no evidence that either party had organized the attacks as part of party decision.
The Awami League was banned from taking part in the national election held on February 12 this year. Of the 300 elected parliamentary seats, the BNP won 209, while Jamaat-e-Islami secured 68. The results showed that the BNP gained strong support in many Hindu-majority areas that were traditionally considered Awami League strongholds.
Netra News analyzed results and voter records from more than 40,000 polling stations. Of these, 1,088 were in areas where more than half of the voters were inferred to be Hindu, based on their names in the electoral rolls. The BNP led in 984 of these polling stations, securing 69.1 percent of the valid votes cast, compared with 14.9 percent for Jamaat-e-Islami. These figures suggest that minority voters migrated to the BNP after the Awami League was banned.
In this year’s election, only four candidates from religious and ethnic minority communities – two Hindus and two Buddhists – were elected to parliament, all nominated by the BNP. Four more women from minority communities were later nominated to parliament through reserved seats, also representing the BNP. This brings the total number of minority lawmakers to eight. Their representation remains low compared with the share of religious and ethnic minorities in Bangladesh’s population. It shows that more needs to be done to ensure meaningful political representation for minority communities, beyond symbolic inclusion.
The peaceful conclusion of Durga Puja should not overshadow concerns about incidents reported before the festival. On October 15, the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad and the Mahanagar Sarbajanin Puja Committee reported 34 alleged incidents across the country, including damage to idols, attacks on temples and other violence. The organizations said arrests had been made in 11 of these cases.
Bangladesh Police later said that investigations into some of the incidents found no evidence of plots to disrupt communal harmony. Instead, they pointed to local leadership disputes, theft, and other causes. Even so, transparent and credible investigations into all the allegations remain important, and those responsible must be brought to justice.
According to the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council, 257 incidents of communal violence were reported across Bangladesh between January and June 2026 (a period covering both the interim government and the BNP government). The organization said 44 people were killed in 40 of these incidents. 
The changing political situation of religious minorities in Bangladesh also has implications for relations with India. Minority security has long been a sensitive issue between the two countries.
During Sheikh Hasina’s rule, close ties between Dhaka and New Delhi were shaped not only by security and strategic cooperation but also by the Awami League’s self-claimed secular political image.
However, Bangladesh-India relations became strained after Hasina fled to India and took refuge there in 2024. Even under Bangladesh’s current elected government, disagreements over Hasina, border issues, trade and water sharing remain unresolved.
Still, this year’s Durga Puja celebrations have drawn approval even from some Indian critics who have long raised concerns about minority security in Bangladesh. Among them is Kolkata-based journalist Mayukh Ranjan Ghosh, who praised the scale and grandeur of the celebrations. Such reactions suggest that perceptions of Bangladesh may be beginning to change across the border.
articles.summary: The largest Hindu religious festival went off smoothly – a credit to the new BNP government.

articles.title: Trial by Fire: The 2025 Thai-Cambodian Border Clashes and the Royal Thai Air Force
articles.full_text:
In two outbreaks of war last year, the RTAF underlined its status as one of the region’s most effective and professional air forces.
A Royal Thai Air Force SAAB Jas 39C Gripen fighter jet performs during at air show at Don Mueang Air Force Base in Bangkok, Thailand, July 2, 2012.
The long-simmering border conflict between Thailand and Cambodia erupted into a higher intensity military clash in July and December 2025, which saw the participation of the Royal Thai Air Force (RTAF) in a high-intensity conflict for the first time since World War II. During the conflict, the RTAF proved its status as a highly professional air force – one that belongs to the front ranks of Southeast Asia’s air forces.
This article uses available open-source information to assesses the RTAF’s air operations against the Royal Cambodian Army (RCA) during the July and December border clashes. It also discusses what the fighting revealed about the RTAF’s current capability today.
Multiple clashes between Thai and Cambodian forces since the spring of 2025 led to a major escalation of hostilities on July 24, when Cambodia fired BM-21 rockets across the border, killing at least 11 Thai civilians and one soldier.
In response, the Thai military launched Operation Yuttha Bodin, a coordinated air and land assault, to defend Thai sovereignty, retaliate against Cambodian military actions along the border, and to reduce Cambodian military capability in order to preserve Thai state security and public safety.
On the first day of the operation, on July 24, the RTAF dispatched two missions totaling 10 strike sorties against RCA military command posts and army positions in the Ta Moan Thom temple area in Oddar Meanchey province.
During the five-day operation, the RTAF operated under a joint tactical plan, with Army Commander Gen. Pana Klaewplodthuk acting as the overall joint force commander. The RTAF provided direct support to a ground offensive by the Royal Thai Army (RTA).
The primary geographic focus of Operation Yuttha Bodin was on the disputed border area adjacent to Thailand’s Surin province and Cambodia’s Oddar Meanchey province (see Table 1). The RTAF provided support to the RTA, specifically in areas of active fighting, conducting air strikes to neutralize Cambodian C2 posts, troop strongholds and artillery positions, and weapons and ammunition supply depots.
Besides the Wing 1 F-16s in Korat, a major RTAF air force base located northeast of Bangkok, the 7 Wing, deployed its key assets from their home base in Surin to the base, including JAS39 Gripen fighters and Saab 340 Erieye AEW&C and Saab 340 ELINT aircraft to support the operation.
Together with the base’s 103 Squadron, 1 Wing, and 403 Squadron, 4 Wing F-16s, which had also dispatched aircraft to Korat from its base in Takhli, northwest of Bangkok, and the Gripen detachment, the three units represented the brunt of the RTAF’s offensive force.
The F-5TH and F-16s from the 21 Wing in Ubon Ratchathani, near the Thai-Cambodian border and the 4 Wing at Takhli executed all-important defensive counter air missions to protect critical military and civilian infrastructure.
The 702 Squadron’s Erieye aircraft flew day and night, providing a unified aerial picture, airspace management, and deconfliction between the different offensive and defensive assets in close coordination with the air force’s Air Command and Control System (ACCS) at Wing 6 Don Mueang base in Bangkok.
Critically, while the RTA led the overall joint force, the RTAF (through the ACCS) held control of all air assets and responded to requests from RTA for air support.
Other critical assets included the Sa Kaeo-based 3 Wing – the RTAF’s dedicated uncrewed aerial systems unit – which operated the Aerostar BP and Dominator XP UAS, and 7 Wing’s Saab 340 electronic intelligence platform, which provided critical intelligence, reconnaissance, surveillance, and targeting  (ISTAR) and battle-damage assessment (BDA) support to the joint force during the operation.
In addition, the RTAF and the Thai Army deployed their ground-based air defense systems to provide additional cover for ground forces and forward bases against air-based threats.
During the operation, the RTA employed multiple types of uncrewed systems that ranged from bomb-dropping quadcopters dropping munitions on RCA trenches to larger DP-20 MALE UAS, which provided additional battlefield surveillance and reconnaissance support.
December 2025 – Resumption of Air Campaign
In December, in response to what Thailand described as the RCA’s continued provocations and movement of heavy equipment and combat forces into disputed border areas, the Thai military launched Operation Sattawat, which aimed to “penetrate and destroy the opposing side’s combat support structures and strategic supply routes.”
To support the RTA’s operation on the ground, the RTAF targeted Cambodian C2, drone control facilities, weapons and ammunition depots, logistics, and equipment that could pose a threat to “national security and civilian safety.”
In a major departure from the more geographically constrained operations against RCA forces and supplies adjacent to Surin province during Operation Yuttha Bodin, the December air campaign saw the RTAF expand its target list to encompass the entire length of the shared border (see Table 2).
In addition to the frequent close air support missions along the border, the RTAF carried out some deep strike operations to destroy selected bridges and weapons depots deep inside Cambodia. For example, on December 24, Thai fighters penetrated as deep as 100 kilometers into Cambodian territory in Battambang Province to hit a weapons depot there.
Although not publicly disclosed like the 1 Wing and 4 Wing F-16s and 7 Wing Gripens use in strike missions, visual evidence of bomb mission marking on other units and combat aircraft like the F-5TH “Super Tigris” and T-50TH from the 21 Wing and 4 Wing verify their active participation in strike missions as well.
During the July operation, the RTAF flew two to three combat missions daily, involving two to four combat aircraft per mission. On the first day of heavy fighting, larger formations (up to 10 combat aircraft in total) were involved in strikes in anticipation of a greater level of resistance (see Table 1). The lower-than-expected opposition allowed required sorties to be reduced to an average of four sorties or two two-ship missions per day. In total, RTAF conducted 28 strike sorties during Operation Yuttha Bodin.
Compared to July, it appears that the RTAF operated at a higher operational tempo in December, based on the known targets struck and the geographic spread of combat operations (see Table 2). For example, during the more active phase of ground fighting on December 18-19, the RTAF flew a larger number of sorties against RCA forces along the length of the shared border, including in Siem Reap, Oddar Meanchey, and Banteay Meanchey provinces.
Critically, the publicly released sorties only consider actual strike sorties. Several supporting sorties, including defensive counter air, airspace surveillance and strike coordination, reconnaissance and target acquisition, electromagnetic domain monitoring, and airlift sorties were carried out simultaneously, even if not publicly acknowledged.
The bombing effort was preceded and supplemented by an attempt to locate any ground-based air defense threats and eliminate them. To achieve this, RTAF deployed crewed and uncrewed ISTAR assets, including the 7 Wing’s Saab 340 ELINT was used to establish the Cambodian forces’ electronic order of battle along the key operational axes opposite Ubon Ratchathani, Buri Ram, Surin, Si Sa Ket, Sa Kaeo, and Chanthaburi Provinces.
The RTAF and RTA uncrewed ISTAR aircraft deployed the Aerostar BP and Dominator XP UAS and Defense Technology Institute (DTI) DP-20 MALE UAS to reconnoiter the border area, locate RCA force disposition, and provide post-strike battle damage assessment.
To reconnoiter targets and provide precision-guidance for PGMs, RTAF combat aircraft employed Litening-III targeting pod (Gripen and F-5TH) and the Sniper ATP pod (F-16 and TA-50TH)—to find, fix, identify, engage, and BDA (battle damage assessment) targets.
The RTAF dropped more than 30 tons of munitions on Cambodian positions during Operation Yuttha Bodin. Munitions employed included unguided general-purpose bombs (GPBs) and precision-guided munitions (PGMs), and direct attack and standoff weapons.
articles.summary: In two outbreaks of war last year, the RTAF underlined its status as one of the region’s most effective and professional air forces.

articles.title: Why China Can’t Fix Its Broken Economy
articles.full_text:
China’s economy has a huge problem: Chinese people aren’t spending enough money. And this is not just a problem for China.
China has a huge problem: Chinese people aren’t spending enough money. China today has the lowest consumption rate of any major economy in the world – in fact, its consumption rate is lower than any major economy in the past 100 years. 
Consumption makes up just about 56 percent of China’s GDP. In most economies, it’s 70 percent or more. To put this in perspective, China’s consumption as a share of GDP is about 10 percentage points lower that Japan’s was in the 1990s, at the worst point in its economic stagnation. 
Why does low consumption matter? Because it’s a flashing warning sign that China’s economic model is fundamentally broken. That’s why GDP growth is coming to a screeching halt, dropping from highs of 10 percent or more in the early 2000s to under 5 percent today. It’s also why China’s debt is growing to alarming levels.
And this is not just a problem for China. Low consumption in China means its people aren’t buying all that much – but China can’t scale back production without mass layoffs. So what does China do with all the extra stuff? It exports more and more abroad, at lower and lower prices. 
The technical term for that is “dumping” – and countries from Europe to Asia are starting to complain about it. China’s huge excess production is killing manufacturing industries around the world.
And all of these problems have the same root cause.

articles.title: Indonesia Reduces Gas Supply to Singapore, Citing Domestic Energy Needs
articles.full_text:
Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said last week that Jakarta would prioritize its own needs, and might cut off supplies to nations that did not respect Indonesia.
A natural gas distribution center in Bontang, East Kalimantan, Indonesia.
Indonesia on Saturday began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore in order to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs, the country’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said.
According to reports by Reuters and Channel News Asia, SKK Migas chairman Djoko Siswanto said that the diversion involves 31 million standard cubic feet of gas per day, which would be redirected to meet electricity needs in Batam, Bintan, and Sumatra. This comprises 15 million standard cubic feet of gas per day from Natuna and 16 million from Sumatra, which makes up around 9 percent of Indonesia’s total exports of natural gas to Singapore.
“In order to safeguard the reliability of domestic gas supplies for electricity generation, effective today, gas supplies previously ​destined for Singapore ​are being redirected ⁠for domestic use,” Djoko said, as per Reuters.
The latest cut comes after a series of serious power outages in Indonesia, including a major blackout across at ​least six provinces in Sumatra in May and rolling ‌outages ⁠in Java and Kalimantan in June and July. More recently, the island of Batam in Riau Islands Province was last week hit with a 16-hour power outage.
Singapore is highly dependent on imported gas for electricity generation, generating more than 90 percent of its power from this source. Last year, around 43 percent of the country’s imported gas was shipped by pipeline from Indonesia and Malaysia, with the remaining 57 percent made up of liquefied natural gas shipped by sea.
Despite Singapore’s reliance on Indonesian gas, the reduction is unlikely to have much impact on the country’s electricity supply. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said on Saturday that the reduction would amount to around 17 billion British thermal units per day over a period of 18 days. This, it said, equated to “less ​than 2 percent of our total daily gas demand.”
Tan See Leng, Singapore’s minister for energy, trade, and industry, said yesterday that Singapore has sufficient gas supply to meet its demand, and was seeking continuously to diversify its sources of gas to guard against any potential future shocks.
“In the short term, the prices would not really affect that much,” he said. “I would like to urge all of our fellow Singaporeans: keep calm and carry on. We have dealt seamlessly with such reductions in the past without any incident, and the government will continue to ensure the reliability and the resilience of Singapore’s energy supply.”
The gas supply cut is consistent with Indonesia’s long-standing policy of prioritizing the use of natural resources for its domestic needs. Under Jakarta’s regime of Domestic Market Obligations, producers of key natural resources and commodities are required to reserve a specific portion of their production for the local market at below-market prices, before being allowed to export the remainder. For instance, in January 2022, the Indonesian government banned coal exports for a month after supplies at domestic power plants ran low.
Indonesia has also banned the export of unprocessed nickel, bauxite and raw copper to encourage companies to refine minerals domestically and boost the local economy.

The following day, he said that the government might also cut off supplies to nations that did not respect Indonesia.
“Don’t come asking for help only when you’re in need, but when other issues that can actually be discussed arrive, act like you have no sense of propriety, like someone who doesn’t know how to conduct yourself properly,” Bahlil said, as per the South China Morning Post.
The minister’s remarks were cryptic, and he made no mention of Singapore, but they come at a time of growing friction between the two neighbors due to the toxic haze resulting from months of Indonesian wildfires, and the recent turbulence in the Indonesian stock market.
In recent weeks, Singaporean citizens have grown increasingly frustrated with the haze, a result of raging forest and peatland fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, and the apparent inaction of the Indonesian authorities – a sentiment that has not been helped by the defensive statements of some Indonesian officials.
Singapore’s government, too, has begun to express its discontent with Jakarta over the haze, albeit in much more measured language. On October 15, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the government was looking into Indonesian companies that could be responsible for the fires in Indonesia, and potentially take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.
Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on October 19 that Singapore will “sustain pressure” on these companies even after the haze passes. “If companies refuse to cooperate, regardless of whether they have a presence in Singapore or do not have a presence in Singapore, we will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters,” he said.
There have also been tensions related to the recent threat of global index provider MSCI to downgrade Indonesia to “Standalone Market” status due to a lack of transparency in its stock market. The possible downgrade, which was announced on October 16, led to an immediate plunge in the Indonesian stock market, which shed 15 percent of its value over two days of trading.

The two firms have denied his claims. Prabowo himself responded to the downgrade threat with strident nationalism, claiming that MSCI “intended to intimidate us.”
Prabowo’s two years in office have been marked by increasingly strident nationalism and rhetoric about national self-sufficiency, which have resulted in ever-more overt state involvement in the economy. While this policy may serve to safeguard Indonesia’s domestic energy and food security in the short term, the longer-term impact will be to undermine business confidence and potentially to generate friction with Indonesia’s neighbors. articles.title: The Strategic Logic Behind Pakistan’s Defense Pacts
articles.full_text:
Last week, Pakistan signed the Badr Pact with Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia, the latest in a string of defense-related agreements with key partners.
Screenshot of a Qatari Ministry of Defense video showing representatives from Turkey, Pakistan, Indonesia and Qatar at the signing of the Badr Memorandum of Understanding in Doha, Qatar, Oct. 21, 2026.
On October 21, Pakistan, Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia signed the Badr Pact, a quadrilateral defense cooperation framework. As per the joint statement issued after the signing of the memorandum of understanding in Doha, the pact is aimed at deepening cooperation in defense manufacturing, joint research and development, technical training, and industrial capacity building among the signatory countries.
The pact is expected to pave the way for deeper technological integration and joint production by leveraging the complementary strengths of the defense sectors of the four countries.
This agreement is the latest addition to Pakistan’s expanding security partnerships. Over the past year, Islamabad has concluded multiple defense pacts with numerous countries in West Asia and neighboring regions.
In September 2025, Pakistan signed the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement with Saudi Arabia, under which aggression against one will be treated as aggression against the other. In August 2026, Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia concluded the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, which contains an explicit collective defense commitment. The same month, Pakistan signed a Protocol Agreement with Kuwait, which has expanded military cooperation in training, capacity building and related areas between the two countries.
The Badr agreement has now added a multilateral industrial cooperation framework with Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia.
There are three interconnected reasons for Pakistan’s participation in these agreements, which highlight the strategic trajectory Islamabad is now pursuing in terms of its defense partnerships.
First, these agreements reflect Islamabad’s growing strategic engagement with key Muslim countries amid rapidly shifting regional security alignments in West Asia. It is important to note that Pakistan’s military performance during last year’s clashes with India demonstrated credible conventional capabilities and helped restore a measure of international strategic credibility. At the same time, Pakistan has played an important and visible mediating role between Iran and the United States, and has helped in keeping channels of communication open at a time when many other actors found themselves constrained by their own alignments.
Arguably, these developments have reinforced perceptions of Pakistan as a useful middle power, which is capable of engaging competing power blocs. In a tumultuous region like West Asia, traditional security umbrellas have shown their limits amid the U.S.-Iran war. Against this backdrop, countries are increasingly seeing value in deepening ties with a state like Pakistan that has maintained working relationships across multiple camps and has proven operational military capabilities in recent years.
Second, Pakistan has long pursued the idea of joint defense production and investment in its defense industry to elevate its security partnerships beyond transactional procurement of weapons. This vision has benefited Pakistan in many ways. For instance, cooperation with China has produced notable results, including the JF-17 fighter program and related industrial capacity. Similarly, ties with Türkiye have expanded into naval shipbuilding along with other technology and production initiatives.
A recent analysis published in Dawn newspaper observed that each of the recent defense agreements signed by Pakistan carried an explicit provision for joint defense production and investment in the defense industry. “This clause in every defense pact reveals Islamabad’s long-term strategic objective of moving from a buyer-seller relationship to a co-production partnership with reliable partners in the region,” it noted.
This essentially means that such opportunities can help Pakistan accelerate its defense modernization and help sustain credible conventional deterrence in a difficult neighborhood.
Third, Pakistan has been working to develop a more competitive defense industry, which is capable of supporting meaningful arms exports to a level where it could compete with major international players. In recent months, there has been a noticeable increase in reporting of export discussions and deals involving countries in Africa, West Asia and other regions, including substantial packages linked to platforms such as the JF-17 and related systems.
Moreover, Pakistan has long participated actively in international defense exhibitions, where it has showcased both domestically developed and jointly produced equipment with partners such as China. In this regard, the new agreements offer Pakistan a way to build on the idea of expanding arms exports, attract investment into the sector, and raise the competitiveness of Pakistani offerings. One can argue that over time these defense deals may also support the further development of Pakistan’s local production capacity, creating a direct link between increased industrial strength, export earnings, and operational self-reliance.
Taken together, the Badr agreement and Pakistan’s recent defense pacts reflect Islamabad’s growing role in shaping an emerging security architecture in West Asia. Arguably, through these frameworks, Pakistan is not only going to play a role in enhancing the security of its partners through military training, operational expertise, and joint manufacturing, but it will also likely benefit by securing foreign investment, technology transfer, and building defense industrial self-reliance.
It will be interesting to watch how Pakistan will navigate the opportunities these arrangements will bring, while also managing the constraints that will inevitably accompany a growing list of commitments.

articles.title: Myanmar War Crimes Survivors Look to Denmark for Justice
articles.full_text:
The country’s legal system may provide one of the few remaining means of bringing Myanmar’s generals to justice.
Prins Jørgens Gård at the Christiansborg Palace in Copenhagen, Denmark, which houses a number of government institutions including the Supreme Court.
Forty homes. That is how many a woman, now living in Denmark, watched burn in her village in Chin State, western Myanmar. Family members and friends were killed or left permanently disabled by landmines planted by the junta. Like tens of thousands of others from Chin State, she was driven across the border into India.
On Monday, October 26, she asked the Danish authorities to investigate the men responsible.
She has filed a criminal complaint in Copenhagen against members of the Myanmar junta. For her safety, she cannot be named. The crimes in the complaint include deliberate killing, mass arson and the forced displacement of tens of thousands of people.
This is possible because of a change in Danish law. Legislation that came into force last year specifically criminalizes war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. It gives Danish prosecutors a route that did not exist before.
Her lawyer, Copenhagen-based Eddie Omar Rosenberg Khawaja, puts it plainly. “Under the new Danish legislation, it no longer matters where the crimes took place, or the nationality of the perpetrators or the victims,” he says. “Victims living in Denmark can request that Danish authorities hold commanders under whose watch atrocities against them occurred responsible.”
That matters because there is nowhere else to go. Myanmar’s courts are controlled by the generals. The Security Council has failed to act. International courts in The Hague – the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice – have also been slow. For the people of Chin State, a Danish police station may be one of the few doors that open.
It also fits Denmark’s own history. Tracy Bawi Hlei, Chairperson of Myanmar Action Group Denmark (MAGD), which supports the case, says, “Denmark has a history of aligning itself with the pro-democracy movement in Myanmar since before the 1990s, through development aid, support of activists, bypassing the military government and standing in solidarity with human rights movements.”
She sees this case as the next step. “Now, Myanmar people and Danish activists who are part of communities and movements in Denmark are taking a stand for accountability and the international rule of law,” she says. Survivors and crucial evidence, she explains, were identified within Denmark through a collaboration of civil society groups, including MAGD and the Chin Community Denmark, which also supports the case.
I run the Myanmar Accountability Project, which supports cases against the junta in Southeast Asia and Europe. I believe the basis for a Danish case is strong.
The Danish government has said so itself. In a statement to the U.N. on September 30, 2025, Denmark said, as a matter of public record, that Myanmar suffers from a lack of accountability and continued impunity. This complaint invites Denmark to act on that.
The timing is pointed. The Danish Foreign Ministry is closing its embassy in Myanmar. This case allows the Danish government to send a signal that it remains engaged with issues of justice and accountability, and that the rightful aspirations of the people of Myanmar to a just, peaceful and dignified life must be respected.
Meanwhile, the junta is seeking legitimacy. Min Aung Hlaing, the general who led the coup, is now president after sham elections that offered the people of Myanmar no real choice. Those who lived through his campaigns of burning and killing are expected to accept this as normal. They do not.
The country’s condition leaves no room for complacency. According to the latest U.N. report, more than 16 million people need aid, and the junta is blocking humanitarian access to vast areas where the need is greatest. Nearly 3.8 million people are estimated to be displaced, many of them several times over. A U.N. Development Programme report published last month found that two-thirds of the population are living in poverty or at immediate risk of falling into it.
The violence is taking place on a scale that few outside the region grasp. More than 100,000 people have died in conflict-related violence since the coup. That makes Myanmar the fourth most deadly conflict in the world. Far from being a frozen conflict, this is a war on civilians, and state-wide repression compounds the inhuman levels of killing, which makes justice and accountability even more important.
What the complainant seeks is limited. She is not asking Denmark to end a war. She is asking its police to open an investigation and its prosecutors to take her evidence seriously. She is asking that the commanders responsible be held accountable.
Denmark has said impunity in Myanmar must end. Its new law now gives it a way to act on that. She has come forward, at a risk to herself that most of us will never face. It is now for Danish authorities to decide whether the law means what it says.

articles.title: Indonesia Seizes More Than 2 Tons of Narcotics in Major Anti-drug Operations
articles.full_text:
In recent years Indonesian waters have become an important route for the trafficking of Golden Triangle drugs to Asian and global markets.
Indonesian anti-narcotics officials hold packets seized during a raid on a liquid methamphetamine lab in Aceh province, Oct. 23, 2026.
Indonesian authorities have made two major drug busts in Sumatra that led to the seizure of more than 2 tons of ketamine and methamphetamine, authorities said on Friday.
National Police Chief Gen. Suyudi Ario Seto told a press conference that police and customs officers intercepted a ship carrying 1.1 tons of ketamine in the waters off Sumatra on October 20, the AFP news agency reported.
The tanker MT Global 168 was intercepted after intelligence officers detected irregularities in its route through the Malacca Strait and the Andaman Sea. It was then taken to Belawan Port in North Sumatra for inspection.
“From this search operation, the joint team managed to seize illicit drugs in the form of ketamine HCL (hydrochloride). The evidence was found in 58 sacks with a total weight reaching 1.16 tonnes,” Suyudi said, adding that the shipment had an estimated value of 3.48 trillion rupiah ($210 million).
The police chief added that the MT Global 168 flew the Mongolian flag but is owned by a company based in Johor Bahru, Malaysia.
The following day, Suyudi added, in what the National Narcotics Board (BNN) described as a joint operation with the National Narcotics Control Commission of China, Indonesian authorities raided a clandestine drug laboratory in Aceh province’s Pidie regency. There, they seized around 1.2 tons of liquid and crystal methamphetamine, assorted equipment for converting liquid into crystal meth, and arrested 11 suspects, including two Chinese nationals. Authorities put the value of the drugs at around 2.16 trillion rupiah ($119 million).
“The back-to-back operations underscore how Indonesia remains a major target for international drug trafficking organizations,” Suyudi said, as per the Associated Press.
The AP added that Indonesian authorities are investigating possible connections between the meth lab and drug syndicates in China, Malaysia, and Indonesia, as well as criminal groups in the Golden Triangle – the tri-border region between Myanmar, Thailand, and Laos – a region long associated with large-scale narcotics production and trafficking.
The two drug operations, which come after the seizure in August of 1.3 tons of ketamine from a ship near the Riau Islands, reflect the booming state of the illicit drug trade in Southeast Asia.
In its most recent annual report on the Asian synthetic drug market, released in June, the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) reported that methamphetamine seizures spiked to a record 349 tons in East and Southeast Asia in 2025, a 48 percent increase over last year’s record of 236 tons. Last year was also notable for a surge in ketamine seizures, which rose to 52.5 tons, a whopping 185 percent increase on 2024’s total.
The majority of last year’s methamphetamine seizures – around 94 percent – occurred in Southeast Asia. As The Diplomat explored in a video last week, most of these narcotics are produced in areas of Myanmar controlled by rebel groups and militias of various stripes. While drug production in Myanmar is nothing new, production and trafficking have spiked since the military coup of 2021.
The resulting conflict, chaos, and economic dysfunction have created lucrative opportunities for criminal syndicates. The civil war has weakened the state’s hold on outlying regions of the country, where most drug production has historically been concentrated, while disrupting law enforcement efforts and heightening the nation’s reliance on drug-related proceeds.
As a result, flows of narcotics from Myanmar have increased in all directions. In its June report, the UNODC noted the increasing trafficking of drugs via maritime routes, for the purposes of “both domestic distribution and transit trafficking to third countries.”
In addition to Indonesia, last year saw record seizures in Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, and the Philippines, including numerous multi-ton seizures.

articles.title: South Korea’s Ruling Democratic Party Is Tumbling in the Polls
articles.full_text:
Its in-house gaffes and disputes are largely to blame for the DP’s plummeting approval ratings.
On October 19, Gyeonggi, South Korea’s most populous province, held a post-funeral ceremony ahead of a firefighter’s internment. More than 2,700 people filled the indoor stadium. Choo Mi-ae, the provincial governor, stood on the green sports surfacing, tears streaming down her face. File after file of uniformed firefighters weaved around her amid dirgeful tributes.
Of course, the firefighter’s burial signified the loss and sacrifice of a serviceman who braved a conflagration to save lives. Yet, it also rang the death knell for the ruling Democratic Party’s approval ratings. 
The same day, Realmeter, an authoritative pollster, released a poll. The DP’s approval rating, at 36.2 percent, was lower than the opposition People Power Party’s 40.9 percent. It was the first time since the June local elections that the PPP had outpolled the DP. 
The alienation of DP supporters happened fast. Less than five months ago, the June local elections handed the DP a resounding victory. Since then, the DP has registered a double-digit plunge in approval ratings.
The party’s fall was particularly steep in Seoul, with the DP polling at 26.7 percent as opposed to the PPP’s 45.7 percent. One-fifth of South Koreans live in Seoul; track records in the capital thus tend to reflect where the swing voters stand. Oh Se-hoon, its current mayor, may lose the post should the Supreme Court uphold the special counsel’s charge that Oh allegedly paid a pollster to rig polls in his favor. (On October 23, the appellate court overturned his guilty verdict. The Supreme Court will rule on the case early next year.) The DP hopes to retake Seoul in a potential by-election, but with these poll numbers success is far from assured. 
The DP’s popularity may still crater further. Given the touchy nature of the reform agenda still ahead for the Lee Jae-myung administration, the rest of this year and next year may not really be a rosy picture for the party. And then it will already be time for the 2028 general elections.
The party’s poor polling performance is of its own making, though. Choo, the governor of Gyeonggi-do, dealt the most immediate damage in a controversy that preceded the firefighter’s funeral.
On October 13, during a parliamentary audit, Choo said that “firefighting is like a financial straw, causing the biggest headache.” She then elaborated on how much firefighters are setting back the province’s coffers. Firefighters’ unions went up in arms, wondering how the sacrifice of constantly putting their lives in jeopardy could be reduced to a budgetary complaint. 
Choo ignored their calls for an apology. The province explained that her remark was in reference to the ballooning budgetary burden on the local government due to decreasing financial contributions from the central government – even though the firefighters are directly employed by the central government. Despite her true intention, Choo’s phrasing was no doubt inappropriate and hurtful. She was already facing steep criticism. Then October 16 changed everything. 
A fire erupted in a metal printing factory in a town in Gyeonggi. Flames engulfed firefighter Kim Jin-seok, who passed away in the line of duty. The nation became even more infuriated with Choo’s callous analogy earlier. 
The next day, Choo attended Kim’s funeral, where she finally apologized: “Since you want an apology, I wholeheartedly apologize.” You have to want to apologize for an apology to feel sincere. But she made it clear she was forced. Her apology duly backfired, to the point where she might have been better off not apologizing at all. 
Making matters worse, when Kim Min-seok, the DP’s leader, arrived at the funeral his car parked in a spot reserved for emergency patients. It was a collective PR disaster for the party.
Choo has also been stirring the pot within the DP. She openly clashed with President Lee Jae-myung on the latter’s choice for head of the Serious Crime Investigation Agency (SCIA). It’s a new institution born out of abolishing the prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor’s office used to wield unchecked political powers through its dual authority to investigate and indict. Lee’s criminal justice reform and the DP’s legislation kiboshed this practice by distributing investigatory powers to the police and the SCIA, and indictment authority to the Prosecution Service, also a new body. 
In September, when Lee picked Kim Ji-yong, a former prosecutor, to lead the SCIA, Choo maligned Lee by wondering out loud, “Why is he shivering before the insurrection forces?” Kim Yong-min, a popular hard-line DP legislator, joined forces with Choo. They believe Kim Ji-yong huddled around former President Yoon Suk-yeol when Yoon was chief prosecutor and that appointing Kim means giving in to the prosecutors and insurrection forces that aided and protected Yoon for his authoritarian practices and failed self-coup. For his part, Lee maintains that Kim was anti-Yoon. 
Their public disagreement continued into this month. “Why appoint someone who can turn their back to the people and justice as the captain of our reform ship?” Choo wrote on October 2. On the same day, Kim Yong-min held a press conference publicly denouncing Kim Ji-yong for having always opposed prosecutorial reform. Meanwhile, Lee made repeated social media posts and a parliamentary submission arguing that the nominee had appropriate qualities needed to establish a trustworthy criminal justice system.
Voices in and out of the DP expressed concerns that such open defiance seemed to challenge Lee’s authority over personnel. The spat peaked in rhetoric on October 9, when Lee made a social media post maligning “those incompetents … who stage internal attacks purportedly for radical reform as a noble cause” when in fact they were complaining because “personnel and national policy didn’t go the way they wanted.”
Separately, the president’s online spat with Cho Kuk, a former justice minister who founded the Rebuilding Korea Party (RKP), further fractured the support for the DP. With 12 legislators in the National Assembly, Cho’s RKP is the third largest party after the DP and the PPP. Cho is also frequently mentioned as a strong contender for the next presidency. The RKP collaborated with the DP to boost liberal voters’ turnout during the 2024 April general elections. 
The DP-RKP alliance became uncomfortable in June, however. When Cho ran for a parliamentary by-election, the DP fielded a candidate of its own – a choice many questioned. Liberal votes naturally split, and the PPP easily nabbed the seat. 
Ever since, talk of merging the two parties has become fraught with grudges. Cho and Lee have also exchanged criticisms over each other’s stance on the extent of prosecutorial reform. Lee must have targeted Cho as well when he wrote on October 5 that his detractors “shouldn’t try to influence personnel choices and specific affairs of investigation and indictment in the name of prosecutorial reform and for selfish reasons.” (Cho and his wife served prison time after the prosecutors dug every dirt on them to stem former President Moon Jae-in’s and Cho’s effort to curtail the prosecutor’s office’s undue investigative and political powers.) Cho retorted that “the sense of crisis over the dissolution of our alliance has reached the boiling point.”
The past couple of months has seen Lee devoting a large portion of his time and energy to putting in place vociferous elements within the liberal camp. There are two reasons the president rolled up his sleeves to personally engage with critics. 
First, Lee must be feeling isolated and betrayed. In September, he shared someone else’s post: “What hurts more are words from within than foes from without … In this chess game, we need to protect the queen that is Lee Jae-myung.” Second, Kim Min-seok, the DP leader who had Lee’s support in the August chair election, has failed to set the party’s house in order. He is kind and voluble but ineffective in quelling the internal unrest. His frequent warnings against those critical of Lee have fallen flat. 
While the DP’s big shots are preoccupied with aggrandizing their own presence, the RPK’s support rating reached 9 percent, its highest since the onset of the Lee administration, according to the October 22 figures released by Media Tomato, another major pollster. On the one hand, it indicates the degree to which the DP let down even its core supporters. On the other hand, at least the overall support for the liberal bloc is still more robust than for the PPP. The most pressing thing would be learning how to coalesce at critical moments.

articles.title: Xi Jinping May Have His Own Reasons to Avert a China-Russia-US Summit
articles.full_text:
A formal trilateral could raise strategic questions that are awkward for the EU, Ukraine – and China itself.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin have put Xi Jinping in an unusual position by expressing interest in a trilateral summit with the Chinese leader at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen mid-November. Xi’s cautious response so far – Moscow and Washington have confirmed discussion, while Beijing has yet to commit publicly – could help Europe and Ukraine avoid the worst: major powers making decisions about the region in their absence.
The idea for a meeting came from Russia and it’s not hard to see why. Moscow’s ideal outcome would reportedly be a “Yalta-style” agreement on Ukraine, echoing the 1945 conference at which the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union discussed the post-war order in Europe. But even much more modest results would count as a success. Simply taking part in such a summit would elevate Russia’s status alongside the U.S. and China, help break its diplomatic isolation, potentially drive a further wedge between the U.S. and Europe, and provide an important platform for its narrative of Western threats to Russia.  
A three-way meeting would play to Trump’s self-regard as a dealmaker and peacemaker – and quite possibly his appetite for economic gain. The United States recently eased sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports, with an initial shipment of 40,000 tonnes reportedly on its way to the U.S. Moscow has also offered to increase fertilizer exports amid shortages caused by the Middle East crisis. But Trump may also have a larger strategic motivation. He has said that nuclear disarmament, not Ukraine, should be at the top of the agenda.
With the APEC summit in China being discussed as the venue, Xi would surely welcome the huge symbolic win of being seen as the world leader capable of hosting such an important gathering – while possibly helping to widen the divide between the U.S. and Europe. But Xi also has very good reasons to avoid such a meeting. China has benefited from dealing with Washington and Moscow separately, and it has in the past insisted that both Russia and Ukraine must be involved in any peace process. A China-Russia-U.S. summit to discuss Ukraine’s future without Kyiv would undermine both those positions.
A high-profile trilateral could overshadow the APEC summit, which Beijing wants to use to showcase its economic leadership and promote openness, innovation, and cooperation. A highly publicized gathering of three major powers also would sit uneasily with Beijing’s repeated calls for inclusive multilateralism, particularly at a forum intended to promote regional economic cooperation. 
A successful trilateral might make the risk worthwhile. But such an outcome is uncertain – not least because of the unpredictability of Trump and Putin. The meeting could end up dominating APEC at the expense of Beijing’s economic agenda, without producing any significant outcomes. 
Lastly, while Putin and Trump have major strategic incentives to meet, Xi has a strategic reason to avoid doing so. Trump’s insistence on putting nuclear arms reduction at the top of the agenda is problematic for China. Beijing has long emphasized that its nuclear arsenal is far smaller than those of the United States and Russia – and that Washington and Moscow must make substantial reductions before China joins any talks. Abandoning this position would risk China being bound by the same rules as Russia and the U.S., despite the gap in nuclear capabilities. 
But Xi may recognize that he cannot dismiss the idea of a meeting altogether. Chinese diplomats have reportedly indicated that they would not rule out a trilateral. If Xi cannot prevent such a meeting, he could at least use his position as host to shape it – a less prominent, more informal encounter with a loose agenda focused on major power relations or the global economy, rather than a formal summit focused on Ukraine or nuclear arms control that would raise public expectations. Xi could even cast himself as the host of a Trump-Putin meeting rather than a participant in three-way talks. 
Such stage-management would not protect Europe and Ukraine from the United States, Russia, and China talking about them behind their backs. But it would allow European governments to frame such a meeting as nothing more than an exchange of views. A formal summit explicitly devoted to Ukraine, by contrast, would risk signaling to the world that the three leaders are entitled – by right or by force – to make strategic decisions about Europe in Europe’s absence. That alone would send a terrible precedent for the continent. 
Much can still happen until the APEC summit next month. Another round of U.S.-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi are reportedly under discussion, while Trump’s views on Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy continue to shift. But whatever summitry emerges in Shenzhen, European governments must continue to insist on Ukrainian participation in any talks about the country’s future. Apart from pressing Washington to take them into account, Kyiv and European capitals should also appeal to Xi’s own reservations about a trilateral summit that also carries many risks for Beijing.
